#10221. AWS Weekly Roundup: AWS Lambda Web Functions, Amazon S3 on the Vercel Marketplace, and more (October 19, 2026)

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Nothing last week added a new kind of compute. What it did instead was shorten the distance between the code you already have and that code being live. AWS Lambda learned to run a plain HTTP server with no adapter in front of it, and Amazon S3 became something you can provision from inside the tool you were already using, without opening the AWS Management Console. Different services, same direction.

The counterweight arrived on Thursday. As it gets easier to put things into production, it matters more that you can say what those things are allowed to do, and this week’s most interesting read is about exactly that. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news…

HeadlinesAWS Lambda Web Functions is a new form factor that runs a standard HTTP web application on Lambda without rewriting it into an event handler. You take a port-listening server built with Express, Hono, Fastify, or Next.js, run aws lambda-web deploy, and get back a live HTTPS URL in under a minute. No adapters, no infrastructure to set up first, no framework lock-in. Lambda now has three form factors on the same Firecracker isolation, which compose inside one application: Event Functions (the model you already know) for async work, Web Functions for the user-facing layer, and MicroVMs for stateful sandboxes running untrusted code.

Two details make this more than repackaging. Each execution environment handles up to 128 concurrent requests, so a burst of traffic shares warm environments instead of mapping one request to one environment, and billing meters the CPU time your code actually uses rather than wall-clock time. For server-side rendering, API backends, and inference endpoints streaming tokens, where most of the elapsed time is spent waiting, that changes the arithmetic. Adding --regions to the same deploy command replicates your code and configures latency-based routing behind a single global URL, and you can split traffic across revisions by weight for a canary rollout. It’s available in five Regions, running Node.js 24 on Arm64 with VPC connectivity. The AWS Compute Blog has a longer walkthrough, and Amazon CloudFront can now use a Web Function endpoint as an origin with origin access control.

The week’s other headline isn’t a launch. Trust in Depth: giving agents more autonomy without losing control makes an argument I keep running into in practice: putting a person in the loop for every agent action works at small scale and then quietly stops working, because people asked to check everything stop catching what matters. The alternative is four questions answered at four moments, which AWS calls scope, know, bound, and observe. The part worth sitting with is that an agent’s limits belong outside its own reasoning, in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore policies enforced at the gateway, because an agent cannot turn off a control it does not run. AWS has run automated reasoning in production for more than a decade, including AWS Identity and Access Management at more than 2.1 billion requests per second, and the case here is for pointing it at the rules you write for agents.

#10219. L’Italia è afflitta da vulnerabilità informatiche, senza una causa chiara

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

I ricercatori non riescono a spiegare del tutto perché le minacce informatiche in Italia siano così diverse rispetto a quelle di qualsiasi altro Paese.

Translation provided by Dark Reading's internal AI translation tool.

Secondo nuovi dati, l’Italia è vittima di un numero sproporzionatamente elevato di attacchi informatici. Non solo: le tipologie di attacchi che colpiscono le organizzazioni nel Paese sono molto diverse da quelle che colpiscono altre località. I ricercatori avanzano tre teorie per spiegarne il motivo.

È vero che alcune regioni e alcuni paesi sono esposti a un rischio informatico maggiore a causa di fattori economici, militari e politici. Israele è una calamita per gli hacktivisti e per le minacce persistenti avanzate (APT) regionali, legate agli Stati. La storia unica del Brasile lo rende un vero e proprio alveare di trojan bancari. L’economia degli Stati Uniti attirerà sempre la massima attenzione da parte dei truffatori. Non è però così ovvio il motivo per cui l’Italia sia un bersaglio così popolare per i criminali informatici.

Related:Cyber Vulnerabilities Besiege Italy, Absent Clear Cause

«Uno dei motivi principali per cui abbiamo deciso di esaminare il panorama delle minacce in Italia è che il Paese continuava a comparire in cima alle nostre statistiche nei rapporti interni mensili», afferma Gianluca Tiepolo, analista di criminalità informatica presso Intel471. In un rapporto condiviso in esclusiva con Dark Reading prima della sua pubblicazione, Intel471 ha rilevato che l’Italia rappresenta un vero e proprio caso a sé stante nel panorama globale delle minacce informatiche. Le organizzazioni italiane subiscono attacchi a un ritmo ben superiore a quanto ci si potrebbe ragionevolmente aspettare, considerando le dimensioni del Paese, la sua economia e la sua situazione politica. Inoltre, gli attacchi sfruttanti le vulnerabilità e le infrastrutture web sono molto più comuni in Italia che altrove.

«Volevamo capire cosa fosse alla base di quelle statistiche», afferma Tiepolo. Alla fine, però, i dati dipingono un quadro quasi inspiegabile di ciò che sta accadendo nella terra della pasta e del Chianti.

L’Italia è il 25° Paese più grande al mondo ma, secondo questi nuovi dati, le sue organizzazioni rappresentano circa il 7% di tutti i dati di accesso iniziale venduti sui forum dei criminali informatici. A livello globale, è seconda solo agli Stati Uniti (30%). L’Italia si colloca inoltre al quarto posto tra i Paesi più presi di mira dal ransomware.

Ancora più strani sono i tipi di intrusioni informatiche che colpiscono le organizzazioni in Italia. Secondo i nuovi dati, gli initial access broker (IAB) hanno ottenuto il loro primo punto d’appoggio sfruttando vulnerabilità nel 57% dei casi. Le credenziali hanno spiegato solo il 23% dei casi. Nel frattempo, gli IAB hanno venduto l’accesso all’infrastruttura web di proprietà delle vittime nel 49% dei casi, con strumenti di accesso remoto e desktop remoto che rappresentano il 26% dei casi.

Related:Aussies Face Reduced Cybercrime Risk, as Pressure Shifts to SMBs

E allora? Forse queste cifre non saltano all’occhio. Ora, però, confrontiamole con i dati di Intel471 tratti dal suo rapporto “2026 Cyber Threat Trends & Outlook”:

A livello globale nel 2025, gli IAB hanno preso di mira gli strumenti di accesso remoto e di desktop remoto nel 67% dei casi — il 41% in più, in termini relativi, rispetto all’Italia. Nel frattempo, l’infrastruttura web — di gran lunga la risorsa più a rischio in Italia — rappresentava una frazione talmente esigua dei dati globali di Intel471 che l’azienda non si è nemmeno preoccupata di citarla nel proprio rapporto.

Allo stesso modo, secondo i dati globali dell’azienda, gli attacchi basati sulle credenziali sono oggi, in generale, otto volte più comuni di qualsiasi altro tipo di attacco. È emerso che il 49% delle inserzioni su IAB indicava le credenziali come tipo di attacco, rispetto al 23% dei dati specifici per l’Italia. E, cosa davvero esilarante, mentre in Italia rappresentano circa il 57% di tutti gli attacchi, le vulnerabilità sfruttate sono emerse solo nel 6,5% dei casi a livello globale.

Related:Europe Evolves Into Ransomware's Favorite Region

Sebbene i dati sulla sicurezza informatica possano essere interpretati in modi diversi a seconda delle circostanze, l’Italia sembra davvero una sorta di “unicorno” del rischio informatico, afferma Tiepolo, aggiungendo che l’Italia è ormai da tempo in ritardo in termini di preparazione informatica.

«Sono italiano», dice. «Ho lavorato con molti clienti italiani diversi. Quello che posso dire è che l’Italia è probabilmente leggermente indietro rispetto ad altri paesi europei, semplicemente in termini di [adozione delle] tecnologie di sicurezza. Ad esempio, le tecnologie di rilevamento e risposta sugli endpoint (EDR) sono diventate popolari in Italia intorno al 2020–2021. Prima del 2020, la maggior parte delle aziende italiane non utilizzava la tecnologia EDR. Quindi, forse storicamente, l’Italia è un po’ indietro nell’investire effettivamente in prodotti e tecnologie di sicurezza informatica».

Inoltre, i criminali informatici opportunisti stanno sfruttando in massa vulnerabilità note, diffuse e spesso piuttosto datate per mietere un numero maggiore di vittime in Italia rispetto ad altri paesi. «I dati che abbiamo visto la scorsa settimana da PHP2Shell, credo, confermano questa valutazione. L’Italia è il paese europeo con il maggior numero di versioni PHP 4, 5 e 7, che sono ormai fuori supporto», osserva Tiepolo.

«Ben il 90% delle offerte di accesso iniziale rivolte all’Italia sono quelle che chiamiamo “offerte all’ingrosso”», ipotizza. «Non si tratta di offerte mirate specificatamente all’Italia, ma semplicemente di sfruttamento delle vulnerabilità. La nostra valutazione è che l’Italia sia probabilmente più lenta di altri paesi nell’applicare le patch ai propri sistemi».

Un’altra possibilità correlata è che l’Italia si trovi vittima di una sorta di effetto rete delle vulnerabilità informatiche. La logica è più o meno questa: se determinate tecnologie sono particolarmente diffuse in un paese come l’Italia e le organizzazioni sono lente nell’affrontare le vulnerabilità di tali tecnologie, allora quel paese diventa un’economia di scala attraente.

Come ha scritto Intel471 nel proprio rapporto: «Una volta che un attore sviluppa un metodo di sfruttamento efficace, può applicare tale metodo ad altri sistemi esposti senza dover condurre un’attività di ricognizione separata ed estesa contro ciascuna organizzazione. Ciò riduce lo sforzo necessario per compromettere aziende la cui dimensione o il cui profilo potrebbero altrimenti offrire un incentivo limitato per un’intrusione mirata».

I ricercatori non hanno potuto specificare esattamente a quali tecnologie, vulnerabilità o metodi di sfruttamento questa teoria possa riferirsi, ma hanno osservato che essa si inserisce nel dato secondo cui il 90% delle offerte di accesso iniziale alle organizzazioni italiane online viene venduto all’ingrosso.

Senza avallare specificatamente i dati o le conclusioni di Intel471, i rappresentanti della società di sicurezza informatica Cleafy, con sede a Milano, hanno dichiarato a Dark Reading di aver osservato modelli sostanzialmente simili.

«La nostra ricerca sulle minacce evidenzia effettivamente un modello correlato: gli autori degli attacchi riutilizzano strumenti, infrastrutture e tecniche per estendere le campagne a diversi obiettivi bancari italiani», ha scritto l’azienda via e-mail. Ha citato casi come il kit di iniezione web drIBAN, che gli autori degli attacchi hanno utilizzato per sfruttare il sistema di Posta Elettronica Certificata (PEC), ampiamente diffuso in Italia. Casi come quello di drIBAN «non dimostrano che l’Italia abbia un mercato di accesso iniziale sproporzionatamente ampio, ma illustrano come le tecniche di attacco e le infrastrutture riutilizzabili possano aiutare i criminali informatici a estendere le operazioni su più obiettivi».

C’è un altro fattore, potenzialmente significativo, che spiega perché l’Italia appaia così diversa dagli altri paesi nei set di dati sugli attacchi informatici: la prevalenza delle piccole imprese.

La maggior parte delle imprese, ovunque, è di piccole dimensioni, ma, almeno rispetto ad altre economie avanzate, ciò è particolarmente vero in Italia. Una “panoramica dei dati per l’Italia” del maggio 2024 redatta da McKinsey ha rilevato che le “MSME” — micro, piccole e medie imprese — hanno contribuito all’economia e all’occupazione italiane in misura superiore di circa il 10% rispetto alla loro quota relativa in altre economie avanzate. Lo scorso marzo, inoltre, l’Organizzazione per la cooperazione e lo sviluppo economico (OCSE) ha pubblicato un rapporto in cui si indicava che nel 2023 il 99,9% delle imprese italiane era costituito da PMI e il 94,8% da microimprese.

«L’Italia ha molte piccole e medie imprese», afferma Tiepolo. «Una delle cose emerse dai dati — in particolare quelli relativi alle estorsioni — è che questi gruppi prendono di mira [in modo sproporzionato] le piccole e medie imprese. Quindi questo potrebbe essere uno dei motivi per cui [l’Italia si distingue] rispetto ad altri paesi che hanno un maggior numero di grandi aziende».

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#10216. Introducing Amazon ECS Gateway: A fully-managed ingress solution for ECS services

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

When platform teams manage containerized applications at scale on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), configuring ingress networking for each service often becomes a bottleneck. For every new service, teams must provision and connect Application Load Balancers (ALBs), AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificates, AWS WAF web ACLs, and security groups, then keep those resources in sync as services scale, update, or operate. This per-service overhead slows down deployment velocity and increases the risk of configuration drift across an organization.

Today, we’re announcing Amazon ECS Gateway, a new account-level resource that simplifies ingress networking for containerized workloads by dynamically provisioning and managing the necessary infrastructure on your behalf, with all resources created directly in your account.

ECS Gateway introduces a clear separation of responsibilities between platform teams and application teams.

ECS Gateway offers host-based routing using ALBs and enables up to 25 services to share a single ALB, optimizing infrastructure costs. ECS manages the full lifecycle of the underlying infrastructure, provisioning the first ALB when your first service connects, adding more ALBs as capacity is reached, and removing them when no longer needed. Each service receives a unique DNS hostname, giving your teams a ready-to-use endpoint the moment provisioning completes.

A first look at ECS Gateway In the ECS console, platform team can create a gateway and sets its configuration. The infrastructure role is an IAM role that ECS assumes to provision and manage networking resources such as ALBs, security groups, and certificates in your account. To create a gateway, provide a gateway name and select an infrastructure role. You can optionally associate the gateway with ECS clusters during creation or later.

Choose a load balancing scheme, either public or VPC-internal traffic routing. Under Additional Settings, you can also set up a listener, port, maximum count of load balancers the gateway can scale to, and a web ACL lets you protect your web applications. Some settings, including the name, scheme, VPC, subnets, IP address type, listener protocol and port cannot be changed after gateway creation.

Using AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), call CreateGateway with a name (unique per account), an infrastructure role, and a configuration object. No infrastructure is provisioned until a service connects with a gateway connector.

Once the gateway is created, you can take a look at the detailed configuration, gateway routes, load balancers, and associated clusters.

Now associate the gateway with one or more clusters (many-to-many), to make it available to ECS services on those clusters.

Use AssociateGatewayWithCluster to make the gateway available to services on a cluster:

To create and manage the ECS Gateway programmatically, including calling APIs and searching documentation, try the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI coding tool. To learn more, visit the Amazon ECS Gateway documentation.

ECS Gateway:Behind the scenesA gateway can be associated with up to 10,000 clusters, and a single cluster supports up to five gateway associations. This many-to-many relationship gives platform teams the flexibility to share a gateway across environments or assign multiple gateways (for example, public and private) to a single cluster.

Platform teams can control access by choosing which gateways to associate with which clusters. For additional control, use IAM policies to restrict who can deploy services to specific clusters.

Application teams add the gateway connector to each service definition in CreateService or UpdateService. If you have an existing ECS service with its own load balancer, you can adopt ECS Gateway incrementally by calling UpdateService to add a gateway connector. Both ingress paths remain available, allowing you to validate the gateway connection before removing the existing load balancer configuration.

At deployment time, Amazon ECS evaluates the gateways associated with the cluster and connects the service to every compatible gateway. A gateway is compatible when its access type matches the service’s connector filter, it is in the same VPC as the service, and it covers all Availability Zones used by the service’s configured subnets.

For each connection, Amazon ECS assigns the service to an ALB with available capacity and provisions the per-service resources: an ACM certificate, a unique DNS hostname, a listener rule routing traffic for that hostname to the service target group, and a service security group allowing inbound traffic only from the ALB security group. If no existing ALB has capacity, ECS creates a new one (up to maxAlbCount referring to quota limit). Once provisioning completes, the gateway route becomes ACTIVE, and the service URL is ready to receive traffic.

ECS Gateway handles common operational scenarios automatically:

Things to Know Here are a few important details to keep in mind:

Now available Amazon ECS Gateway is available now in all commercial AWS Regions where ECS is available at no additional charge. You pay only for the underlying infrastructure provisioned in your account when services connect to a gateway, including applicable ALB charges, CloudWatch logs and metrics, ACM certificates, and data transfer charges. To learn more, visit the Amazon ECS Pricing page.

To get started, create your first gateway today in the ECS console, and send feedback to AWS re:Post for ECS or through your usual AWS Support contacts.

#10215. Linus Torvalds sees signs AI-prompted patch flood has peaked

Fixes are arriving faster than new bug reports for one major Linux project

The worst of the patchpocalypse may be behind us, according to Linus Torvalds.

Writing in his weekly kernel update post, the Linux kernel dev leader delivered Linux 7.4 rc2 – the second rough cut of the next kernel – which he rated as a big release for two reasons.

One is that he left some code out of rc1, because he was busy and because it was already the largest such release in the history of the kernel.

The other is what Torvalds described as “various AI fixes.”

Such fixes are necessary because ever since Anthropic launched its Mythos bug-finding model in April, developers have been able to find more software flaws than was previously possible.

Microsoft, for example, addressed a record 974 flaws in September – its third record fixing spree this year after it whacked 622 flaws in July and 206 in June. Oracle addressed 1,449 flaws in a single month.

That’s many more patches than IT teams are set up to handle, yet they must find ways to deal with bugs more quickly because attackers are increasingly targeting flaws found by AI.

Torvalds’ post suggests that, perhaps, the worst of this is behind us.

“This time around Alexei claims that on the bpf side at least the fixes are now coming in faster than the new reports, and that sounds lovely if true,” he wrote.

That’s a reference to Alexei Starovoitov, co-creator and lead dev on the Extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF), the project that makes it possible to run sandboxed programs within the Linux kernel.

“I think most other areas haven't reached that point yet, but it's at least a sign that we _may_ be starting to see the tide starting to turn,” he added. “Don't hold your breath, but maybe cross your fingers we'll be getting there in the not entirely distant future.”

If Torvalds is correct, that’s welcome news. The Linux kernel’s 40-million-plus lines of code makes it one of the world’s bigger software projects. If AI soon stops finding flaws in other parts of the kernel beyond eBPF, perhaps the deluge of fixes developers and users alike will need to handle has peaked. ®

#10213. AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now generally available

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Today, we’re announcing the general availability of AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities. AWS Continuum is a security service that finds and validates code vulnerabilities, then delivers fixes as patches you can automate or as pull requests in your repositories. AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities confirms which findings are exploitable in your environment, ranks the resulting issues by business impact, and proposes a fix for each one. Every remediation starts in a mode where Continuum proposes the fix and a person approves it before it ships. In the future, you will be able to decide which actions Continuum can take on its own, within the guardrails you define.

Using frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models, threat actors can turn a vulnerability disclosure into working exploit code in minutes, and the same tools that speed up development also increase the volume of findings your teams must process. If your organization runs a large application estate, your scanners likely produce thousands of findings a day, and many of them need no action. A finding can be unreachable, unexploitable, or already mitigated by a runtime control. Generic severity scores don’t tell you which resources a threat actor can actually reach, so a critical score on a dev-only utility looks the same as a medium score on a service one step away from a payments database. Previously, confirming whether a finding was exploitable took hours of manual investigation, and shipping a fix with confidence took days of coordination across security, infrastructure, and application teams, because the blast radius of a change is hard to assess without business context. To close that gap, Continuum proves which findings are exploitable and bounds the risk of each fix it proposes.

Continuum builds a context graph from two primary sources: your code repositories and your AWS environment. For AWS, you set up a collector in the account and Region where your code runs. The collector gathers resource details such as AWS Config resources and network configuration so Continuum can judge whether a vulnerability is reachable over the network and what a threat actor could reach from it. From this graph, Continuum learns which systems are business-critical, who owns them, how services depend on one another, and which data each one touches. It uses that picture to identify your highest-value systems, such as customer data stores, payment pipelines, and authentication services, and then ranks each resulting issue by how close its attack path runs to those systems.

Continuum analyzes each finding against your code and its environment context and assigns an evidence level, such as a verdict proven by static analysis of the vulnerable code path. For findings it can reproduce, Continuum runs the exploit in an isolated sandbox and attaches proof-of-concept code with the reproduction steps. It produces the attack path, the supporting source analysis, and a blast radius assessment instead of a risk score alone. It also evaluates whether your existing defenses would detect and stop the validated path.

For each confirmed issue, Continuum generates a fix (a code patch, a dependency upgrade, or a configuration change) and opens it as a pull request in your connected repository, ready to review. Every fix requires human approval: you review and merge the pull request, so the final decision stays with your team. In the future, you will be able to build confidence in specific remediation classes and let Continuum apply those fixes automatically once its confidence gates pass, such as test coverage, scope bounds, and historical success rate.

AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities in actionTo show how this works, I open AWS Continuum in the console and go to Code vulnerabilities. Before I can review issues, I set up an environment. I connect a code source, either a GitHub integration or an Amazon S3 bucket, and then create an environment that scans it on a schedule I choose. An Amazon S3 source has a couple of prerequisites: the bucket sits in the same account and AWS Region where I turn on AWS Continuum, and I grant access through an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role that AWS Continuum assumes. I can optionally add AWS infrastructure context by setting up an AWS Continuum collector in the account and Region where my code runs and authorizing my environment to use it. For the full requirements and steps, see the AWS Continuum User Guide.

The Overview page brings these pieces together in one place, showing my Code integrations, the Environments built on them, and the status of any AWS collector that supplies AWS resource context.

I open one of my environments. The Issues tab lists validated, prioritized issues rather than raw scanner output, each with a severity, a status, and the time it was created. I choose one of the issues.

The Overview rates it High severity, with the status Completed and the remediation already Delivered to GitHub. The Risk assessment explains why. Continuum rates its Exploitability as Exploitable, with an evidence level of Static proven and a validation run status of Completed. Likelihood is High, since the service is reachable from an attacker, requires no authentication, and needs no user interaction. Impact is Moderate, which means an attacker gains the ability to modify business data, with a blast radius reaching other users in the same tenant. A Proof section includes the source analysis behind the verdict.

The Remediation section shows a fix already delivered as a pull request in GitHub, changing four files, with 50 lines added and 24 removed across the cart service. Continuum opens the fix as a pull request titled Continuum fix, and I choose View pull request to open it in GitHub. The console is explicit that a generated patch does not mean the issue is fixed. I still review and merge it, which keeps the final decision with my team. A Contributing findings section lists the specific scanner finding this issue was built from.

The pull request description carries the same risk assessment, remediation summary, and proof from the console, so whoever reviews it in GitHub sees the evidence without leaving their workflow.

The Findings tab lists the raw scanner findings across the environment, the evidence that issues are built from.

The Scans tab shows the history of each scan with its status, origin, and request and completion times, and I use Configure scan frequency to change the cadence or Queue scan to run one on demand. The Configuration tab is where I manage the environment: the code and context sources it reads from, its code integrations, environment settings such as whether Continuum creates remediation patches, and the AWS collectors it uses for AWS context.

In a single workflow, I work through the validated issues in priority order with each scan, reviewing the evidence and scope behind each one before I approve and merge the fixes I trust. Every fix waits for my approval, so the backlog keeps shrinking while my team keeps control of what ships.

Now available AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is available today in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon) Regions. For pricing, visit the pricing page.

To learn more, visit the AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities product page and the User Guide. Give it a try in the AWS Continuum console today, and send us feedback through your usual AWS Support contacts.

Esra Kayabali is a Principal Solutions Architect at AWS, specializing in analytics, including data warehousing, data lakes, big data analytics, batch and real-time data streaming, and data integration. She has more than ten years of software development and solution architecture experience. She is passionate about collaborative learning, knowledge sharing, and guiding community in their cloud technologies journey.

#10211. Dev error bricked 600 PCs, caused $1M CD-ROM write-off

One lucky engineer scored a free dinner during the frantic fix, the rest got to explain their mistake

Welcome to Monday, the day upon which The Register offers a new instalment of "Who, Me?" – our reader-contributed column that shares your stories of messing up, 'fessing up, and somehow finding redress.

This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Oriel" who told us he once worked for a vendor of small business accounting software.

This story comes from a time when software shipped on CD-ROMs and users bought it off the shelf in actual shops. The vendor released a new version each year and always shipped it before a major holiday that's celebrated with a giant meal.

Oriel was part of the team whose job it was to get the package ready on time.

In the previous year, they flubbed the job because the program didn't always install itself on some PCs running Windows 95 or Windows ME machines system due to registry corruption.

"We wanted to increase our successful installation metrics, so in conjunction with the installation team, a key decision was made – by me – to force the updating of registry keys to enable the install," Oriel admitted. In his email to The Register, he asked the portentous question: "What could possibly go wrong?"

What went wrong was that not long after the software was shipped, the vendor's support lines started getting calls from customers who complained that after installing the accounting package none of their other software would work.

"Installing a new version of our application had borked the customer's machine completely," Oriel wrote.

The company decided the best thing to do was to tell affected customers they should go and buy a new PC – and that it would pick up the bill, no questions asked.

"In the week prior to the holiday, we replaced over 600 machines," Oriel told The Register.

Oriel and his developer colleagues were of course told to fix the problem but couldn't reproduce it nor figure out their mistake.

"To get a reproduction case we need a user's machine where the user had created a Windows Registry restore point prior to installing our application," Oriel explained. If the developers could find such a machine, the plan was to roll it back to the restore point, verify everything was in order before the customer installed the update, install the accounting software, and figure out the problem.

The company tasked its support agents with finding a customer willing to surrender their PC, which proved difficult because few bothered to create a registry restore point.

The day before the holiday, a customer volunteered their machine.

This customer was located a few hours away by road, so an engineer got the job of visiting on the morning of the holiday to pick up the stricken machine, give the customer a shiny new system and configure it to their specifications.

Said engineer did the job, which took so long he was invited to stay for the holiday meal, then returned to HQ with the broken box.

The next day, Oriel and his colleagues got to work and found a fix, then created a version of the accounting application that wouldn't break any more PCs.

Oriel was, of course, summoned into a meeting with senior execs to explain the situation and watched as they decided the best course of action was to pull buggy CDs from stores – which meant trashing CDs and packaging valued at $1 million.

Have you made a mistake that broke customers' kit, or cost millions? If so, don't make the mistake of not sharing your story with The Register and click here to email the column. ®

#10209. AWS Weekly Roundup: Amazon Polly Generative engine, TorchNeuron for Trainium, and more (October 26, 2026)

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

A few weeks ago I presented to a small group of commercial and technology leaders from Brazilian agribusiness at the AWS office in São Paulo. My talk ran through where generative AI fits across the different stages of an agribusiness operation, and the point I kept returning to is that the markets we call traditional are exactly the ones where keeping up with this technology decides who ends up ahead of the curve. Nobody there was arguing about whether AI belongs in agriculture. The questions were about delivery: who receives the output, in which language, on which device, often while driving between farms. That is why a launch I might otherwise have filed under routine leads my list this week. The Amazon Polly Generative engine upgrade added 14 new voices, two of them in Brazilian Portuguese. When your user has both hands on a steering wheel, the interface is a voice.

Presenting “GenAI no Agronegócio Brasileiro” at the AWS office in São Paulo.

The rest of the week had a sharper edge. The biggest launch is a security service built on the premise that the gap between a vulnerability being disclosed and a vulnerability being exploited has effectively closed, and AWS published the honeypot evidence for exactly that in the same week. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news…

AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now generally available AWS Continuum reframes vulnerability management as an end-to-end job rather than a scanner that hands you a list. It builds a context graph from your repositories and your AWS environment, assigns each finding an evidence level, and reproduces exploitable findings in an isolated sandbox with proof-of-concept code so you see the issue rather than a severity label. It ranks issues by how close the attack path runs to business-critical systems, then opens the fix as a pull request. The control boundary matters: every remediation currently requires human approval, so you review and merge the pull request, with autonomous classes of fix gated behind confidence thresholds for the future.

The “why now” came from AWS’s own honeypots in the same week. Amazon Threat Intelligence found a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt in MadPot telemetry dated October 17, four days before CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 were publicly disclosed, and on disclosure day proof-of-concept exploits were circulating around 02:00 UTC, roughly twelve hours before the embargo was due to lift at 14:00 UTC. The practical reading is direct: a patch window measured in days assumes a delay that no longer exists, and an investigation should start from the earliest known exploitation rather than from the disclosure date. AWS also published the AWS WAF mitigations for the same CVEs. Continuum is available in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon).

Introducing Amazon ECS Gateway Amazon ECS Gateway splits the work of exposing a service between the people who own the network and the people who own the application. Platform teams define one gateway with the organization’s subnets, security groups, TLS certificates, listener settings, and AWS WAF web ACLs. Application teams opt in by adding a gateway connector to the service definition, and ECS gives them an ACM certificate, a unique DNS hostname, listener rules, a target group, and a security group that admits traffic only from the Application Load Balancer.

The numbers make the economics clear: up to 25 services share a single ALB, ECS provisions the first ALB on first connect and removes ALBs when they are no longer needed, and a gateway can associate with up to 10,000 clusters, with five gateways per cluster. You can adopt it incrementally with UpdateService while your existing load balancer stays in place. Amazon ECS Gateway is available in all commercial Regions where Amazon ECS is available, at no additional charge.

Last week’s launches Here are some launches that caught my attention this week.

Amazon Polly delivers a major upgrade to its Generative engine – The Generative engine now runs a larger, more expressive catalog: 57 generative voices across 11 languages and 25 locales, with 14 new voices across 9 locales and Hindi and Finnish generally available for the first time. Two of the new voices are Brazilian Portuguese, Leo and Carolina. It is a drop-in upgrade, so the voice names, the same SynthesizeSpeech call, and the price all stay the same while the output gets more natural.

AWS announces TorchNeuron: native PyTorch support for AWS Trainium (public beta) – TorchNeuron is an open source PyTorch backend that lets you run your model on Trainium by switching to .to(‘neuron’), a configuration change instead of a rewrite, with eager execution and torch.compile intact. It integrates with the Neuron Kernel Interface for custom operators, and it works on Trainium2 and Trainium3 instances. If you want the bigger picture on why hardware choice should not lock in your software, the AWS Insights piece on that theme is a good companion read, and the release lands alongside AWS Neuron 2.33.

New ways to customize models with Amazon SageMaker AI, without managing GPUs – Training sessions are now generally available, giving you control of the post-training loop, including custom loss functions and reward signals, while SageMaker AI handles GPU allocation, distributed execution, fault recovery, and checkpoint storage. You pay for the tokens SageMaker AI processes, and the meter stops while your reward function scores a batch. There is a full technical walkthrough, the training session APIs, and new support for Muse Glimmer, Qwen 3.8, and Ministral 3.

Structured outputs for Claude models available on Amazon Bedrock – You can now get schema-compliant JSON back from any Anthropic Claude model on Amazon Bedrock, across both the bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle endpoints, without custom parsing, retry logic, or post-processing. That makes jobs like pulling every required field from a financial report, parsing clinical notes, or routing support tickets by intent far more reliable to automate.

Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey now supports online migration with zero downtime – You can migrate self-managed Valkey or Redis OSS on Amazon EC2 into ElastiCache Serverless with zero downtime, meaning zero errors returned to the client during the move, measured the way the ElastiCache SLA measures availability. You prepare the migration, start the data sync, then choose a manual or automatic cutover, with no third-party replication tools. It is available in all commercial Regions, the China Regions, and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions.

Other AWS news Here are some additional projects and posts that you might find interesting.

Discover tools at runtime with AWS Agent Registry – AWS Agent Registry is a managed catalog for MCP servers, agents, and agent skills, so an orchestrator can search approved capabilities at runtime instead of compiling every tool in at build time. This walkthrough shows the discover, instantiate, and execute loop in a working sample, with search results that return connection metadata but never invocation credentials.

Tokenomics for coding agents: benchmark cost and quality on your own code – Coding assistants replay a growing transcript on every turn, so their cost math is nothing like ordinary inference. This post gives you open source tooling to measure model, harness, and hosting choices on your own repositories and build a cost-and-quality frontier you own, with sample results where routing came out 44.7 percent cheaper for 4.8 percent lower mean quality.

How U.S. Bank migrated 119 TB from Oracle Exadata to Amazon RDS for Oracle – U.S. Bank moved four Oracle Exadata databases totaling about 119 TB to Amazon RDS for Oracle using a config-driven pipeline built on Oracle XTTS, AWS DataSync, and Amazon EFS. The initial baseline copy finished in about 7 days with zero data loss and cutovers averaging roughly four hours per database, over a bandwidth-capped Direct Connect link.

Upcoming AWS events Mark your calendars for these upcoming events.

AWS re:Invent – AWS re:Invent runs November 30 to December 4 in Las Vegas, with more than 2,200 sessions. The session catalog is live and reserved seating is open, so now is the time to build your schedule.

AWS Community Days – AWS Community Day Brasil Norte takes place in Belém on October 31, closing out the 2026 Brazilian community season. Check the hub for events near you.

That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup!

This post is part of our Weekly Roundup series. Check back each week for a quick roundup of interesting news and announcements from AWS!

#10206. AWS Weekly Roundup: GPT-6.1 Terra on Bedrock, Step Functions as agent tools, and more (November 2, 2026)

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

The agentic launches that stayed with me last week had nothing to do with how capable a model is. They were about reach. AWS Step Functions, which already orchestrates over 220 AWS services, can now be handed to an agent as a tool, so workflows teams already trust became callable without a rewrite. In the same week, the AI blog published how one engagement platform exposed roughly 400 internal API operations the same way. Neither story involves rebuilding anything, only describing what exists and letting the agent find it.

The other thread was cost. OpenAI’s newest Terra model reached Amazon Bedrock priced well below the model beside it, and two post-quantum launches landed for a deadline nobody can put on a calendar yet. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news…

HeadlinesOpenAI GPT-6.1 Terra is now generally available on Amazon Bedrock, and what interests me is where it sits rather than what it tops. Terra is the everyday-workload line of the GPT-6 family. In OpenAI’s Agents’ Last Exam evaluation it scored 15 percentage points higher than GPT-5.6 Terra, performed on par with GPT-6 Astra, and completed tasks more than three times faster than both. Those are OpenAI’s figures, not an independent test. The price is what I would check first: input and output tokens are at least 50% lower than GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-5.6 Terra. It takes up to 1 million input tokens with text and image input, and you can reach it from the Bedrock APIs or ChatGPT Work and Codex.

AWS Step Functions workflows are now available as AI agent tools through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, which connects agents to tools over the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The division of labor is the idea: the agent decides when to run a workflow and what input to pass; Step Functions runs each step exactly as you defined it. A support agent can trigger a refund, and the eligibility check, the manager approval, and the credit still happen in that order every time, because the ordering was never the model’s to improvise. Your existing Standard and Express workflows qualify as connector targets, and agents can also look up runs. It’s available in all Regions where AgentCore Gateway is, at standard rates.

Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention:

AWS Key Management Service now supports ML-KEM for post-quantum key encapsulation – You can now establish a shared secret with a post-quantum algorithm using AWS KMS keys, with private keys in FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated HSMs. All three NIST FIPS 203 parameter sets are supported through Encapsulate, which produces a random 32-byte shared secret and its ciphertext, and Decapsulate, which recovers it. The threat is harvest now, decrypt later: an adversary records today’s key exchange and recovers the secret once quantum computers are powerful enough. It’s available everywhere KMS runs except the Middle East (UAE and Bahrain) and China Regions. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL added post-quantum TLS key exchange the same week, on versions 18 and higher.

AWS IAM Identity Center now supports cross-Region trusted identity propagation – You can now carry a user’s identity with their request to AWS services in another Region. This removes a genuine architectural constraint: trusted identity propagation used to require every service accessing that identity to sit in the same Region, which left two unappealing options, broad IAM roles that cannot distinguish individual users, or consolidating all your services into a single Region. Now the identity travels with the request automatically, so you grant access by user and group membership and audit who accessed what. It’s available at no additional cost everywhere IAM Identity Center runs.

Amazon ECS now supports GPU sharing with NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS) – You can now run multiple Amazon ECS tasks concurrently on a single NVIDIA GPU, the practical answer to work that only ever uses a fraction of one, like small-model inference and multi-model serving. You declare the GPU memory each container needs and can optionally cap its share of GPU compute, and ECS places tasks on GPUs with available capacity as your services scale, with no code changes. It works on ECS Managed Instances and ECS on Amazon EC2, and on Managed Instances it watches the MPS control daemon and replaces the instance if it turns unhealthy. It’s available in all commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions.

AWS Lambda supports Seekable OCI (SOCI) lazy loading for Lambda Managed Instances – You can now have AWS Lambda fetch only the files needed at each stage of startup instead of pulling a whole container image first, which AWS puts at up to 70% off container startup time. You create a SOCI index, push it to Amazon ECR, point the image URI at the indexed tag, and Lambda detects it automatically. The technique also reached Amazon SageMaker AI training and processing jobs, with benchmarks: lazy loading held at 3 to 11 seconds regardless of image size, against a median 3 minutes 42 seconds for a 13.2 GB image, a range they report as 8x to 46x.

Amazon EKS Auto Mode now supports Kubernetes Gateway API – You can now declare how traffic reaches your applications with Gateway and HTTPRoute resources on Amazon EKS without installing a separate controller, and EKS Auto Mode provisions and manages the underlying AWS load balancing infrastructure. You get HTTP and gRPC routing, cross-namespace routing, weighted traffic splitting, header-based routing, and automatic TLS certificate discovery through AWS Certificate Manager. Existing Ingress workloads keep working alongside them, so this is additive rather than a migration. Gateway API support is included with EKS Auto Mode; standard load balancing charges apply.

For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page.

Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting:

How Nubank automated disaster recovery with the AWS DevOps Agent – Nubank serves more than 140 million customers across Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia, and classifies over 300 business flows as critical, each tested on a regulator’s schedule. Nubank reports that handing evidence collection and report writing to the AWS DevOps Agent cut a test cycle from about 4.3 hours to roughly 40 minutes, and quadrupled flow coverage in 2026 to more than 160. One execution terminated more than 900 EKS instances under synthetic traffic with AWS Fault Injection Service, producing the evidence its regulator needed.

How MoEngage turned over 400 APIs into agent tools with AgentCore Gateway – Roughly 400 internal REST API operations, built by 25 teams, sitting in private VPCs across seven Regions, with tenant identity that could never become a parameter the model gets to set. MoEngage estimates the managed path saved about six months of platform engineering. The detail worth stealing: a full tool listing would have crossed 20,000 tokens per connection, so agents search for tools by describing a task instead of receiving the catalog.

Reducing petabyte-scale S3 storage costs with evidence-based lifecycle rules – The hard part isn’t deciding to act, it’s knowing which data has gone cold and where it can safely live. This uses S3 Storage Lens groups and Storage Class Analysis to prove access patterns before moving anything. In the engagement described, 5.8 PB of logs in Amazon S3 Standard at approximately $241,000 per month showed an access ratio below 0.1% past 90 days, and a 90-day transition to Glacier Instant Retrieval cut the bill by roughly 70%, a figure the author ties to that workload.

Upcoming AWS events Check your calendar and sign up for upcoming AWS events:

AWS re:Invent – re:Invent returns to Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4, with more than 2,200 sessions. The event catalog is live and reserved seating is open, so register and claim your spots before they fill up.

AWS Community Days – Community-led conferences planned and delivered by community leaders. The 2026 season is winding down as re:Invent approaches, so check the hub for what’s still on.

Join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events.

That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup!

#10204. What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

Today, we announce the General Availability of Pathways on Google Cloud Platform. In this post, you will learn about Pathways, the distributed system Google built to train its own large models, including Gemini. We discuss how Pathways addresses the coordination challenge by introducing one client that describes the whole computation as a graph, and how the distributed runtime places it, moves the tensors, and keeps the accelerators busy.

Most large-model training runs as Single Program, Multiple Data (SPMD) programs. Every accelerator runs the same program in lockstep and coordinates through collectives like AllReduce.

It works well when your job is the same program running on every device. It struggles when the job is no longer uniform, like a pipeline whose stages wait on each other or an RL loop where a sampler, a reward model, and a trainer are different programs that have to overlap.

Large runs also have to survive hardware failures, which interrupted Gemini 2.5 training multiple times per hour. In SPMD, one lost machine stops every process and sends the run back to its last checkpoint. In each case, the challenge is coordination. You have to decide what runs where and in what order, how tensors move between devices, and how the job keeps going when a machine drops out.

In this post of the series “Pathways on Google Cloud”, you will learn about Pathways, the distributed system Google built to train its own large models, including Gemini. The post discusses how Pathways addresses the coordination challenge by introducing one client that describes the whole computation as a graph, and how the distributed runtime places it, moves the tensors, and keeps the accelerators busy.

By the end, you'll know where SPMD is suboptimal, what single-controller execution changes, and how Pathways coordinates a whole training job across a cluster.

If you train PyTorch models, you almost certainly use Distributed Data Parallel (DDP) or Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP). DDP runs a copy of your script on every accelerator and averages gradients with a collective operation such as AllReduce. FSDP shards parameters, gradients, and optimizer states across workers so that the model fits at all.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

DDP and FSDP both follow the Single Program, Multiple Data (SPMD) execution model. Every process runs the same copy of your script, owns its accelerators for the whole run, and moves in lockstep with the others, because the only way they coordinate is through collectives like AllReduce. Inside one tightly connected group of accelerators those collectives run over a fast interconnect and are cheap. Scale the job across groups and the same collectives cross the datacenter network, which is far slower. On a TPU v5p, for example, each chip gets 1,200 GB/s of bidirectional chip-to-chip bandwidth inside its group, but only 50 Gb/s (gigabits, about 6 GB/s) to the datacenter network which is roughly two orders of magnitude less.

And because every step blocks on its collectives, that communication lands directly in step time. The more groups you span, the larger the share of each step spent moving data, so throughput grows slower than the number of accelerators you add.

As long as your training job is one program that fills the hardware you give it, this execution model fits well. You write your model as if there were one device, and the collectives do the rest. But fitting a model into memory is only part of the problem. Keeping every accelerator busy is the harder part, and this is where the SPMD model starts to show its limits.

Take pipeline parallelism as an example. You split a model into blocks across devices, and each device now runs different code over smaller micro-batches. Activations flow forward, activation gradients flow back, and while device 0 works on the first micro-batch, devices 1 and 2 wait. Apart from the idle accelerators you keep paying for, this drops utilization and throughput, even though every device has work in the steady state.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

Another example is RL post-training for an LLM. You have a sampler that generates rollouts, a reward model that scores them, and a trainer that updates the policy and sends the new weights back to the sampler. These are three different programs that should overlap; otherwise the sampler is idle while the trainer runs, and the trainer is idle while the sampler generates.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

In both scenarios, the job is now several different programs running on different devices, and their dependencies can no longer be managed through a single collective. You now have to coordinate which devices share which tensors, which processes run while others are still finishing, and how early to enqueue the next buffer so an accelerator never waits for input. Because each worker only has visibility into its local devices and data, no individual process can manage all of these dependencies itself. That has several consequences.

First, because each process owns its accelerators for the whole run and every collective blocks until all devices finish, one failed machine prevents the collective from completing and stops the entire job, forcing a restart from the last checkpoint. You cannot add devices mid-run, and you cannot give devices back.

Second, because each process holds its accelerators from start to finish, capacity can't move to where it's needed. Within one job, a stage that needs fewer chips than another still keeps the extra ones. They sit idle, you keep paying for them, and no other part of the job can use them until the run ends. Across a team, the same happens at cluster scale. Every job owns its accelerators for as long as it runs, so sharing a cluster means splitting it into per-job allocations, and each new job brings up its own processes on its own hosts.

Finally, the development process itself gets harder. On one host you iterate fast because you run the script, drop into a Python shell, set a breakpoint, and debug. This is not true once the job spans many hosts. You need a launcher to push your script to every host, you hit coordination bugs that never showed up on one machine, and there's no single process to break into. When something hangs, each worker is stuck at a collective waiting for the others, with no one place that shows the whole job.

So the common challenge here is the coordination itself. As soon as the job stops being one program in lockstep, you have to decide what runs where, in what order, and how tensors get from one device to the next.

One way to describe this is as a graph, where each block is a node, each tensor that moves between blocks is an edge, and the devices are where the nodes are placed. You can wire that graph up by hand in SPMD, one process at a time. But what if a single client declared that graph, including what each block does, what it needs, and where it runs, and a distributed runtime handled the transfers, dependencies, and ordering along its edges?

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

That is the idea behind Pathways, the distributed system Google built to train its own largest models, including Gemini. Pathways runs JAX programs on TPUs and it is available on Google Cloud.

With Pathways, you define the end-to-end computation from a single Python client, without writing custom coordination code, and a distributed runtime executes it. That client is decoupled from the hardware. It runs on an ordinary CPU machine and you write your program against virtual devices; a resource manager maps them onto real chips, and a worker on each accelerator host runs the compiled programs it receives.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

Because your code refers to virtual devices rather than physical ones, the runtime is flexible to allow users to change the devices used for a given computation. This allows you to stay in control while the runtime handles the mapping to hardware. In an RL loop, for example, the trainer and the samplers rarely want the same number of chips, so you can give the sampler stage more chips by asking for more virtual devices.

Also, the same capability helps when a host fails or the hardware isn't ready yet. If a host dies, the resource manager remaps the work onto healthy chips and the run keeps going instead of relaunching the whole job, which is the basis for elastic training. And because the program targets virtual devices, compilation can start before the physical chips are provisioned, so setup overlaps with provisioning instead of waiting on it.

The resource manager owning the chips also means one Pathways cluster can serve several clients, so researchers on a team can share its capacity. With the Shared Pathways Service, the cluster stays up as a long running service, which lets you develop interactively on TPUs hosted on GKE. Each client connects on demand from a laptop or VM, gets its own slices (groups of tightly connected TPU chips) from the shared pool, and hands them back when it disconnects. When every chip is busy, the next workload waits until capacity frees up.

Take the three-block model from Figure 2. Block A runs on one group of devices, block B on a second, block C on a third. You declare what each block computes, its target devices, and where its outputs go. Pathways expresses those dependencies as a distributed dataflow graph, in which each block is a compiled SPMD program and each edge is a tensor the runtime has to deliver.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

In a single SPMD program, the framework handles the collectives that keep the devices in sync within a group, with or without Pathways, and your code doesn't change. The difference shows up once the job runs several programs on different groups (Multiple Programs, Multiple Data, MPMD), like these three blocks or the sampler, reward model, and trainer of an RL loop. Then no single process sees both sides (the same limit from before, where each worker only knows its own devices), so getting a tensor from block A to block B is a hand-off you have to coordinate yourself.

Pathways closes that gap. You declare the dependency once, and the runtime moves and reshards the tensor for you, over the fast interconnect within a group and over the datacenter network between groups.

To keep the accelerators busy, Pathways prepares launches ahead of time with futures and parallel asynchronous dispatch. While block A is still computing, block B can't run yet, but its input shapes and dtypes are already known, so the runtime allocates B's buffers and schedules the transfer before A's output even exists. Host-side setup for every block happens up front, and each block launches when its inputs arrive.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

This is also what keeps the single client from becoming a bottleneck. Because dispatch is asynchronous, the coordination work overlaps with the compute already running on the chips, so the client stays off the critical path instead of stalling the accelerators between steps.

In Pathways, the runtime decides execution order when a group has more than one operation ready. In pipelined training, B's devices often hold both the forward pass for an upcoming micro-batch and the backward pass for an earlier one. If each device picked on its own, their collectives would conflict and the group would stall.

Pathways has a central scheduler that puts every program's operations into one consistent order, so operations that must communicate start together instead of deadlocking.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

And because it's still one client, the development loop we mentioned before comes back. It's the same single Python process whether you drive one host or thousands of hosts, so you can drop into a shell, set a breakpoint, and inspect the run as it goes. When something stalls, there's one place that knows what's queued on every device and which dependency hasn't been met, instead of a hang spread across separate processes.

Put together, Pathways separates model building from execution. You choose how the model partitions across hardware using the client. And the runtime handles the transfers, ordering, and scheduling that keep accelerators busy, across the whole cluster rather than just your slice of it.

Described this way, Pathways can start to sound like an orchestrator you already know. If scheduling work, moving tensors, and keeping a whole cluster busy brings Ray to mind, it should. But the two work at different layers.

Ray is an open-source framework for orchestrating Python-native AI workloads across large clusters. It provisions the cluster, schedules your Python code as tasks and actors, and launches your workload across hosts, holding data loading, training, serving, and tuning under one control plane. To Ray, an accelerator is a resource to schedule.

What Ray doesn't change is how your training runs on the chips. The job inside each worker still runs as SPMD. The framework inserts the collectives, and each process sees only its own devices. Ray places and starts that job but it doesn't turn it into a single program that drives the whole cluster.

That is the layer Pathways works at. It changes the execution model underneath, so one client coordinates every chip. Because they sit at different layers, the two are complementary. In principle, Ray can orchestrate the cluster and the pipeline while Pathways handles how the training step executes.

So concretely, Ray's job is about orchestration while Pathways' job is about execution. With Ray, you tie your data, training, serving, and tuning together and spread heterogeneous work across accelerators and clouds. With Pathways, you run one model across many groups of chips, express patterns beyond SPMD, and recover from a failed host instead of relaunching the whole job.

When a training job stops being one uniform program, the challenge becomes coordinating the dependencies between stages, the tensors that cross the network, and the ordering that keeps every accelerator fed.

SPMD requires you to address these dependencies. With Pathways, you describe the computation once, from a single client, as a graph of blocks and the tensors between them. And you have a runtime that places the blocks on virtual devices, moves and reshards the tensors, orders the work across the cluster, and remaps around a failed host.

With Pathways, model building and execution are separated and you reason about the whole cluster instead of one slice of it.

#10202. Amazon S3 Tables now offer managed migration of Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Today, we’re announcing a simple, cost-effective path for data lake modernization. Amazon S3 Tables now support managed migration of your Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg. Migration works with Parquet tables in Amazon S3 that are registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog and allows you to upgrade your data lake with no pipelines to build or compute to provision, while production workloads keep running.

Apache Iceberg has become the open standard for large analytics datasets. It lets you manage petabyte-scale tables with features like schema evolution, hidden partitioning, and time travel queries, while keeping your data open and queryable with any Iceberg-compatible engine. Amazon S3 Tables offer fully managed storage purpose-built to keep Iceberg tables performant and cost-effective as they grow, with features like automatic maintenance, optimization, replication, and S3 Intelligent-Tiering built-in.

What is new Previously, migrating Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg could take weeks of engineering work to build and manage the required infrastructure. Converting data types and building rollback capabilities added operational complexity. Now, this is available as a managed, API-driven operation.

S3 Tables handle the entire migration workflow, including data validation, compatibility checks, type conversions, file recompression, and compaction. Before copying any data, S3 Tables identify every source object in scope and generate a compatibility report. You can sync as many times as you need without stopping writes to your source table, except for a few minutes during cutover. Once you are ready, you can complete the migration, minimizing time that tables are offline.

Compared to self-managed approaches, S3 Tables managed migrations are cost-effective because you pay only for the data copied, with no charge for the Hive-to-Iceberg conversion, and source objects in S3 Intelligent-Tiering stay in their current access tier.

A first look at the migration To migrate an AWS Glue Hive table, choose your destination table bucket in the S3 console, then choose Create table from migration.

Create a namespace and table name for your destination Iceberg table. The destination table is created using recommended default settings tuned for query performance and storage efficiency.

When you start the migration, S3 Tables validate the source table, generate a compatibility report, and begin copying data. The destination table is read-only during the migration. Once you complete migration, the destination table is promoted to read-write.

You can begin working with your data right away using a direct integration with Amazon Athena and Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio in the AWS console, or use any tool compatible with the Apache Iceberg REST API to directly query the tables. To learn more, visit the S3 Tables migration documentation.

You can also use AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), AWS SDKs, or the Agent Toolkit for AWS. For example, set up migration jobs and call the start-table-migration command.

To catch up the destination table with changes in the source, call sync-table-migration as many times as you need before you complete the migration. Each sync copies only what changed.

If you’re using coding agents like Kiro, the migrating-hive-tables-to-s3-tables skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS provides step-by-step migration guidance with safety guardrails for agents. The skill can:

To learn more, visit the GitHub README page for the skill.

Now available Amazon S3 Tables managed migration is available today in US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Mumbai, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo), and Europe (Frankfurt, Ireland, Stockholm) Regions. At launch, the capability supports AWS Glue-registered Hive tables stored in Parquet format within the same AWS account and AWS Region. If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, or troubleshoot about this new feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool.

Try it in the Amazon S3 console today and send feedback to AWS re:Post for Amazon S3 or through your usual AWS Support contacts.

Channy is a Lead Blogger of AWS News Blog and Principal Developer Advocate for AWS Cloud. As an open web enthusiast and blogger at heart, he loves community-driven learning and sharing of technology.
