#10154. Investors Dish on New Startups & What They'd Back Next

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

The cybersecurity market is difficult to predict, but a glimpse into the annual DataTribe Challenge shows what's trending and what's not.

Startups have been battling it out on the DataTribe Challenge stage for the past nine years, but this year's event still saw some firsts.

A cyber insurance company made the top five finalists, and attendees got to vote for their favorite finalist with the People's Choice Award. Both of these firsts highlighted how people are looking for answers to new risks introduced by artificial intelligence (AI).

The DataTribe Challenge, hosted by the cyber startup foundry and venture capital firm, is one of the signature events of its annual Cyber Innovation Conference. The meeting, which took place in October, aims to unite the cybersecurity ecosystem, from founders to investors and — since it's held in Washington, D.C. — some policymakers, too.

Cybersecurity conferences pop up on the calendar more frequently these days; that momentum is important "to keep the information fresh" as the industry and threat landscape transforms rapidly, explains Robert Ackerman, co-founder and managing partner at DataTribe. Game-changing incidents that require sharing information emerge almost daily now, he adds, pointing to the more recent PHP2Shell vulnerability that attackers jumped on and proved difficult for organizations to patch.

Related:AI Agents as Insider Threats: Inside Microsoft's Bet on a Unified Security Stack

An expanding pool of cyber-related startups is also driving industry transformation. Nearly 700 rising companies submitted entries or were considered for this year's Challenge, which pairs startups with mentors before they pitch to judges who crown the winner.

As Ackerman and Leo Scott, managing director at DataTribe, filtered down the contestants into the top five list, they found it interesting that many of the startups focused on the dynamics around how AI is driving the market as organizations transition from AI adoption to managing the technology.

Some companies had a more direct tie. This year's winner, Sondera, aims to solve agentic architecture challenges like improving guardrails and security controls.

But cyber insurance company Navasana, which made the top five for the first time ever, was an example of a company indirectly focused on AI. Instead, Navasana launched to handle new risk dynamics that AI created, speaking to broader industry trends.

At one level, everyone's been thinking about cyber insurance for a long time, Ackerman adds. But looking at how policies are written in cyber, he has noticed a shift in risk as they add disclaimers and exemptions.

"What makes cyber attractive from an investment perspective is you never really solve it," Ackerman tells Dark Reading. "You never mitigate risk fully. It's a very hard puzzle piece to put together. The hope with AI is you get this real-time data to understand posture and environments. I still think there's a real lag though because insurance doesn't operate in real time."

Related:RemoteThreat Bets Security Teams Need to Test What Happens After Defenses Fail

Navasna marked the first cyber insurer to make the top five due to the end-to-end, continuous services it offers in a space where organizations manage such a broad umbrella of needs. As an early-stage investor, Ackerman is not looking to "feed the consensus machine" but wants to anticipate what's next. In venture capital, that's hard right now, he adds. Still, the conference and DataTribe Challenge look to showcase companies that are currently topical and addressing real needs.

Navasana is an example of more emerging needs, says Ackerman, while Sondera is in the "sweet spot" by addressing current challenges, as attacks make it clear that agentic AI needs more guardrails.

Sondera is "doing some really interesting things in that space that are well beyond what others are doing," says Scott. What resonated with the audience was how much research Sondera put into understanding what organizations actually need, he adds.

Rather than operating at the rule level, Sondera's approach starts at a much higher level, beginning with the human's underlying intent and what they're trying to achieve. Then organizations can work with users to generate the specific rules.

Related:Deception by Design: CISA's Guide to Tricking Cybercriminals

It's increasingly evident that agents can be very persistent and act independently, so control is essential. That may be one reason that Sondera took home the trophy — people really understand the problems they've seen in their environments, Ackerman adds.

Ackerman sees two timelines in cybersecurity right now. Discussions over the past 18 to 24 months centered around concerns that offense has more of an advantage as attackers use AI to become faster and more advanced. Defense will catch up, but he believes that what the industry knows about cybersecurity — how to protect systems, and layer defense and zero trust — still work.

"We just have to apply them efficiently all the time," he urges.

The other timeline is what happens after 24 months. What issues will emerge then? Those are the core concepts, like protecting Internet infrastructure, that DataTribe wants to showcase in these events.

And the long-term lens is what the investors are betting on right now.

"It's not about what is going to get picked up in the next three to four months," Ackerman says. The startups and investments "have more of a five- to 10-year time horizon," he says.

One of Ackerman's favorite pastimes once startups wrap up their Challenge pitches is to walk around the floor while everyone's waiting for the judges to cast their votes and announce the winner. He considers the disconnect: He has spent weeks with the companies, coaching and prepping, yet the audience full of people from across the industry only get to know them for 20 minutes.

That's what makes storytelling so important, not just the cybersecurity and technical points. Learning what the judges and audience think of these companies is important for DataTribe, as well as for the startups which is the true value of cyber competitions.

For Ackerman, it's always great to hear that people had been thinking about a problem one of the contestants was trying to solve, but no one had developed a solution.

"That's validating," Ackerman says. "We're sort of directionally correct, which maybe in this market is the best you can do on any given day."

Arielle spent the last decade working as a reporter, transitioning from human interest stories to covering all things cybersecurity related in 2020. Now, as a features writer for Dark Reading, she delves into the security problems enterprises face daily, providing context and actionable steps. She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

She previously lived in Florida where she wrote for the Tampa Bay Times before returning to Boston where her cybersecurity career took off at TechTarget SearchSecurity. When she's not writing about cybersecurity, she pursues personal projects that include a mystery novel and poetry collection.

The Fine Print: The following comments are owned by whoever posted them. We are not responsible for them in any way.

The license can be legally worked around:

1. Have one AI agent document the code fully by explaining how it works in plain english2. Copy that new documentation to an entirely segregated second agent3. Instruct the new agent to write brand new code according to the documentation

It's unlikely this will be done for all OSS projects since the result usually has bugs and inconsistencies. But spend a week or two doing passes over it for improvement and you get a functional reimplementation. (What license that can use will depend on how the law around AI code shakes out in the future)

I would say as soon as even one line of the original code was in the training data, this becomes a copyright violation. "Clean room" means nothing of the inner workings of the original besides the spec ever made it to the implementation team. And you have to be able to prove that.

First off, you can always just use a LLM with an open training dataset (OLMo, Pythia, etc) to prove that the data isn't in it, and have that handle the "clean" side of the equation.

Secondly, you are under the mistaken impression that a LLM that has been exposed (which, BTW, does not mean "memorized", or even any rough understandings of the workings - ask the LLM (ideally an abliterated one to avoid refusals) to reproduce the original code verbatim, it'll almost certainly fail badly) automatically fails in such a suit. It does not. There is no such thing as "homeopathic copyright contamination". Copyvio requires substantial similarity. LLMs will tend to have common algos memorized, but those are the very things that tend to be simultaneously not copyrightable.

The cleanroom is an evidentiary shield, not a pillar of copyright law. If you can prove that the cleanroom team had no access to the original, then you can prove that they didn't copy it, and potentially get summary judgement. If you can't prove that, that doesn't mean that it's not copyvio, it just means that you instead have to focus on substantial-similarity defenses. Access without substantial similiarity is not copyvio. If you read an open-source codebase, close it, and then later write a new program purely on your own that looks nothing like the original, you had "access", but still did not infringe. The same applies to LLMs - but even moreso, because humans are much better at learning from brief, limited exposures to content than LLMs are. A court will usually apply an "Abstraction-Filtration-Comparison" test - they break the code down into layers (source code, parameters, architecture, algos, etc) (abstraction), remove everything that copyright law does not protect (ideas and common algos, things where there's only a limited number of ways to possibly do it, etc) (filtration), and then compare the creative expression that remains to see if there exists sufficient similarity to count as infringement. It is highly unlikely that a LLM-implemented version will fail that.

(That said, you're talking about a long, expensive legal battle if you get to that point, so you obviously prefer to be able to get summary judgement if you can)

Oh, also, as pointed out further downthread [slashdot.org], any LLM with a training cutoff before the license change date is pretty much assured to be okay for use in a cleanroom implementation. Copyright holders cannot make retroactive copyright changes, and open source licenses generally explicitly grant rights in perpetuity anyway. The threat would be new code. But since the cleanroom side has never seen that new code (it was released after the training date), it remains untainted. And training cutoffs generally lag

You have the workings of the law backwards. The litigant is the one who has to do the proving. The defendant doesn't have to prove they didn't access it, because that is called "proving a negative" which is impossible. This is why they don't arrest someone for murder and start the trial with "OK, defendant, prove you didn't commit the murder or we are going to execute you for murder." Sometimes you do have to prove your innocence, because you invoked a strong defense that is only available if you can prove it.

In civil law, the preponderance of evidence wins. If I accuse you of being a poopy-pants, and your only defense is something you would have to prove (self defense, etc), and you fail to prove it, then I already won. That's why lawyers say things like, "My client did not kill that man, and even if he did, he had a permissible reason!" It sounds stupid if you don't understand the law.

The license can be legally worked around:

1. Have one AI agent document the code fully by explaining how it works in plain english 2. Copy that new documentation to an entirely segregated second agent 3. Instruct the new agent to write brand new code according to the documentation

It's unlikely this will be done for all OSS projects since the result usually has bugs and inconsistencies. But spend a week or two doing passes over it for improvement and you get a functional reimplementation. (What license that can use will depend on how the law around AI code shakes out in the future)

A and B in this case are both black boxes. The way clean room protocol works is to gaurentee that the surfaces of A and B are identical. Everything you can see, looks exactly the same. If however, you open up the boxes, you will very likely find entirely different contents that just happen to produce the same surface behaviour. If you were to clean room something, and produce identical A and B - i.e. not only is the behaviour exactly the same, but the code is exactly the same too, you would *very* likely find a court taking an extremely sceptical view of the idea that your clean room was in any way clean. That is, you'd still get found liable for the copyright infringement.

The purpose of the clean room is not merely to provide plausible deniability, it is to provide *actual* deniability. The thing you plead to the judge is not "Your Honor, we didn't look at the code, we pinky promise", it is "Your Honor, this can't be copyright infringement, look, the implementations are entirely different." The implementations necessarily will be different because without the system being trivially simple to the point of uncopyrightability, there are so many different ways to implement the same behaviour, that the chance of selecting the exact same one will be basically 0.

While your argument has some merits, there are counter arguments.

If I as a company hold patents, I will likely avoid GPLv3 code like the plague. I don't want to accidentally give up the rights to my patents because I happened to touch some GPLv3 code that was in vaguely the same area.

A good example of this would be Apple. They dropped bash for zsh, dropped gcc and wrote clang instead, dropped gdb and wrote lldb instead, dropped samba and wrote SMBClient and SMBX instead, dropped GNU tar and used libarchive/bsdtar instead, dropped GNU rsync and used openrsync instead,

- For zsh they appear to have contributed relatively little code upstream, but that's maybe expected for a mature project that is maintaining stability at this point rather than adding exciting new features.- For gcc/gdb, they appear to have voluntarily given away *massive* amounts of code, clang and lldb simply didn't exist before Apple created them and open sourced them.- For openrsync despite only having adopted it last year, they've contributed quite a lot of feature parity code to it (not just macOS compatibility code)- For bsdgrep, it seems like you may be more right - it seems like Apple prefers to maintain a fork there rather than substantially contribute upstream.- Samba seems to be a mixed bag - they went from a GPLv3 implementation to a BSD/APSLv2 client, and a proprietary server. The client they are contributing code actively. The server they're keeping all to themselves.- For libarchive, it looks like Apple's made a ton of fixes, and contributed them upstream, same for bsdtar.

WebKit didn't replace a GPLed project, but Apple has written about 80% of the code in the repository, and licensed it mostly as BSD (with some licensed as LGPL to comply with KHTML's original licensing). BSD is their default license for new WebKit code.

With CUPS/OpenPrinting the story is similar - they adopted a GPLv2 project, relicensed it more permissively, and then proceeded to contribute massive amounts of code.

There's a bunch more cases of the same thing going on.   - XNU - weak copyleft licensed, continues to upstream changes   - Swift - permissively licensed, continues to upstream changes   - libdispatch - permissively licensed, continues to upstream changes   - mDNSResponder - permissively licensed, continues to upstream changes   - dyld - weak copyleft licensed, continues to upstream changes   - launchd - weak copyleft licensed, continues to upstream changes   - Swift Foundation - permissively licensed, continues to upstream changes   - bsd libc - BSDed apple contirbutes heavily upstream   - OpenSSH - BSDed, apple contributes upstream   - curl - BSDed, apple contributes upstream   - sqlite - public domain, apple contributes upstream   - libxml and libxslt - apple adopted them, and actively maintain them.   - Heimdal - Apple appears to have forked it, the license remains BSD in their fork, and all their changes are there.   - OpenPAM - looks like apple keeps its changes to itself here.

The overall picture is that despite all these BSDed projects, Apple in particular still contributes code upstream heavily. This is of course one anecdotal example, but at least from it, it doesn't appear that the motivating factor for changes being contributed upstream is being forced to with a copyleft license. Instead, it looks much more likely that it's simply that having the community all work together on single, standardised components is much more efficient for the industry than everyone having their own implementations, with incompatible quirks, bugs etc.

They also aren't exclusive. Asahi Linux could make parts of their code available to other projects under their choice of license on a "by request" basis. It depend on whether, e.g., the BSD project needs things available that Asahi considers too significant. That would still mean the scrapers (What's a better word for that?) would be scraping GPL licensed code.

#10150. Datacenters, Elon Musk, and AI are all on the chopping block once Congress changes hands in 2027

Rage, rage against the dying of the right

Hey, did you hear about those elections in the US this past week?

The Democratic party has seized control of Congress and state governments around the country. It's easy to see this entirely as a rebuke of Trump and his policies, but blowback against AI, datacenters, and the tech industry played a role too, if the past week of chaos in markets and Silicon Valley is any indication.

Join host Brandon Vigliarolo, El Reg Editor In Chief Matt Rosoff, and special guest, senior reporter at The Verge, Elizabeth Lopatto, to talk about what the winds of political change mean for the tech industry.

Hey everyone, and welcome to the latest episode of The Register's Kettle Podcast. I'm your host, Reg Reporter Brandon Vigliarolo, and hey, chances are you've heard about those elections we had in the US this week. The Democratic Party dealt a pretty hearty rebuke to Donald Trump, Republicans, and the MAGA movement, with Dems winning elections in states that haven't gone blue in decades. Now it's easy to see this as a blowback against Trump and Republican politics. There's a lot of indication that the tech industry was kind of on the ballot this year, too.

After all, they cozied up hard to Trump in his first two years in office in a bid to push AI and promote datacenter projects, and people have been none too happy about any of that. With me to discuss the elections and what they mean for Silicon Valley is Reg editor-in-chief Matt Rosoff and a special guest this week, senior reporter from The Verge, Elizabeth Lopatto. Thank you both for coming on, and welcome, Liz.

I was so glad we could make this work. So let's start off by dissecting the degree to which AI datacenters and attitudes toward the tech industry in general sort of played a role in this election. I mean, were those major elements in the Democratic sweep or just part of the equation?

I think they were part of the equation. I think first and foremost people were pissed off about the corruption. And second, people were pissed off about ICE. Having people snatched from your community is the sort of thing that kind of sticks with you. So I think those were probably the two biggest issues. But the corruption is not totally separate from the tech industry, given the way that the tech industry has been cozying up with Donald Trump, the fact that Elon Musk and DOGE were cruising through the federal government, destroying stuff. So those things are related.

And then obviously there's the datacenter stuff, which is universally unpopular, not the only bipartisan issue in the US right now, but certainly a big one. So it's in there, I think.

I thought it was interesting that of something like 47 anti-datacenter initiatives on local ballots, 45 of them passed and only one failed. So that seems to me to be some indication that people at least don't like whatever these things are being shoved down their throats, which is funny because two years ago nobody knew what a datacenter was.

I think that there are sort of two things happening here, right? The first is that a lot of these datacenters have been popping up in people's communities without a robust public comment period. There have been a lot of NDAs being used and backroom deals. And I think most people don't like that stuff anyway. But add to that how frustrated I think a lot of people are with the tech industry right now. And suddenly this is the avatar of the tech industry doing a bunch of things that people don't like. And they can't get rid of Elon Musk. They can't pry Sundar Pichai out of his CEO role. There's not a lot you can really do, but you can stop the datacenter.

They can't get rid of AI results in search.

I think that's just an expression of that frustration, right?

Yeah, and I think the industry at least has to see it a little bit, right? Because I think it was maybe the day after the elections, OpenAI came out right away and was like, "Hey, you know what we're going to do? We're going to really try to be better civic citizens in our communities. We're going to stop signing NDAs." And then they're also trying to rebrand datacenters as "compute campuses" to make them more attractive, as these aren't just big warehouses where we're doing AI processing. We're trying to do all this other stuff there, too. It just seemed like there's very much an awareness that, "Oh wow, this may have been a bit of a blowback against us, or at the very least, something we're going to need to adapt to in a new political cycle."

I found it really interesting: I saw a study yesterday, maybe the day before, that said 41 percent of active datacenter projects are in states that Democrats took control of this election cycle, including Texas and my home state of Michigan, where Democrats didn't just capture federal offices, but state-level legislatures and offices as well. That could potentially mean that a lot of datacenter projects are going to be slowed or stalled completely in the next few years. Is there any indication that that could happen, you think?

Well, maybe. I think that the frustration with datacenters has really been growing over the last two years. And you've seen things like Project Jupiter in New Mexico where the locals didn't even know who was coming in, right? There was total secrecy. And then as soon as people figured out what was going on, they made the moves they could to start blocking access to power.

And so I think anybody who's politically ambitious picks up on that and says, "Okay, this is a way to really channel some populist frustration. I can probably ride this." So there's that part of it. But I also think these people got elected a couple days ago. And in some cases, I think this was a race in Iowa, the Democrat had dropped out because he was sick and got elected anyway. So there's a certain amount of just pure rage being expressed here.

I've heard a lot of people saying that it wasn't even necessarily a vote for Democrats in many cases as it was a vote against Republicans and their policies.

Yeah, so I think that using that as a way to consolidate power is a smart move, right? So you see even before election night's out, there are these statements like "lawyer up." And  I imagine investigating DOGE is going to be super popular because a lot of people lost their jobs, right? Separately from all of the people who died because USAID stopped. I think that there is just a real political will for investigations, for some of this stuff becoming public. And specifically in Texas, you have these emails between Elon Musk and Greg Abbott that have been really heavily redacted. You want a fast and easy political win, you unredact those emails.

And I can't imagine that the new governor of Texas isn't going to — leave it to the Democrats to take something like this and completely squander it by sitting on their thumbs and trying to compromise. So part of me is like, "Wow, what a mandate you have. Let's see how badly you mess this up." I'm hoping that isn't the case. I'm hoping that we see some actual drive from Democrats to do things like unredact those emails. Give voters a reason to actually say you did something good, right? It's easy, like we were talking a couple of minutes ago again about datacenters kind of being a scapegoat for the tech industry right now. And Elon Musk is easily that as well, right? He's the person you can point to and say, "Look at this asshole," and all the things he's been doing, especially in Texas, right?  I'm hoping that they do take that and run with it. He's been—

I think it's interesting. Texas didn't just elect a couple Democrats. It was a Democratic slate from top to bottom. And I think a lot of Trump voters showed up specifically to vote against Republicans this time. So I don't know if that's all—some of that is related to Paxton being on the ballot and the sort of known history of corruption that he's shown and the fact that the MAGA movement backed him so boldly. But some of it is, I think, Elon being so loud and so belligerent and charging in and saying we're just going to do whatever we want and get out of the way. And there has kind of been an arrogance among the tech industry and the tech executives for the past few years, but I think it's really become loud in the last couple of years. And I think to some degree, datacenters are a backlash against that and some of the ire directed towards Elon Musk is a backlash against that.

We all live in the same society, right? We've been hearing Sam Altman out here like, "Well, some people are going to die because of AI, and we're just going to have to accept that as a cost." And it's like, well, Sam, is that you? Are you planning to die for AI? Because it kind of sounds like you're talking about me and I don't like it.

Right. Yeah, it's the same sort of thing with wars. Some of you are going to have to die. Me and my kids, we're fine. Politicians are never going to send their sons and daughters to fight these wars.

I was recently in Washington and talking to some folks there who are involved with federal agencies and the difference between how Silicon Valley and tech companies and startups think of and use AI. I mean, it's $10,000 token budgets per developer and everybody's using agents to automate workflows and everything. And in Washington, it's like, this went way too far, way too fast. How do we stop it? And meanwhile, now AI is uncovering flaws and vulnerabilities in all of this software and all of these online services and web servers that we've been using for 25 years. So we've got to figure out how to patch all of that. We've got people entering confidential information into Chinese models like DeepSeek. So I think that the tech industry got way ahead of itself and the rest of the country is just starting to catch up. And yeah, maybe in five or ten years we will all be using agents and the infrastructure will have been built out to a point where the costs make sense and the ROI makes sense. But right now there's just this huge disconnect it seems between tech insiders in Silicon Valley and how people actually are using the technology today. So there may be some of that as well.

I think that there is a bubble, an intellectual bubble around Silicon Valley where all of these people are talking to each other and hanging out on X and assuring each other they're the smartest. And they're saying things like, "Oh, this is going to totally change your life." And the normal person who is using ChatGPT to try to replace their search engine is noticing that ChatGPT kind of hallucinates and it's not it's not that good. And there is this impulse on the part of these evangelists to be like, "Well, that's your problem because you don't know how to properly prompt the AI." And it's like, uh-uh, that's not how you get people to adopt technology. If you remember the internet, when the World Wide Web first happened, people didn't start using it until it made sense for them to use it. There were people who liked it because tech was their hobby and they thought it was a cool toy. But it wasn't until there was a reason for ordinary people to start using it that ordinary people started using it. Even online shopping, which I think is one of the very obvious use cases for the internet and was very early on, didn't catch up to in-person shopping for 20 years. So all of this hyperventilating around AI and how it's going to change the entire society and eliminate everybody's job and all of this other stuff, I feel like it's really misplaced. And it's not just misplaced because it underestimates the experience the rest of us are having with AI, which is frankly not that great. You're going to replace my job with this? Good luck.

Also there's just this sort of reality check. If you think about what AI is, it does certain kinds of intellectual work really well. Programming, for instance. Mathematics. But those are not things that require human relationships or resources outside of a computer. Almost all of the rest of us are involved in industries where those things are required. And so, how do you fit AI into that is a really different question. So there are blinders on in Silicon Valley and you can even see it — I live in Oakland and as soon as you leave San Francisco and go to Oakland, you start talking to normal people and they're just like, "I don't see the point of this AI. Why are we doing this?"

Yeah, I mean most people I talk to agree it's kind of useless to a degree, right? The way I think of it is it's almost like it's replaced Wikipedia for me, right? It's replaced — it hasn't even replaced search, it's replaced Wikipedia. It's the place I can go to get a basic overview of something to then do my own research because I can't trust the information that a Google search overview gives me, but at least it's going to maybe surface some resources that I didn't know were there, right?

It's good for summarizing certain kinds of documents. I do hear about it being used in the legal profession pretty extensively. So you don't have to read every line of every briefing. You have to check its work, because sometimes it makes stuff up or invents citations. I think it's gotten better at that.

You know, it's good for things like cleaning up text and it is good for programming. I hear a lot of programmers saying, "Hey, we were using this internal software or we were using a couple of our licenses of a particular enterprise piece of software to accomplish one very specific task and it was too expensive and we vibe coded a replacement for it over the weekend and it actually works. It's good enough. And we don't have to pay enterprise vendor X ten thousand dollars a month or something anymore."

Yeah, just make sure it's not exposed to the internet or next thing you know.

Right. It's not handling any sensitive data that you care about. Right, exactly.

Yeah, I mean I generally think of AI, at least in my experience, because I tend to not use it actually. I have moved to Kagi so that I can just get the old Google search circa 2012, primary source document type deal, because Google search sucks so much.

I think of it as being kind of a shitty intern, right? I occasionally use AI to transcribe my interviews and it's good enough. I have to double check it. I've got to listen to the part that I want to quote to make sure that it got it right, because sometimes it really doesn't. But it beats doing the transcription myself. So I have this kind of shitty intern now that I have to keep an eye on. And that's fine because that can be time saving if you need to change a format in an Excel spreadsheet. That feels like it's about the level at which the shitty intern does okay. But anything more serious than that, and I'm like, "I don't know about this. I think I'd better do it if it's going to be done right."

But is it worth $1,000 a month or $10,000 a month?

With the election and at the same time the finances of Anthropic becoming clearer and clearer and these increasing commitments. They filed their S-1 at precisely the right time when they had this growth spike and they were profitable for one quarter and then you looked at Q3 and lo and behold, they're back in the red again. I just wonder if some of this infrastructure buildout is going to be stalled and how that sort of affects pricing and how that affects competitiveness versus open weights models and those kinds of things. I don't know, I know Liz, you've looked at some of the financing in the industry, particularly around the CoreWeaves of the world, the neo-clouds, what do you think's going on there?

I think that those are only going to live as long as Nvidia wants them to live. You look at CoreWeave and it just doesn't make sense as a business. It's paying too much for debt to make sense as a business. There's just no way to get out from under that debt. And so, as long as Nvidia is willing to continue bailing them out, because it is basically an Nvidia client state – Nvidia is the reason that they were able to have an IPO at all. So as long as Nvidia is willing to bail them out, sure, they're going to continue being a going concern. But if you look at the bond market, people are pretty nervous about those bonds and I think they're right to be nervous. We saw here today – today is Friday – we saw Microsoft pulling out of a deal with Oracle for datacenter capacity for compute. The excuse that they gave was that Oracle had old chips. And maybe that is part of the decision-making, I don't know. I don't live in Microsoft. But it's also possible that Microsoft, who is building its own datacenters, is like, "Well, I don't need to give money to a competitor. We'll figure out something smarter to do in the meantime. And then once our datacenters are built, we'll just use our own."

And that has been the case for all of those neo-clouds for a while now, that their clients are about to become their competitors as the buildout happens. So if the buildout slows down, then every existing datacenter becomes more valuable. And so maybe that gives CoreWeave a lease on life. But maybe not, because who knows what's going to happen with the interest rates.

And how do you feel about Oracle? Their borrowing is getting more and more expensive and it seems like people are sort of walking away. Could Oracle actually be in some kind of real financial trouble?

I think that Oracle has enough going on in its legacy businesses that I doubt bankruptcy is on the table, but I could be wrong. I do think that they have made a really big bet on AI generally and OpenAI specifically, and I'm not sure that OpenAI was a super smart bet. Again, depending on how the buildout goes and what comes online and what doesn't, it might turn out that Oracle can turn around and flip that compute to somebody else if OpenAI isn't good for their money. It might also be the case that Oracle can use that compute itself for its other businesses. I am a little less worried about Oracle than I am about the pure play neo-clouds that basically pivoted from bitcoin mining and have no other business.

We've been talking about that almost weekly, because I feel like so often the Kettle ends up being about AI, right? Because that's the big topic right now. And almost every week we mention the fact that Oracle, Google, Microsoft, these companies are going to be fine if all this AI financing and circular investing starts to shrivel up, right? Who's not going to be fine is OpenAI and Anthropic. And the neo-clouds, right? They're all making these huge bets on AI and they have no other business to fall back on. It's not like someone's going to try to fall back on bitcoin at this point, I don't think.

Certainly not at this point. I mean, just looking at looking at what bitcoin did this week, I feel like it's not super valuable to be a bitcoin miner right now.

Let's talk about Elon Musk. Is this sort of the beginning of the bursting of the Musk worship bubble? Are we sort of seeing him lose his influence and power a little bit?

I know Liz wrote an article on all of the things he could have spent whatever it was, $500 million on.

Obviously he doesn't really know how to have a lot of fun, but the fact that he lost so completely everywhere that he bet, and the fact that Democrats are starting to whisper about indictments and investigations, is this sort of the end of his reign as the king of tech?

It's a good question. One of the things that's been interesting to me is that the Twitter acquisition really made the public turn on Elon Musk, right? That was when people were like, "Is he a genius? Because that doesn't seem like the move of a — why is he doing this?" And then of course, following that, the stuff with the Trump administration, people started protesting Tesla, like he kind of skunked his brand. So there is the popular view of Elon Musk, which is that this guy sucks. And then there is Silicon Valley, where for some reason he is still held in really high esteem. And I don't know why that is, except that maybe he's very good at raising money.

But that's real and that's still a thing. And so I am interested to see what happens here because if these sweetheart deals do start getting unearthed and we start seeing some of the private correspondence and like, "Oops, there might have been a little bit of bribery here and there," or "Oops, there might have been something else that was quasi-legal," those are things that are significant that become risks to his companies because they are so closely tied to him, right? For a long time, Tesla didn't have to buy advertising because Elon Musk's Twitter account was good enough. You know, and so you live with Elon Musk, you die with Elon Musk. That's just what it is. He can delete all the tweets he wants, but it doesn't change what we all saw over the last two years. And so I do think that there is a very real chance that he's got Texas where he's got an attorney general who entered basically with a mandate to investigate him. He has a senator who is like, "Hey, I'm proof that Texas can't be bought."

He's got a governor who isn't that fond of him either. And there's that. And then broadly across the country, again, this man is unpopular, so he's a great target for investigations.

I think we are looking at a real change of his fortunes. And whether that will stick or not is anybody's guess. Because one of the things that has certainly been true for the entire time that I have covered Elon Musk, which at this point is more than a decade, is that you discover which laws have teeth and which ones do not. Turns out copyright law really matters. Turns out the Chancery Court of Delaware counts. That one matters too.

I don't know about the SEC. I don't know that that's real.

Or like when he was smoking weed on camera and then got a slap on the wrist. I guess our drug laws around contractors, if you're rich enough, they don't matter. So there's a real sense in which we're going to find out exactly which laws apply to Elon Musk and which ones do not.

I also think it was interesting his purchase of Twitter and the way he sort of tilted the platform or the way the platform got tilted, so it kind of became this center-right, right-wing, Silicon Valley echo chamber. And I think a lot of people were surprised by the election results on Tuesday. As a result of that, if you're only on Twitter and talking to your very rich friends in VC, you might not actually know what real people think.

Yeah, there was a whole story I read about Bluesky basically saying, "Hey, we were right the whole time. Twitter's become this echo chamber of right-wing thought that doesn't realize that the rest of the world is a little pissed off at the tech industry." It's been kind of—

I think there isn't what Twitter used to be, which was where everyone was, right? After Musk bought Twitter, I think the social networks really fragmented. So I'm not going to sit here and — I like Bluesky, I use Bluesky. I don't think it's necessarily representative of the entire country. I think it is representative of a lot of people who are left-wing. And I think it can be useful in that way, in the same way that the left-wing blogosphere was useful in the early 2000s. That's a great way to organize, it's a great way to strategize. Fantastic. But similarly, I'm watching with a lot of schadenfreude the right-wing infighting on Twitter right now. They did not see this coming. And to be honest, neither did I. I knew there was going to be a blue wave; I did not think that my home state of Iowa was going to elect a bunch of Democrats. I didn't see Texas coming.

Yeah, no. I mean I figured [Texas Senator Elect James] Talarico was maybe a toss-up, right? But he beat [Republican Attorney General Ken] Paxton handily. You know, it was insane to see the degree to which people really blew back on Trump and, like we were saying, on the tech industry too, to a degree.

And if you think about the differences between Bluesky and X, there's another significant one, which is that X has an algorithm that is being tweaked by Elon Musk to show Elon Musk things he likes. And Bluesky, there are a bunch of algorithms that you can adopt, but I'm just using the same reverse chronology timeline that I have used forever on social media. And that again It's not going to show me just things I want to see. And so like again, like there are uses for algorithms, there are uses for filters, but you have to keep in mind that if you're being shown things you like, you're being shown things you like.

I think it's going to be interesting to see kind of what happens in the next — well, it's going to be at least a few months before things start happening, right? Because the new politicians who've been elected don't really take office until the beginning of the year. But once that happens, will the Democrats actually manage to do anything with this mandate they've been given? Will Elon Musk face some degree of accountability and will datacenter projects be stalled? Don't know.

Could happen, might not. Either way, we're gonna be here on the kettle to talk about it and we hope that you'll join us. Thanks for coming on, guys, and we'll talk soon. ®

#10144. Japanese homeware giant pulls online store after cloud breach puts 7.7M records at risk

No reopening date as orders face delays and some customers are told to refuse deliveries to cancel purchases

Japanese electronics giant Iris Ohyama has taken down its online store after discovering that attackers may have accessed the personal information of 7.7 million customers, leaving shoppers unable to place orders.

The retailer, which sells everything from home appliances and furniture to pet supplies, first disclosed the incident on October 29, a day after discovering a suspicious file on a third-party cloud service used by its Iris Plaza ecommerce operation.

Iris Plaza immediately suspended its website and associated systems and began investigating, subsequently confirming unauthorized access.

Iris Ohyama has since revealed that the potentially compromised cloud environment contained personal information belonging to approximately 5.8 million registered customers, including former members, and another 1.9 million people who had purchased products without creating an account or participated in promotional campaigns.

The potentially exposed information includes names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, dates of birth, gender, and passwords, although the company says the exact information at risk varies between customers.

Some of that data, including passwords, was encrypted, but Iris Ohyama hasn't explained what protection was used. It has advised customers who reused their Iris Plaza passwords elsewhere to change them, presumably before someone else gets the opportunity.

There is some good news for anyone who has handed over their credit card details, as the retailer says it didn't store payment information in the affected cloud service and that it hasn't been compromised.

It remains unclear whether the attackers actually made off with any personal information. In its FAQ, Iris Plaza says it is still investigating the possibility of a data leak and has yet to establish the full extent of the intrusion.

Meanwhile, Iris Plaza's website is still down, and the company isn't saying when it'll be back. Orders are also taking longer to ship, while customers trying to cancel a purchase have been told they may have to turn the delivery driver away if their parcel arrives before the cancellation is processed.

Fortunately for anyone desperate to buy a new rice cooker, Iris Plaza's stores on Rakuten, Yahoo! Shopping, and auPAY Market are still operating. The company says it has found no evidence that those stores were affected.

Iris Ohyama has reported the incident to Japanese authorities and says it will contact potentially affected customers individually. It has also warned shoppers to watch out for phishing emails, fraudulent calls, and fake websites impersonating the retailer.

The company has yet to identify the cloud provider involved, explain how the attackers got in, or establish whether any of those 7.7 million records actually left its systems. ®

#10141. Who can still open your files after they've left?

EVENT: Peers compare how they find the shares nobody closed, over dinner with The Register in London.

Someone left your organisation in the spring. Can they still open the project share? Most infrastructure leads would want to check before answering, and that pause is the subject of a dinner The Register and LucidLink are hosting for senior technology, infrastructure, and data leaders at the Covent Garden Hotel on Tuesday 24 November. Joe Fay of The Register is in the chair.

The trouble is the copies. A busy folder lives on the file server, in a sync client, on a couple of laptops and in the share set up for an agency last year, and each copy carries its own permissions. Locking down one leaves the others as they were. Then there's the tool a team built for itself because the approved one was too slow, which IT may not know exists.

The evening runs under the Chatham House Rule, and that's what makes it worth going. People say what actually happened in their own shop and how they caught it. Alan Marshall, Strategic Director, EMEA at LucidLink, joins a small group of peers round the table. Nobody presents.

The talk moves on to unstructured data that keeps growing, the duplicate storage that comes with it, and how to get access back under control without throwing out the storage and governance you've already paid for.

Drinks are at 6.30pm and dinner around one table runs until 9pm. Places are limited.

Request a place at the 24 November dinner

Places go by invitation and each one is confirmed personally.

#10138. Outlook.com bounces legit emails as Microsoft's authentication crackdown goes sideways

Missing DMARC or wobbly SPF means your mail may be treated as suspicious

A validation error has stopped Outlook.com from accepting legitimate emails.

The problem appears widespread and, according to reports from affected users, can result in non-delivery reports with error codes related to SPF (Sender Policy Framework) validation failures.

Other users have reported errors highlighting a lack of DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance) information.

The troubles began at the end of last week and appear to be the result of Microsoft tightening the rules (or at least attempting to do so) for accepting emails. The company's consumer email services are affected, and it appears that if a domain doesn't have working SPF or if it has a missing DMARC record, then Outlook.com and its ilk will treat it as suspicious and not accept emails.

The rules are designed to deal with spam, bulk senders, and the like. In 2025, Microsoft announced new rules designed to strengthen email authentication for domains sending more than 5,000 emails per day. In addition to DMARC and SPF compliance, DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) was also required.

Although this seemed like a good idea to ward off spammers, small senders now appear to be affected. According to complainants in the Outlook forum, a single email with just one line might now be rejected. Furthermore, Microsoft has not issued any advisory to customers explaining how the rules have changed.

Although some customers insist their DMARC, SPF, and DKIM settings are compliant, many more have reported that once they set them to Microsoft's requirments, email began flowing once more.

SPF must pass for the sending domain (the domain's DNS record should accurately list authorized IP addresses/hosts). DKIM must pass to validate email integrity and authenticity. DMARC must have at least p=none and align with either SPF or DKIM (preferably both).

The Register asked the Windows giant for more information, but we have yet to receive a response.

To make matters worse, the glitch also appears to be intermittent. A resend attempt might succeed following a rejection. To compound the situation, the rejection error message may also be vague about what caused the bounce in the first place.

A moderator in Microsoft's support forum acknowledged the bug and said it was "classified as a service degradation."

"Microsoft is actively investigating the underlying cause of this email delivery issue, and engineering teams are actively analyzing service telemetry and customer-provided data to identify the source of the issue."

Still. It could be worse. Earlier today, several users in Europe, the Middle East, and Africa were affected by another Microsoft whoopsie – a "recent service change" that caused some connections to be abruptly terminated. Outlook on the web, as well as the Purview and Defender portals were all affected.

Microsoft reverted the change in the Exchange Online front-end infrastructure, and all was well.

It has yet to say what else, if anything, might have changed in its email services to cause legitimate messages to bounce back. ®

Microsoft has confirmed that this was a fault. In its incident report (EX1545193), the company wrote: "A recent update to the spam enforcement rules caused email messages to be incorrectly marked and blocked, which led to impact."It also said it would review its update procedures. This will be of great comfort to customers who found legitimate emails rejected by Microsoft's servers as a result of the latest whoopsie.

Thanks to Aliaksandr Markau at DMARKOFF for the tip.

#10136. PapRAT Cyber-Espionage Campaign Leaves a 'Bitter' Taste in South Asia

Organizations in the region face growing cyberattacks from the known India-linked threat group, which leverages legitimate Windows functionality in three distinct attack chains.

A known South Asian cyber-espionage group has been targeting organizations across the region with attacks designed to compromise Windows systems, establish persistence, and give attackers remote control over infected machines using custom malware.

The attacks, attributed "with high confidence" to the South Asian threat group known as Bitter (aka TA397), involve three distinct infection chains and demonstrate the group's expanding malware capabilities, according to new research from FortiGuard Labs published today.

Bitter, one of several threat groups linked to India, has been active since at least 2013 and has historically targeted government, energy, and engineering organizations. The group is known for using tailored attack campaigns to gain persistent access to victim networks, collect information, and maintain remote control over compromised systems.

At the center of the latest threat campaign is PapRAT, a custom remote access Trojan (RAT) that gives attackers extensive control over compromised Windows systems, including the ability to execute commands, manipulate files, capture screenshots, and download additional payloads, according to FortiGuard Labs.

Related:CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents

"This campaign illustrates how Bitter combines native Windows tools with custom malware to establish and maintain access to targeted systems," Cara Lin, a FortiGuard Labs threat researcher, wrote in the post.

Bitter has recently revamped PapRAT from a C++ code base to Rust, expanding its functionality in the process from eight commands to 11, according to the report. Additional capabilities in the latest version include PowerShell execution, a sleep directive, and a clean-exit command.

"PapRAT's C++ and Rust implementations indicate continued investment in Bitter's toolset," Lin wrote.

Indeed, attackers have increasingly adopted Rust for malware development for various reasons, including its cross-platform development capabilities and potential evasion advantages.

The latest updates to PapRAT also underscore the importance of certain defensive measures, including "monitoring malicious behavior across scripting tools, scheduled tasks, and installer activity alongside detecting known malware signatures," Lin wrote.

Researchers observed three distinct attack chains being used by Bitter, all of which exploit legitimate Windows functionality to disguise malicious behavior.

These tactics demonstrate "how advanced cyberespionage operations deliberately abuse native system tools to evade traditional endpoint detection," notes Shane Barney, chief information security officer at Keeper Security.

Related:Operação de influência russa tem como alvo generalizado a América Latina

The first attack chain uses a malicious LNK file that abuses the native Windows ftp.exe utility to execute scripts and create scheduled tasks that maintain contact with the attackers' command-and-control (C2) server.

The second uses a VHDX disk image containing an LNK file that opens a decoy spreadsheet while silently launching an MSI installer to deploy PapRAT.

The third attack begins with a URL shortcut that retrieves an LNK file through WebDAV, leading to an MSI installer that deploys PapRAT. In this chain, PapRAT also delivers WmRAT, a secondary implant previously documented by other researchers, according to FortiGuard Labs.

"By co-opting native Windows utilities like ftp.exe and scheduled tasks to establish initial command-and-control communication, threat actors operate within trusted administrative channels before deploying custom malware," Barney observes. "When an intrusion leverages trusted system processes, signature-based controls simply have nothing to alert on."

This so-called "hybrid tradecraft," which combines legitimate Windows functionality with custom malware, requires organizations to focus on strict privilege boundaries and identity security rather than relying on endpoint signatures alone as part of a comprehensive defense strategy, Barney says.

Related:Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

To defend against these attacks, organizations should treat unexpected LNK files, URL shortcuts, disk images, and MSI packages with caution, particularly when delivered through unsolicited messages, Lin recommended in the post.

"Combining user awareness with controls that detect suspicious execution chains and outbound C2 traffic can help limit exposure to campaigns that blend legitimate Windows functionality with custom malware," she wrote.

The third attack chain is particularly problematic for defenders because removing PapRAT from compromised systems may not eliminate the attacker's access, observes Jason Soroko, senior fellow at Sectigo.

This means defenders need to look deeper into their systems "to check what else was installed and identify scripts and scheduled tasks that could keep fetching commands," he says. A comprehensive recovery effort must look beyond the file that triggered the original alert to identify any additional payloads, persistence mechanisms, or other components of the compromise.

The solution, then, is highly restrictive moderation to keep the outrage out of the space. Many vBulletin-style bulletin boards did exactly that to keep users on topic throughout the 2000s and 2010s...but such a heavy-handed moderation system requires dedicated moderators and a group of people who generally agree with the moderation for the sake of group cohesion on the topic. #10133. The AI bubble can wait, but your exit plan can't

Infrastructure spending outruns measurable returns, with supplier finances key to judging when trouble arrives

The AI bubble isn't about to burst, Forrester reckons, although businesses should prepare for a correction that could upend their suppliers, contracts, and prices.

Spending on infrastructure has raced ahead of measurable returns, the analyst says, yet the financial strength of the companies funding the build-out is what keep Forrester from predicting an imminent crash.

"Fears that an AI bubble is about to burst are premature," said Forrester emerging technology veep Brian Hopkins.

"About nine-tenths of the money building today's AI computing infrastructure comes from large, healthy technology companies paying out of their own cash flow. The risk is concentrated in a few places: a small number of builders under real financial strain, and circular financing deals with the AI labs."

Conveniently, Forrester has developed an AI Bubble Model to help technology leaders monitor the risks and prepare.

Its latest report, "An AI Bubble Burst Is Not Imminent," notes what many in the IT industry, including The Register, have been saying for a while: that the hyperscale operators are committing a record share of revenue into capital expenditure to bring online more infrastructure to support AI development and use.

At the same time, the boost in productivity doesn't justify this supplier capacity build-out. Forrester calculates that the infrastructure investments break even only if AI raises US GDP by 5 percent by 2035. Published estimates suggest productivity improvements could provide about two percentage points of that uplift, leaving roughly $1.3 trillion to come from other sources of value.

A recent report from management consultants Bain & Company came to similar conclusions, estimating the AI industry needs to generate $6 trillion in annual revenue by 2031 to keep funding all the infrastructure it needs, and this will require new uses beyond simply enhancing employee productivity.

Forrester also claims that the forces making AI abundant also make parts of the market unstable, and says that enterprise users should take heed of how prices collapsed as major providers like Anthropic slashed token costs in response to competition from open source models.

If demand disappoints as new capacity comes online, suppliers could cut investment, merge, change prices, or discontinue products. Customers could find themselves rebuilding AI plans around suppliers and services that no longer exist.

Forrester advises businesses to track whether their AI projects deliver measurable value and limit their exposure to vulnerable suppliers – with its help, of course.

Companies can judge how things are going by looking at the gap between suppliers' contracted business and revenue actually recognized, along with how they fund their build-outs. If a vendor leans more on outside investment and customer prepayments, as Oracle and CoreWeave have, this is a red flag to cut back dependencies on them, Forrester says.

Enterprises should also stress-test AI plans against scenarios such as a key vendor announcing end of support in 12 months, and an AI model supplier defaulting on payments to its compute vendor and cutting back service-level agreements for enterprise workloads. Companies should know in advance which AI use cases to drop, what data and workloads need to be moved, and at what cost.

But Hopkins sounded a further note of caution: "Oversupply on its own won't decide whether a correction comes. Demand will, and that's the biggest unknown, because it depends on enterprises finding lasting value in AI beyond simple productivity gains."

Organizations shouldn't pull back, he insists. They should keep investing where AI delivers value that can be demonstrated, closely monitor the financial health of the companies building AI computing, and be ready for corrections.

Recently, the International Monetary Fund started ringing alarm bells that financial markets are increasingly exposed to an AI-driven correction that could lead to widespread economic disruption.

Earlier this year, the Bank for International Settlements also raised concerns that the current situation with the AI industry bore the hallmarks of historical economic bubbles and presented a risk to global economic stability. ®

#10130. Who Gives A Crap? Hackers, apparently, after toilet paper maker's customer data exposed

UK shoppers caught up in third-party security mess, and nobody knows whether the data was flushed away

Toilet paper purveyor Who Gives A Crap has found itself in a bit of a mess after an intruder accessed customer information through a third-party software provider, leaving the company scrambling to clean up a breach affecting shoppers in the UK, US, and Australia.

In an email sent to affected customers over the weekend, seen by The Register, the loo roll seller warns that personal information was accessed without authorization after a security incident at an unnamed US-based marketing software provider.

The email explains that the intruder gained access to the supplier's systems on October 30. The provider spotted the intrusion the following day and says it secured its systems by November 1, although Who Gives A Crap wasn't told until November 6. It's unclear why the supplier sat on the bad news for another five days before passing it on.

The exposed information includes customers' names, email addresses, phone numbers, mailing addresses, and total spending with the company. In other words, someone may now know not only where you live, but just how much of your hard-earned cash you've flushed down the crapper.

Payment information, order details, and passwords were not involved, and customers' accounts were not directly accessed. That's something of a relief, although whether the intruder actually made off with the data remains a pressing question.

"We don't yet know whether the information was copied or downloaded," the company told customers, adding that it had found no evidence of misuse.

In a separate public statement, Who Gives A Crap co-founder and CEO Simon Griffiths confirmed that the incident affected customers across the company's Australian, UK, and US stores. Canadian customers, meanwhile, appear to have escaped this particular toilet emergency, with the supplier reporting that no personal information belonging to shoppers in the country was accessed.

Who Gives A Crap says it has since disconnected the provider from its systems, changed access credentials, and begun warning affected customers to watch out for suspicious emails, texts, calls, and other unsolicited communications.

"The main concern is scam or phishing messages that use your real details to look convincing," the company warned in its customer email.

While Who Gives A Crap has been busy cleaning up, the supplier at the center of this particular stink remains a mystery. The company hasn't identified the software provider or disclosed how many customers were affected, including those in the UK, and didn’t respond to our questions.

Griffiths said the company is "engaging with the relevant regulatory authorities, as required." In the UK, the ICO told The Register: "We can confirm Who Gives A Crap Limited has reported an incident and we are assessing the information provided."

Who Gives A Crap has plenty of toilet paper to hand, although cleaning up this particular situation might require more than a few rolls. ®

Architecturally RISC-V is quite MIPS-like, but organized better for adding extensions. The aarch64 instruction set is a little more MIPS like and less ARM-like than its 32-bit counterpart. (XZR/WZR being kind of like $zero, and the removal of shift operations that leaves behind a big ARM heritage).

The interesting part for ASIC and embedded processors is that RISC-V has a reasonable system for vendor extensions. Allowing one to add some custom instructions or to implement an extension on a lower end core that helps it compete with a higher end configuration. The vendor instructions are always a bit of a compromise and make the tooling difficult. Thankfully it occurs less often, as there are quite a few standardized configurations now. (I maintain a small rv32 emulator that can do a few configurations, it can do accurate single-precision floating point, but it has to fake the double-precision stuff with the host's hardware. good enough to run a typical program but not good enough to get golden CRCs for simulation)

#10126. Microsoft's Azure Linux gets 470-plus security fixes in one almighty patching session

A mountain of CVEs, a certificate cleanup, and yet more work for Microsoft's patching teams

Microsoft has unleashed a whopper of an update for Azure Linux, packing more than 470 CVE fixes into a single release as the software industry's ever-growing pile of vulnerabilities shows little sign of shrinking.

Over the weekend, Microsoft rolled out Azure Linux 3.0.2022 with fixes covering everything from the Linux kernel to open source packages and container software. The changelog runs to hundreds of entries, so anyone planning to read the whole thing might want to put the kettle on.

Microsoft's release notes contain more than 470 CVE references, although some vulnerabilities appear multiple times because they affect different packages. So that's not necessarily 470 separate security holes, but it's still an impressive amount of patching for one release.

The fixes span OpenSSL, curl, Kubernetes, Docker, QEMU, and a lengthy list of other packages that underpin modern Linux environments. The generic Linux kernel has been updated to version 6.6.161.1.

There's also been some housekeeping following the eMudhra certificate incident, tracked as CVE-2026-114406. Microsoft has removed or distrusted root certificates that could validate compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates, while adding checks in Python and Go to reject the affected certificates. It has also preserved SSL.com TLS trust where required, presumably to avoid fixing one certificate headache by creating another.

Container infrastructure gets plenty of attention, too, with fixes spanning KubeVirt, containerd, Docker Compose, and other components used to keep cloud workloads running. Several CVEs crop up repeatedly across these packages, helping explain the eye-watering number of entries in the changelog.

The release includes less security-focused changes too, including new Dockerfiles, an OpenVMM patch for confidential computing support, fixes for systemd hangs, and adjustments to GRUB Secure Boot metadata.

The hefty release comes amid an AI-fueled surge in vulnerability discovery that has left developers struggling to keep up with the resulting patch workload. As The Register reported earlier today, Linux creator Linus Torvalds reckons there may finally be signs that the flood is easing, at least in some corners of the kernel.

Torvalds said fixes are now arriving faster than new bug reports in the kernel's eBPF subsystem, although he noted that most other areas haven't reached that point. Whether the wider software industry is anywhere close to catching up is another matter, and Microsoft hasn't said if AI-assisted research contributed to the vulnerabilities addressed in this release.

Azure Linux, formerly known as CBL-Mariner, is Microsoft's own Linux distribution, developed primarily for its cloud infrastructure and services. That makes keeping its many components patched rather more important than the modest version-number bump might suggest.

And judging by the size of this latest changelog, Microsoft's patching teams aren't likely to be putting their feet up anytime soon. ®

The cost of a will varies dramatically based on how you create it and how complex your estate is. Here is a comprehensive comparison of every method, from free options to premium attorney packages.

Several factors push will costs toward the higher end of each range:

The will vs trust decision is primarily a financial calculation: does the upfront cost of a trust save more than it costs by avoiding probate?

When you die with only a will (no trust), your estate must go through probate — a court-supervised process where a judge validates your will, your executor inventories assets, debts are paid, and remaining assets are distributed. Probate costs include:

Probate also takes 6-18 months on average and is a public proceeding — anyone can look up your will, your assets, and who inherited what.

A revocable living trust costs $1,500-$5,000 upfront but avoids probate entirely. The math is straightforward:

For most FI-focused households who are building wealth toward financial independence, the trust pays for itself many times over. If your net worth exceeds $100,000-$200,000 and you own real estate, a trust is almost certainly the better financial decision.

Even with a trust, you still need a pour-over will — a short document that catches any assets not transferred into the trust during your lifetime and directs them into the trust at death. You also still need a healthcare directive and durable power of attorney. Most estate plan packages include all four documents together.

The sticker price of a will is only part of the total cost of estate planning. Several hidden costs catch people off guard:

The FI-optimized approach to estate planning minimizes cost without sacrificing protection:

Start with an online will now. A $159 Trust & Will plan gives you a will, healthcare directive, and power of attorney today. Do not let perfect be the enemy of done — having a basic will is infinitely better than having no will while you save up for an attorney.

Upgrade to a trust when your net worth exceeds $200,000. At this point, the probate avoidance savings justify the $1,500-$3,500 cost of adding a trust.

Shop attorney fees aggressively. Estate planning is a competitive market. Get quotes from at least three attorneys. Many offer flat-fee packages, and prices can vary by 50-100% for the same work in the same city. Ask specifically whether the quote includes trust funding assistance and deed transfers.

Use online services for updates. Rather than paying an attorney $200-$500 for a codicil, many online platforms let you update your will for free or for a small annual subscription ($19-$39/year). Trust & Will, for example, includes one year of free updates.

Bundle documents. An estate plan package (will + trust + POA + healthcare directive) typically costs 20-40% less than purchasing each document separately. If you are going to see an attorney, get everything done in one engagement.

Here is the counterintuitive truth: the most expensive estate plan is the one you never create. Dying without a will (intestate) triggers state default rules that may not match your wishes, longer and more expensive probate proceedings, and potential family conflict. For parents of minor children, it means a judge — not you — decides who raises your kids. The $0-$259 cost of an online will is trivially small compared to these consequences.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Yes. FreeWill (freewill.com) offers a free basic will funded by nonprofit partners. Some states also accept handwritten (holographic) wills that cost nothing. Military personnel can get free wills through the JAG office on any military installation. Many bar associations and legal aid societies offer free will clinics several times per year. While these free options work for simple estates, you may want to pay $99-$259 for a more comprehensive online service that includes healthcare directives and power of attorney.

Attorneys charge $300-$750 for a simple will and $750-$1,500 for a complex will with special provisions. A complete estate plan package (will, trust, power of attorney, healthcare directive) runs $1,500-$5,000. Fees vary significantly by location — attorneys in major metros charge 2-3 times more than attorneys in smaller cities for the same work. Always ask for a flat fee rather than hourly billing for estate planning.

For straightforward estates, yes. Major online will makers like Trust & Will, Nolo WillMaker, and LegalZoom produce documents that are legally valid in all 50 states and cover the same core elements an attorney would include. The difference is that an attorney can provide customized advice, handle complex situations, and anticipate issues specific to your state law. If your estate is simple, an online will is functionally equivalent. If your situation has any complexity, the attorney consultation is worth the additional cost.

Online services typically include free updates for one year and then charge $19-$39 per year for ongoing access. An attorney charges $100-$500 for a codicil (formal amendment) or $300-$1,000 to draft a new will. For minor changes, a codicil is sufficient. For major changes (new spouse, additional children, significant asset changes), creating an entirely new will is cleaner and reduces the risk of conflicting instructions.

The most expensive part of estate planning is NOT the documents — it is probate. Probate costs 3-7% of your estate value ($15,000-$72,000 on a $500,000-$1,000,000 estate) and takes 6-18 months. By comparison, even the most expensive estate plan package ($5,000-$10,000) is a fraction of what your family would spend navigating probate without a trust. The second most expensive mistake is outdated beneficiary designations on retirement accounts, which can send six or seven figures to the wrong person with no legal recourse.

The cost of a will ranges from $0 to $10,000+ depending on your method and complexity, but the most expensive option is always having no will at all. For most FI-focused households, start with an online will for $0-$259 to get basic protection in place immediately. As your net worth grows beyond $200,000, invest $1,500-$5,000 in a comprehensive estate plan with a revocable living trust — the probate savings alone deliver a 300-1,000% return. Update your beneficiary designations today (free), review your plan every 3-5 years, and remember: the goal of estate planning is not to create perfect documents. It is to protect the people you love from financial chaos during the worst moment of their lives.

#10121. NASA keeps its PROMISE to raid Mars testbeds for parts

Cut-and-shut trundlebot with spiffy new paint job meant to be headed to the Moon in 2028

NASA is moving ahead with its plan to repurpose a Mars rover engineering model as a lunar trundlebot for less than $400 million.

The robot, dubbed PROMISE (Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration), is a cut-and-shut of engineering test articles used for the Perseverance and Curiosity rovers, currently rolling around the Red Planet.

During a weekend briefing, NASA outlined the plan for PROMISE: to land the robot on the lunar surface by late 2028 for an 18-month mission. PROMISE will be preceded by NASA's VIPER trundlebot, which is expected to survive only 100 days on the Moon's surface. PROMISE will carry copies of VIPER's science instruments, including a drill capable of boring 1 meter into the lunar regolith.

Power will come from a Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator (RTG) left over from the Cassini mission. NASA acknowledged the fuel was processed some time ago – the Cassini mission to Saturn was launched in 1997 – but anticipates there will be plenty of heat and power for PROMISE's components.

Blue Origin is to deposit the rover on the Moon. NASA awarded the company a $94 million base contract, "with an option period worth an additional $140 million based on performance to deliver PROMISE to the lunar South Pole."

The figures make it difficult to ascertain the exact cost of the PROMISE mission. However, during the briefing, NASA said it had "a pretty firm agreement with JPL to basically deliver the rover to the surface under $400 million." The $400 million includes the lander, which will be Blue Origin's Mark 1.

Earlier this year, The Planetary Society's chief of space policy, Casey Drier, estimated that the mission (including repurposing the hardware developed for Mars and landing it on the Moon) would cost at least $723 million. At the time, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said: "if PROMISE costs even 20 percent of your low-end estimate, we simply will not fly it."

Assuming Isaacman was only talking about the rover, Drier's figure drops to $489 million without launch and landing costs. 20 percent of that is… not going to be enough.

That also doesn't account for the impact of taking away the hardware built for the Mars program. During the briefing, NASA said it was "pretty comfortable" with how the Mars rovers were going and so was happy about repurposing the hardware or, as one speaker put it, "can we give it a new paint job?"

A source told The Register that morale at the agency's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) was not high at present. Raiding successful programs to fulfill the administration's whims is unlikely to have improved the mood of engineers.

Still. Another trundlebot on the Moon. Far better than using that spare RTG for yet another deep space mission, right? ®
