#10117. Microsoft takes three decades to make Sticky Keys less sticky

Windows preview adds a 'don't ask again' option to accessibility prompts, sparing users a trip through Settings

Windows testers are getting a new option in the Sticky Keys and Filter Keys dialogs – one to banish the pop-ups without needing to venture deep into Settings.

It's only taken several decades for Microsoft to put the off switch where the interruption actually happens. The accessibility features themselves are useful, though triggering their activation prompts by accident is another matter.

Once enabled, Sticky Keys let users press modifier keys (such as Control) one at a time instead of holding them down together. For example, rather than holding Control and pressing C to copy, a user can press and release Control, then press C. Filter Keys, meanwhile, ignores brief or repeated keystrokes and adjusts the keyboard's repeat behavior.

However, the dialogs are of little use to people who don't need the features, and they can pop up at the most inconvenient moments. Tap Shift five times, and you'll see what we mean: Windows chimes and shows a dialog asking whether you'd like to turn on Sticky Keys. Dismiss it, hit Shift five times, and there it is again.

Or hold down the right Shift key for eight seconds to be treated to the Filter Keys pop-up.

You can stop this behavior elsewhere in the system, but it requires a trek through Windows settings. The change, introduced in the Experimental Windows Insider Build 26340.9882, adds an option to the Sticky Keys or Filter Keys dialogs to dismiss the prompts permanently.

It's a small change, but one that should spare users an irritating interruption. Better late than never – even if "never ask me again" has taken roughly three decades to reach the dialog.

Former Microsoft engineer Charles Opperman said he wrote the dialog in early 1995 "after @bradsilverberg kids kept activating StickeyKeys [sic] while playing Space Cadet pinball."

Opperman added that a link to Settings was added in Windows 98 or what would become Windows 2000, and a checkbox was considered even then, but it wasn't deemed a priority. Users could turn off the prompt via settings. Now the option is front and center.

The option is also rolling out in the Windows Insider Beta channel, although Microsoft has not announced a general release date. ®

The latest "Digital Defense Report" identifies government agencies as prime targets for AI attacks, but it doesn't mention that they are broadly being targeted through Microsoft bugs.

AI is changing cybersecurity. The hope is that software will eventually ship with fewer vulnerabilities, while the expectation in the meantime is that vendors will issue eye-popping volumes of software patches as a result of using AI to identify flaws in existing products. Software customers will increasingly use AI to more effectively and efficiently protect their networks. These promising developments will take time to unfold, as vendors and their customers learn how to incorporate AI into their software development and cybersecurity risk management workflows.

Attackers, meanwhile, are already using AI to generate novel attacks and orchestrate increasingly complex and large-scale hacking campaigns. AI is already enabling criminal groups to achieve hacking successes normally reserved for patient, highly resourced nation-state threat actors. And nation-state threat actors are using AI to increase the scale and sophistication of their cyber operations. The threat level is rising at an alarming rate.

Related:CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents

Microsoft flagged the impacts of AI on cybersecurity in its recently released "2026 Digital Defense Report." Among its findings, it assessed that government agencies and services were the most affected by cyber threats and frequently targeted for nation-state activity.

Microsoft's report has a major blind spot, however: the impact of legacy software, especially its own, on organizations' cyber-risk. Legacy software will remain the substrate of organizations' attack surface for the foreseeable future. Vendors need to up their security game, and their customers need to demand better security from their vendors, particularly as AI heightens the threat landscape.

For example, with an 85% market share, Microsoft is the most dominant player in the US public sector productivity software market. Its products are therefore a prime target for state-sponsored groups seeking access to US government agencies and the data and secrets they are charged with protecting. So we should expect attackers to prize vulnerabilities in Microsoft's products and devote a substantial proportion of their hacking efforts to these popular products.

But there is more to the story than Microsoft's sheer prevalence in federal IT. Microsoft's grip on the federal IT market exposes the US government to a disproportionate share of cyber vulnerabilities. According to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Microsoft accounts for nearly 16% of known exploited vulnerabilities (KEVs) so far this year — the most of any company. Microsoft accounts for nearly 23% of known exploited vulnerabilities from November 2021 (when CISA began tracking KEVs) to October 2026.

Related:Operação de influência russa tem como alvo generalizado a América Latina

By comparison, the next-highest vendor, Cisco, is responsible for approximately 7% in 2026 and 6% total, less than half of Microsoft's share.

Some agencies even rely on Microsoft as their single software vendor. This isn't particularly surprising — Microsoft has a track record of locking customers into its ecosystem by bundling its cloud computing offerings with office and security products (bundling is one area of focus of the Federal Trade Commission’s ongoing antitrust investigation into Microsoft) and then making it too difficult or costly for customers to switch vendors.

In 2023, the US Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) discontinued its Data Loss Prevention program after moving to bundle security tools into a sole-source Microsoft enterprise license. The move reportedly put 18 million veterans' personal records at risk of leakage. The VA has now moved to reverse course by seeking alternatives to Microsoft, having recognized the consequences of a Microsoft monoculture. Lesson learned.

Related:Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

Microsoft's Digital Defense Report identifies how frequently government agencies are affected by cyber threats and targeted for nation-state activity. Microsoft knows this firsthand. Since 2023, Chinese state-sponsored actors have compromised Microsoft products in at least two significant instances, accessing over two dozen US government agencies' emails in one attack and compromising at least seven agencies in another in July 2025.

Russian state-backed actors have also exploited Microsoft's weak security at least three times since 2020, including the infamous SolarWinds attack and an operation to exfiltrate emails between Microsoft personnel and government agencies. US government officials and advisory bodies have concluded that these breaches were preventable and caused by Microsoft's negligence. The reach and severity of breaches will only grow as China, Russia, and other nation-state threat actors become AI-native and AI tools become increasingly sophisticated.

Microsoft deserves some credit for using AI to evaluate products it has already deployed: its record-setting Patch Tuesday count of 974 vulnerabilities disclosed last month is no doubt the result of using AI to identify flaws. But that's not good enough.

All software vendors, including Microsoft, should invest more in the security of their products before they are released, even if it comes at the expense of slowing the rollout of new product features. And they should all be transparent to customers about these processes to enable customers to make more informed purchasing decisions. Otherwise, Microsoft's "2027 Digital Defense Report" will paint an even darker picture of the threat environment.

Director of the Program on Geopolitics, Technology, and Governance, Stanford University

Andrew Grotto founded and directs the Program on Geopolitics, Technology, and Governance at Stanford University's Center for International Security and Cooperation. He serves as the faculty lead for the Cyber Policy and Security specialization in Stanford’s master’s in international policy program, where he teaches courses on cyber policy and economic statecraft. He is also a visiting fellow at the Hoover Institution. Previously, he was senior advisor to the Secretary of Commerce for technology policy during the Obama administration and Senior Director for Cyber Policy on the National Security Council in the Obama and Trump administrations. He advises technology companies on digital risks, including companies that compete with Microsoft.

#10107. Insight about how 'nature makes no leaps' promises better robot predictions

Machine learning researchers have developed a technique that allows world models to make better predictions about how objects will behave.

World models are used to train physical AI systems like robots how to navigate the real world. They predict the consequences of actions. But they do so based on observed data. These models could provide better direction to robots if they were able to make inferences about possible actions without being trained for all the possible outcomes.

Randall Balestriero (Brown University, AMI Labs), Kerda Varaku, and Turing Award winner Yann LeCun (NYU, AMI Labs) describe an approach that might allow that to happen in a pre-print paper, "Counterfactual World Models: Natura Non Facit Saltus."

The Latin refers to Gottfried Leibniz's axiom "nature makes no leaps," which had a good run until it ran headlong into quantum mechanics. Yet for the authors, the saying explains how they have been able to devise a method for zero-shot physics inference.

Counterfactual world models, said Balestriero in an email to The Register use "the mismatch between your prediction and the real world to figure out what did you get wrong, and from that you can better understand what happened for better future predictions, debugging, reasoning, all at test time."

Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) models, developed by LeCun and colleagues back in 2023, have been proposed for robots because they can take an action as input and ask what the world would be like with that action.

But a JEPA world model produces an average of outcomes and would not be able to anticipate counterfactual scenarios – events that didn't happen. The technique that the researchers developed is not specific to JEPAs – it can be applied to any world model that predicts the average next state under any action. But JEPA models are particularly well suited to being adapted.

Balestriero said that the counterfactual world model experiments were done using off-the-shelf encoders (DINOv2 and MAE) without any fine-tuning and only a small predictor trained on top. Creating a counterfactual world model from that starting point would only require minor additions.

Counterfactual world models predict alternative scenarios more effectively by inferring possibilities from what did occur.

"In causal inference, answering 'What would have happened had I acted differently?' takes three steps," explained Balestriero. "You use what you observed to learn something about those hidden factors, you change the action, and you predict again with the hidden factors kept exactly as they were.

"Our counterfactual world model does all three steps with one subtraction."

Balestriero cited an example from the paper: a boat crossing a river with a hidden current and how the JEPA world model and counterfactual world model predicted the boat's movements.

"The world model predicted where the boat would end up after steering left, and it actually ended up two meters further downstream," he explained. "Those two meters are the signature of the current that occurred. To answer 'where would the boat be had I steered right?', we take the world model's prediction for steering right and add the same two meters. In other words, the counterfactual is what actually happened, plus the difference between the model's predictions for the alternative action and for the action taken.

"Physics enters to justify this rule, not as an equation the model fits. Over a short time, the effect of the action and the effect of the current each grow in proportion to the duration, while their interaction grows only with its square, so over short steps they simply add up, like forces.

"We prove that the fraction of the disturbance's effect that this rule gets wrong shrinks with the square of the time step, and that no method using the same ordinary data can do better than this rate in the worst case."

Counterfactual world models have three likely uses, according to Balestriero. The first is having a robot retry an action after a surprise event.

"When an attempt fails because of something the robot could not see, such as an unexpected load, a current or a weak motor, the counterfactual world model lets it estimate which action would have worked in that same situation," he explained. "In our simulated tasks, choosing the action this way reaches the goal in 35 to 69 percent of events, against 14 to 23 percent for a planner that knows the true simulator but ignores the observed outcome. With two more attempts on the same event, success rises to 51 to 97 percent."

He also sees these models being useful for adapting to persistent fault, like a miscalibrated motor, and helping people understand failures.

"World models are trained to predict, and they are getting good at it," said Balestriero. "But a robot, a car or a drone acting in the real world is constantly surprised by things it could not see coming. After a surprise, the useful question is no longer what was expected, but what would have happened had it acted differently in that same situation. You need that answer to debug a failure, to tell a bad decision from bad luck, or to decide what to do on the next attempt, and prediction alone does not provide it."

The researchers initial attempts to address the issue involved adding a learned component to the world model that infers whatever hidden disturbance (e.g. the current in the boat scenario) affected the anticipated outcome. But that approach was too fragile.

"Trying to understand why led to the theory," explained Balestriero. "Learning the disturbance from ordinary data is not just hard, it is impossible in general: the hidden noise can be relabeled differently for each action without changing a single prediction, so the data cannot tell you which labeling is the right one. The missing piece has to come from outside the data. For physical systems, it comes from the fact that forces add and that their interaction builds up slowly in time. Once you accept that, the learned disturbance model becomes unnecessary: the gap between what happened and what was predicted already carries the information you need, and you carry it over to the other action."

Balestriero said that control engineers have been implementing corrections of this sort for decades, to tune hand-built models.

"What was missing was why the same correction is justified for learned world models that see the world through images, what can and cannot be recovered without paired data, and where it breaks," he said. "The paper answers these questions by connecting causal inference, control and world models. The title comes from Leibniz's law of continuity, natura non facit saltus, 'nature makes no leaps,' which is precisely the property that makes all of this work."

The researchers' paper was provided to The Register prior to its release on ArXiv. It is expected to be released this week. ®

#10100. One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning

The record theft shows how weak system separation, inadequate controls, and untested attack possibilities can turn one breach into systemic loss.

Last week's $6.3 billion breach at Binance underscores why effective security often depends not just on what an organization's controls are designed to block, but also on what they are configured to allow.

Details from Binance's disclosures thus far show that a threat actor, whom the FBI has identified as North Korea's TraderTraitor group, compromised a developer's laptop to access an internal service container with the permissions to initiate withdrawal requests.

Using that access as a starting point, the attackers exploited additional points of compromise and an Ethereum account-delegation mechanism to gain transaction approval authority over a hot wallet. And in around 20 minutes, the threat actors drained billions of dollars in assets.

In the process, the attackers appear to have bypassed Binance's normal approval controls. The company itself has said there's no evidence the attackers used any leaked wallet keys to carry out the massive theft.

Related:CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents

"Binance's initial findings pointed to a compromised laptop belonging to an employee as the starting point. Its subsequent investigation has identified additional points of breach, showing the incident went beyond one device," the cryptocurrency exchange noted.

The incident, at least based on available details so far, has raised questions about whether Binance had sufficient independent safeguards to prevent a compromised system from approving and executing unauthorized withdrawals.

"At a minimum, a platform holding digital assets should have multiple layers of security so no single compromise, such as a hacked employee laptop, can authorize a transfer," says Tim Rawlins, senior adviser and director of security at NCC Group. "Those layers need to be independent of one another."

Funds, for instance, should be separated across hot and cold wallets to limit the impact of a compromise. Developers and administrators should have privileged access workstations to ensure systems they used for critical operations are separate from those they use for other activities such as email and Web browsing, he says. Also critical is 24/7 monitoring for anomalous behavior to help detect compromised endpoints and suspicious activity before attackers can exploit privileged access.

The focus should be on identifying single points of compromise, such as components or privileged roles whose compromise could give an attacker control over funds. "Protecting private keys is only part of the challenge. The systems that request and approve their use must also be secured. A properly secured system has layered, independent controls, hot/cold separation, and has been through threat modelling and end-to-end security testing," Rawlins says.

Related:Operação de influência russa tem como alvo generalizado a América Latina

For now, much remains unclear about exactly how the unauthorized transactions occurred and what safeguards Binance had in place to protect against them. Following the attack, the cryptocurrency exchange moved quickly to freeze some $3 billion. It has also claimed to have replenished — though not recovered — approximately 95% of the affected assets, meaning it has used its own funds to replace the stolen assets.

Cryptocurrency exchanges face many of the same threats as traditional financial institutions. But unlike banks and other financial institutions, which have long been subject to regulations governing operational risk and security, crypto exchanges have not yet faced the same level of oversight, making them a popular target for attackers.

John Bruggeman, vCISO at IT services firm CBTS, says large cryptocurrenct exchanges like Binance have to know that they are constantly being targeted by threat actors. In addition to controls that protect the perimeter or authenticate users, these companies also need to know what trusted identities and systems can do, verify high-impact actions, and prevent one compromised component from becoming a path to valuable assets.

Related:Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

That means segregation of duties, management of private keys that authorize transfers, limits on the size of a transfer, MFA on the use of the private key monitoring, alerting for large transfers, and endpoint detection on all employee devices, Bruggeman says.

Also key is user behavior analysis for all users. Architecturally, organizations like Binance should have custody mechanisms for protecting the cryptocurrency and wallets themselves, transaction controls on how to move the cryptocurrency, some kind of rate limits on withdrawals, identity and access controls, and segregation of duties so no one user can initiate and also finalize a transfer, Bruggeman says.

The Binance breach is an important reminder of why all organizations need to test the path that attackers can potentially take after gaining initial access to an environment and not assume that individual controls, each working as they should, are sufficient protection, analysts said. "The entry point and the damage can sit very far apart, so stop grading your security by how well the front door holds," says Waseem Ahmed, head of engineering at Secure.com.

The traditional approach to security is to check whether a request is valid. It almost never checks whether the action behind it should happen, he says. Available information suggests the attackers used Binance's own signing system to sign the transfers, so they looked valid on the way out. It was the "correct math, wrong decision," Ahmed says.

Security has to move from proving identity to governing consequences, he says. That means putting a human approval gate in front of any action that moves money or data, with limits that count across every system at once. "And test the whole route from laptop to payout, not each box on its own," Ahmed advises.

The Binance attack scenario can play out in any enterprise, too. "Swap out the withdrawal service for a payment system, a customer database, or a deployment pipeline, and this is an ordinary enterprise breach," he says. "A clean report from every tool you own tells you nothing about whether someone can walk from a laptop to the money, because no single tool is asked that question."

Robert Coles, senior manager of threat intelligence security at Black Duck, says the broader takeaway for organizations isn't really about cryptocurrency or the attack on Binance itself. Rather, it's about the blast radius, or what happens after initial break-in. It's one thing, he says, for an attacker to gain initial access. But turning that into a theft of billions of dollars is another entirely.

"Every organization has critical systems and privileged accounts where a compromise can have a much bigger impact," Coles says. "We spend a lot of time asking how we keep attackers out. We should spend just as much time asking, ‘If they do get in, what stops them next?'"

Security teams must assume something eventually will get compromised and make sure that one compromise doesn't become a catastrophic business event, Coles noted.

The Binance breach, the biggest ever by magnitude, is by no means the first to affect a major cryptocurrency exchange. In February 2025, Bybit lost approximately $1.5 billion in cryptocurrency after attackers manipulated a transaction approval process involving an Ethereum cold wallet. In May 2019, Binance itself lost 7,000 bitcoin after attackers obtained user API keys and two-factor authentication codes to bypass existing security checks. In October this year, attackers compromised a third-party script on Polymarket's website and used it to move funds from some user wallets.

North Korean threat actors have been especially aggressive in targeting crypto exchanges and wallets in general and account for 76% of all the money that traders have reported as stolen so far in 2026. In six of the past nine years, groups from the cash-strapped nation have accounted for at least one-third of all reported cryptocurrency theft.

#10094. Researchers pwn automakers’ Android apps to remotely unlock cars, honk horns

Pair of researchers chain WAF bypasses and default logins to command vehicles in Australia and the US

Security researchers exploited flaws in Android apps to gain remote access to connected cars from two major automakers, allowing them to start engines, flash headlights, and sound horns.

Shubham Shah, co-founder at Assetnote, and researcher Sam Curry worked together on the exploits earlier this year. By tinkering with the cars’ Android apps, they devised exploit paths to issue remote commands to vehicles in Australia and the US.

The pair published separate blogs covering different aspects of the research; Shah said the US attack "required a lot more work" because the automaker "spent much more time securing the US, Canadian, and European OpenIDM environments."

Both exploit chains centered around weaknesses in the ForgeRock identity platform relied upon by both automakers, the identities of which were kept anonymous by the researchers, who have previously highlighted flaws in the likes of Hyundai, Kia, Subaru, and many others.

In the Australian version of the app, the researchers first found a vehicle identification number (VIN) using public licence plate checkers, and used those in queries to internal APIs, which provided personal information and owner email addresses.

They also found hardcoded admin credentials for the ForgeRock OpenIDM that were meant for the staging environment but also worked in production. After bypassing the heavy WAF filtering by exploiting path traversal flaws, they were able to invoke the internal admin APIs and take over target accounts using only their email addresses.

This let them mint authentication tokens, which they could issue to send arbitrary commands to affected vehicles through the mobile app.

Issuing commands on the US version also required bypassing WAF filtering through a path traversal, though with a more involved technique: exploiting path confusion to reach the Apache Felix admin console.

The researchers used factory default credentials in Felix’s OSGi Web Console to gain admin privileges. They then used Felix configuration manager to schedule a task that executed an inline Groovy script, giving them shell access to the identity servers.

The researchers then queried local admin API endpoints, allowing them to view or modify user account data. From there, they logged into car owners’ accounts, and gained the ability to issue the same commands as demonstrated in the Australian version.

According to Curry’s disclosure timeline, he and Shah approached the affected automakers in "early 2026," and the exploits were patched within two hours of receiving the report.

Although the automakers wished to remain anonymous, it didn’t take long for some petrolheads to speculate that the partially blurred car in Shah’s demo video was a Toyota, citing the shape of the wing mirror and the unlock sound it made.

Onlookers claimed that the two automakers in question were likely Toyota and its luxury brand Lexus. Asked wether the claims were accurate, a spokesperson for Toyota Motor Corporation neither confirmed nor denied them.

Curry said he and Shah chose to uphold the manufacturers’ requests to remain anonymous out of concern for infoseccers’ current workloads.

He said: "Obviously, they have asked not to be named, and while normally we would fight to actually include the company names, it's a busy time in the security world and I don't like the idea of them diverting resources because they are worried about something with this disclosure." ®

#10089. Attackers backdoor trusted AWS integrations to steal secrets

Wiz researchers uncovered the secret-stealing supply-chain attack

Unknown attackers used compromised identity and access management (IAM) credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account to access customer AWS environments, stealing secrets and other sensitive data from S3 buckets.

Qubole is a cloud data processing platform that uses cross-account IAM roles to manage compute and access storage in customers' AWS environments without requiring customers to provide long-lived AWS access keys. The supply-chain attack abused this third-party, cross-account trust relationship.

Google’s cloud-security shop Wiz declined to tell us how many organizations were affected, but called it a “broad, opportunistic supply chain campaign” that hit “multiple” customer environments.

“Because many organizations left trust policies active even after deprecating the platform, the attacker was able to successfully assume integration roles, enumerate cloud resources, harvest secrets, and siphon data,” the researchers told The Register in an emailed response to questions.

Neither AWS nor Qubole responded to The Register's inquiries.

Wiz, working with Google's Mandiant incident responders after AI data security company Sentra flagged suspicious activity, traced the malicious activity back to October 14, when credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account were used to call the sts:AssumeRole API to obtain temporary credentials for customer-managed integration roles.

The calls originated from Qubole AWS account 805246085872, and used IAM user ID AIDA3W7DIFLYOLTK63SFS, Wiz analysts Zack Morrow, Sean Johnstone, and Benjamin Read said in a Monday blog about the supply chain attack. “Across the affected environments, Wiz CIRT has not observed this IAM user in any activity other than that associated with this threat actor,” the trio wrote.

This activity continued on October 15, and on October 18, the digital intruders began using a second IAM user from the same account.

Once inside customers’ environments, the crooks began probing a ton of AWS services and stealing credentials, keys, and other secrets stored across Lambda, Secrets Manager, and SSM Parameter Store.

The miscreants also used TruffleHog to test AWS credentials belonging to victim organizations, discover their Microsoft Entra ID secrets, and request OAuth tokens using Okta client credentials also uncovered while snooping around the AWS environments.

Abusing the integration roles also allowed the criminals to steal data from customers’ S3 storage, although it seems they were largely opportunistic attackers, in some cases downloading entire buckets, as opposed to state-sponsored spies looking for specific data.

The threat hunters haven’t attributed the supply chain attack to any particular group, and say they don’t have any insight into how the miscreants are using the stolen data.

While investigating this incident, Wiz spotted a separate campaign between October 8 and October 11 that also used customer-owned AWS access keys for Qubole integrations. While a “small number” of these also resulted in the intruders compromising victim organizations’ AWS environments, Wiz said it can’t definitively connect the two sets of malicious activity.

Organizations that have integrated with Qubole should rotate credentials - although rotating a credential does not end temporary sessions that were already issued.

Customers should also review CloudTrail from October 1 onward, looking for AssumeRole events where userIdentity.accountId matches Qubole's AWS account ID, 805246085872, particularly those originating from non-AWS IP addresses.

“For every role session you find, review all subsequent activity from that session, especially Secrets Manager, SSM Parameter Store, Lambda and S3,” the researchers wrote. “If the threat actor assumed an integration role, rotate every secret, parameter and Lambda environment variable the role could read, and revoke active sessions for the role.”®

The $30,000 average wedding figure you see everywhere is misleading. That number is skewed upward by luxury weddings in expensive metros like New York, San Francisco, and Los Angeles. The national median — the number where half of weddings cost more and half cost less — sits closer to $10,000 to $15,000. That distinction matters because it means a beautiful, memorable wedding is absolutely possible without spending five figures you do not have.

The FI perspective adds another layer: every dollar spent on a wedding is a dollar that cannot compound for decades. A $30,000 wedding invested for 30 years at a 7% average annual return grows to roughly $228,000. That does not mean you should elope in a courthouse (unless you want to), but it does mean you should spend intentionally on the categories that matter most to you and cut ruthlessly everywhere else.

Here is where the typical wedding dollar goes:

The biggest takeaway from this table: venue and catering are 60-70% of the total. If you can reduce those two categories, you change the entire math.

Not all wedding spending creates equal memories. Research consistently shows that couples remember three things most vividly years later: the ceremony itself, the food and drinks, and the photographs. Almost nobody remembers the chair covers, the napkin folds, or the custom monogram on the cocktail napkins.

That insight creates a clear FI-aligned strategy: splurge on what creates lasting memories (photographer, food, music) and minimize everything else.

The golden rule of wedding budgeting: if you cannot remember whether a detail was present at the last three weddings you attended, your guests will not notice either. Cut it without guilt.

The biggest financial mistake couples make is not setting a firm budget before visiting any vendors. Venues and vendors are skilled at upselling, and without a hard number in mind, costs spiral quickly. Start with a number you can pay in cash — wedding debt is one of the worst ways to begin a marriage and a direct threat to your FI timeline.

Follow this payment timeline to manage cash flow without credit card debt:

A practical savings strategy: divide your total budget by the number of months until the wedding and automate that transfer to a dedicated savings account. If your budget is $15,000 and your wedding is 15 months away, that is $1,000 per month. Treat it like any other savings goal on your FI path — automate, do not touch, and watch it grow.

For couples on the FI path, consider this reframe: every dollar you shave from the wedding budget is a dollar that starts compounding immediately. Cutting $5,000 from a $20,000 wedding and investing that savings at 7% for 25 years creates roughly $27,000 in future wealth. You can have a wonderful wedding and build wealth simultaneously — but only if you plan intentionally from the start.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Before finalizing your wedding budget, run the compound interest math on any amount you are considering spending. A $30,000 wedding invested at 7% for 30 years becomes roughly $228,000. A $15,000 wedding invested at 7% for 30 years becomes roughly $114,000. This is not an argument against celebrating — it is an argument for spending intentionally on what matters to you and cutting everything else. The couple who spends $15,000 on a joyful celebration and invests the other $15,000 gets both the wedding and a significant head start on financial independence.

There is no single right number, but the median US wedding cost of $10,000 to $15,000 is achievable for most couples without going into debt. Focus on what matters most to you and cut everything else. A $10,000 wedding with great food, a good photographer, and people you love is better than a $30,000 wedding that starts your marriage with financial stress.

No. Wedding debt is one of the worst forms of consumer debt because it funds a single day with no residual asset value. The average couple who finances their wedding on credit cards at 22% interest turns a $20,000 wedding into a $28,000 expense over 4 years of payments. Set a cash budget and stick to it.

Any contribution from parents is a gift, not an obligation. If parents offer to contribute, have an honest conversation about the total amount and whether it comes with expectations about the guest list or style. Budget based on what you can afford independently, then treat any parental contribution as a bonus.

Yes. Friday and Sunday weddings typically cost 20-30% less than Saturday weddings for the same venue and vendors. Some venues offer discounts of 40% or more for weekday weddings (Monday through Thursday). Off-season months like January, February, March, and November also offer significant savings.

Tips for vendors (plan 15-20% for catering staff, bartenders, and drivers), alterations for wedding attire ($200-$500), marriage license fees ($30-$100), and overtime charges if the reception runs past the contracted time. Build a 10% contingency buffer into your total budget for these surprises.

Set your budget privately as a couple before discussing with family. Present it as a decision, not a discussion. If family members want upgrades, they are welcome to fund those specific additions. Protect your financial foundation — the marriage matters more than the wedding, and starting debt-free sets up your partnership for success.

A meaningful wedding does not require $30,000 or any specific dollar amount. Set a cash budget based on what you can afford without debt, allocate spending toward what creates lasting memories (food, photography, people), and cut everything else. Every dollar you save on the wedding is a dollar that starts compounding toward your financial independence. The couples with the strongest financial futures are the ones who celebrate joyfully within their means and invest the difference.

To say that these drugs are too risky and overprescribed based on rare but serious side effects is to dismiss huge benefits for a population of patients whose comorbidities were uncontrolled and essentially had one foot in the grave.

#10072. 3AM Affiliate Embraces AI-Like Loops in European School Attack

Evidence suggests a model may have generated and revised commands during the ransom gang's breach, though researchers stopped short of claiming full automation.

A 3AM ransomware attack targeting a UK school estate may provide an early look at how cybercriminals could use AI as a force multiplier rather than a replacement for human operators.

Bitdefender today published research concerning a "hybrid AI ransomware attack" observed in the wild, attributing certain actions taken to human or agentic elements. On the surface, the attack is fairly straightforward. As a blog post explained, a 3AM ransomware affiliate attacked a school in the UK, "then used ordinary Windows tools to build domain trusts and reach other schools."

Attackers stole backup credentials, created rogue domain-admin accounts, established trusts between previously separate Active Directory domains, moved between schools, stole data, and deployed 3AM ransomware. In other words, the attack largely followed a familiar ransomware playbook, despite Bitdefender's claims that AI helped execute parts of the operation.

Related:'AdFection' Turns Ad Impressions Into Zero-Click Spyware Delivery

Where the attack got more interesting was how, as the security vendor argued, it didn't fit neatly into pre-existing buckets for attacks involving AI. It wasn't exactly an AI-generated attack where the malware was fully or largely created by a large language model (LLM); it wasn't exactly an AI-assisted attack where human engineers built the tools while using AI to speed up work; and it wasn't exactly an AI-operated attack where the LLM orchestrates actions and runs the show, as it were.

In this case, Bitdefender argued an AI system appeared to handle repetitive command generation and troubleshooting while a human operator made high-level decisions.

Many elements of the attack were ordinary for ransomware, such as significant use of living-off-the-land (LOTL) techniques, where attackers abuse tools already present on the victim's machine rather than relying on malware — in this case PowerShell, Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI), reg, netsh, rundll32, and other domain and scheduling utilities preinstalled on Windows. The attacker also used "an Impacket-style remote-execution tool," as well as Mimikatz and a previously published Veeam script.

But despite the attack's ordinary nature, Bitdefender assessed that several things suggest the use of an agentic loop, the control structure that makes an AI agent work. Certain actions appeared to be taken by a program rather than a human operator.

"The commands carry the usual tells of a model: a call to the backup software's web interface (Veeam, a widely used enterprise backup product) on a port and with a login method that do not match the vendor’s documentation, a mistake typical of writing from memory rather than from the manual (Veeam REST API authorization), along with confirmation files, self-labeled output and numbered revisions of the same script," the blog post read. "The retries behave like a loop too."

Related:Biomemory Launches DNA Shield, First Commercial Product Built on Its Molecular IT Platform

In another example, researchers assessed that the time taken between PowerShell command attempts was shorter than a human would take if issuing them by hand, but longer than if an LLM was orchestrating by itself. The longer time taken between individual tasks but the shorter time between retries "is what it looks like if a person is choosing the next step and a model is handling the retries."

Bitdefender caveated its findings by noting that it was unable to access the machine the attacker worked from, so it couldn't document anything tangible involving the AI model itself. The research acts as an argument that this attack behaves like a human operating alongside an agent, which is a working model defenders may wish to plan around.

With that in mind, Martin Zugec, technical solutions director at Bitdefender, tells Dark Reading that "a hybrid model is more reasonable for financially motivated cybercriminals, technically and economically, than a fully autonomous attack."

Related:Foul Language: WordlistLoader Disguises Malware as Ordinary Text

But even as a one-off, the situation is notable because the primary victim was an organization in a critical sector, and Bitdefender's anecdote suggests the affiliate may have used an AI agent to scale the attack by handling repetitive troubleshooting and command generation, although the report stops short of showing AI-enabled capabilities the attacker otherwise lacked.

Moreover, other similar institutions could fall in the crosshairs. "From a domain controller it enumerated trust relationships between domains and searched SYSVOL (the shared folder where Active Directory stores logon scripts, readable by any domain user) for the names and subnets of other schools," according to the research blog post.

The good news is that because much of this attack followed the typical ransomware playbook, the defender recommendations that stop regular ransomware would also stop the attack described in this research.

Zugec adds that agentic loops are noisy from an indicator standpoint, as many of their actions are repetitive and brute force in nature. "An agentic loop doesn’t make an attack quiet; it makes it repetitive: the same command re-run, small tweaks, numbered scripts and probe files left on disk. Even the quickest retries took 40 seconds or more. 'Machine speed' is mostly a marketing phrase about very expensive incidents; in real attacks, especially with local models, we expect this slower and noisier pattern. Speed isn't the giveaway; repetition is."

The vendor recommends focusing on prevention: Keep admin credentials of different domains separate, treat backups as a possible target, restrict remote execution and administrative shares to known management hosts, block interpreters and shells on machines that never use them, and put endpoint security tooling on every machine.

"Prefer controls that work regardless of volume and speed," the blog post read, "because they stop an action the first time and the hundredth."

#10063. LLMjacking Emerges as Thriving Cybercriminal Enterprise

Cybercriminals have turned reselling cloud access to LLMs into a lucrative business model, with some victims paying as much as $1 million in resource consumption before access was revoked.

Cybercriminals have created a thriving business model out of stealing cloud access to commercial large language models (LLMs) and reselling it to paying customers, with the resource cost for victims reaching high as $1 million before access to their LLM was revoked.

The practice, called LLMjacking, has been around almost as long as LLMs themselves. However, now it's become an illicit enterprise on the underground market, providing a lucrative source of revenue for cybercriminals while victims are left to absorb the high cost of model usage, according to a report published Monday by Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant.

LLMjacking can create a massive spike in computing resources in a matter of hours, differentiating it from its more well-known cousin, cryptojacking, which gradually consumes resources. This has made it an attractive revenue stream for "a diverse set of financially motivated threat clusters operating out of multiple regions globally," Google researchers shared in the report.

Related:External Teams Chats Anchor 15-Minute Malware Delivery

"Across individual incidents, we observed fraudulent charges associated with resource consumption exceeding $100,000 USD in a single day, with cumulative charges at some organizations reaching $1 million USD before access was revoked," they wrote.

The report details how attackers gain initial access to LLMs and achieve persistence on targeted networks, and describes the service model around LLMjacking that has become a lucrative endeavor for cybercriminals.

To gain initial access to an organization's LLM, attackers typically identify publicly exposed LLM endpoints or obtain valid LLM application programming interface (API) keys, according to Google.

"The dominant initial access vector has been exposed or stolen cloud identity tokens — including identity and access management (IAM) credentials, service account keys, GitHub personal access tokens (PATs), and active session tokens — which threat actors leverage to establish an initial foothold into target organizations' infrastructure," the researchers wrote.

Some attackers also deliberately keep their initial activity quiet to gain access to an organization's LLM, according to Google. The researchers observed the use of minimal API requests, sometimes containing just one output token, to validate stolen credentials without generating significant consumption.

This sneaky way to gain and then sell access to the LLM could mean organizations are giving up valuable resources without even knowing, while the attacker is cashing in, notes Nick Tausek, lead security automation architect at agentic AI firm Swimlane.

Related:TiDB Breach Exposes Flawed Cloud Security Assumptions

"By the time someone asks why the cloud bill has exploded, the attacker may already have paying customers," he says. "Selling stolen model access gives criminals a reason to keep that access working for as long as possible, which makes the quiet activity before the spending spike especially important."

This notably represents a detection challenge for organizations that need to identify early indicators of compromised identities, unauthorized permissions, and suspicious access to AI services rather than just look for unusual consumption, he says.

The report outlines several examples of how attackers compromised and LLMjacked organizations, demonstrating that there is not just one route to take for successfully and illicitly gaining access to an LLM.

In the middle of the year, for example, a threat cluster tracked as UNC6993 compromised a cloud instance through a misconfigured service account key and used it to grant further access to an LLM API. Attackers also hosted a session hijacking page mimicking an application portal to join a group of LLM users.

"This page tricks users into navigating to the legitimate LLM service website, and pasting their raw JSON payload containing an active access token, which was then posted to the backend API to bypass password and multifactor authentication (MFA) controls," the researchers explained.

Related:Marvell, Microsoft & Oracle Work to Standardize Data Center Hardware Security

In another instance, a threat actor gained initial entry by combining a stolen personal access token (PAT) to access private code repositories and a suspected Web application vulnerability in a package running within a containerized cloud environment.

Similarly, a different threat actor used compromised cloud federation tokens to programmatically generate new access keys that allowed the attacker to bypass MFA protections, according to Google.

Once access to an LLM has been gained, it then needs to be sold for attackers to make money. The key to this part of the LLMjacking business model is what is called an LLM Mixer, which is an underground service that turns stolen access to commercial AI models into a subscription business, according to Google. These services aggregate compromised credentials, route customer requests through victim environments, and offer access to premium models at prices significantly below legitimate market rates.

As the researchers describe it, LLM mixers act as illicit middlemen, allowing cybercriminals to resell access to compromised enterprise LLM accounts without their customers needing their own legitimate API credentials or cloud infrastructure.

"In one investigation, GTIG observed two distinct operational clusters coordinating to compromise and monetize enterprise LLM infrastructure, demonstrating the sophisticated specialization emerging in this space," the researchers wrote.

Indeed, LLM Mixers are an important part of the emerging LLMjacking ecosystem because they provide the monetization layer that makes stealing enterprise AI access financially attractive.

Since LLMjacking relies on victims being unaware for as long as possible, the key to not getting dinged with a huge resource-consumption bill is to catch on as quickly as possible to the intrusion.

To do this, defenders should prioritize IAM and supply chain security, two of the most common pathways for gaining access to and abusing cloud services, according to Google.

Other best practices for preventing LLMjacking in a cloud environment include good credential hygiene by using a centralized secrets-management platform; least privilege by ensuring users and service accounts only possess the permissions necessary for their specific role and required tasks; and code monitoring by automating secret scanning within codebases such as GitHub and GitLab.

Routine configuration audits, rate limiting, network allow listing, budget alerts, and MFA are also good defense strategies, according to Google.

Elizabeth Montalbano is freelance writer, editor, and journalist with 30 years of professional experience and a master's degree from Arizona State University. Her areas of expertise include enterprise technology, cybersecurity, business, and culture. During her long career, Elizabeth has lived and worked as a full-time journalist in Phoenix, San Francisco, and New York City. She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. She currently resides in a village on the southwest coast of Portugal, where in her free time she enjoys surfing, hiking with her dogs, growing plants, and playing and performing as a singer and musician.

#10061. 9 Cyber Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Maze of Threats

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

Practical guidance on safer search, stronger login security, better executive protection, and other habits can reduce enterprise risk.

9 Cybersecurity Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Threats

Cybersecurity Awareness Month tends to bring no shortage of advice, but the most useful guidance for business readers is the kind that maps to the way attacks actually happen now: through everyday habits, trusted workflows, and small moments of inattention. Risks show up when employees trust a search result, follow a fake CAPTCHA prompt, scan a login QR code, click a social ad, reuse a weak recovery method, or assume that an artificial intelligence (AI) model, executive device, or home network is secure by default. This article, compiled by the Dark Reading staff, and the accompanying videos bring those risks together in one place and focus on the practical behaviors and controls that can reduce them.

In October, a Dark Reading poll asked site visitors, "What's your biggest Cybersecurity Awareness Month challenge?" Readers identified phishing and social engineering as the top risk (39.1% of respondents), but that was neck-and-neck with shadow AI and risky data sharing (38.2%). A distant third was training fatigue and weak follow-through, identified as the top problem by 13.5% of respondents, and third-party and contractor access, with 9.2% of the vote.

Reader responses when asked, "What's your biggest Cybersecurity Awareness Month challenge?" Source: Dark Reading

The following nine tips can move the dial on that enterprise risk in very real ways. A common thread for all of these is the fact that attackers win by abusing convenience, familiarity, and human trust, whether the issue is SEO poisoning, ClickFix, session hijacking, dark patterns, or dodgy ads on Facebook. That's why awareness training still matters. It shouldn't be a once-a-year affair either, but rather an everyday focus on a set of specific, repeatable habits backed by stronger enterprise safeguards.

For security leaders, Cybersecurity Awareness Month gives them the chance to do more than remind users to "be careful." It is an opportunity to push for better defaults: phishing-resistant multifactor authentication (MFA), tighter privilege controls, better reporting paths, safer browsing habits, stronger executive protection, and more realistic guidance for work that happens outside the office. The goal is to make the safe action the default action and to help employees recognize the red flags before a routine click becomes a business problem.

Embrace cybersecurity awareness in October and beyond with Dark Reading's curated hub for security leaders — featuring expert news, analysis, and insights for hardening enterprise defenses in areas like identity security, AI risk, social engineering, supply chain, and more.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Becky Bracken, Media & Projects Director at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

As enterprises look to embrace agentic AI, they're sorting through frontier models, open-weight alternatives, and overseas offerings. Much of the focus is on evaluating the safeguards that, say, Claude might have vs. an open-weight alternative, like Meta's Llama series. But for business leaders, the key question is not which model is inherently safe; it's whether your organization has put adequate controls around it. That means treating AI just like any other high-impact enterprise system that can be misconfigured, manipulated, abused, or compromised.

Every model type comes with trade-offs. Frontier models may offer stronger vendor tooling, safety features, and governance support, but they can also introduce concentration and third-party risk. Open-weight models can give enterprises more transparency and control, but that control comes with more responsibility for hardening, patching, monitoring, and misuse prevention. Either way, the burden is on the enterprise.

For Cybersecurity Awareness Month, the practical takeaway is to assume compromise and build from there. Security teams should treat model weights, code, training data, prompts, plug-ins, APIs, and downstream applications as one attack surface. Limit what models can access. Restrict permissions. Segment AI workloads from critical systems. Log activity aggressively. Test for prompt injection, data leakage, and identity abuse. And keep humans in the loop for consequential actions, especially when money, customer data, or operational decisions are involved.

This is a golden opportunity for cybersecurity teams to become business enablers in the best sense of the term. AI will move fast, vendors will keep promising better safeguards, and the market will keep generating noise. But the durable security advantage will come from steady internal discipline. AI models can help the business, but they cannot be trusted to protect the business.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Alex Culafi, Senior News Writer at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

ClickFix is a simple but effective attack because it exploits something security teams deal with every day: people trying to solve a problem quickly. The user lands on a compromised or malicious Web site, a phishing page, or a fake browser-based meeting screen and sees what looks like a normal verification or troubleshooting prompt.

But instead of asking them to check a box, the page tells them to open a system tool — often with Windows + R — and paste in a command that the site has already copied to their clipboard. Once they do, they can trigger the compromise themselves. Security researchers note that this technique has risen sharply and often relies on fake CAPTCHA or error messages that make the request seem routine.

No legitimate CAPTCHA, website, or meeting platform should ever ask a user to open Run, PowerShell, Terminal, or Command Prompt and paste in a script. A request like that should be treated as an immediate red flag. The attack works precisely because it looks like a harmless fix and can sidestep some browser-based protections by pushing the user to execute the command themselves.

Organizations should build this into awareness training now. Tell employees to stop immediately if a website asks them to copy and paste commands, press unusual key combinations, or "fix" an issue through a local system tool. Reinforce a simple rule: If a prompt moves from the browser into the operating system, assume it's suspicious until IT says otherwise. Also, make it easy to report these incidents fast because early notification can help security teams contain the damage and identify affected users quickly. Restricting access to system tools where appropriate can add another layer of defense.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Rob Wright, Senior News Director at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

For Cybersecurity Awareness Month, here's a useful reminder for business leaders and employees alike: Treat social media ads as untrusted content. According to Gen Digital research, nearly one in three (31%) ads on Instagram and Facebook lead to scams, phishing pages, or malware.

And according to Reuters, Meta is charging higher premiums for advertisers that are considered risky. So not only have these platforms turned into a virtual minefield of scams, but Meta has a financial incentive to keep these ads online.

That matters because malicious ads often don't look malicious. They may mimic legitimate brands, use convincing creative, and point to spoofed URLs that appear credible at first glance. Even security-aware users can get caught. The real danger is that these ads exploit trust, urgency, and familiarity — exactly the tactics that work on busy professionals who are clicking quickly on personal devices outside the protections of corporate security tools.

The best defensive habit is simple: Do not click directly from social ads to make purchases, log in, or share payment information. If an offer looks legitimate, navigate to the brand's site manually, use a bookmarked link, or search for the company independently. Before entering credentials or card details, verify the domain carefully. Organizations should reinforce this behavior in security awareness training, especially for executives and remote workers who often blend personal and professional device use.

Caution remains the first line of defense. Encourage employees to use payment cards with fraud alerts, enable MFA on shopping and social accounts, and maintain healthy skepticism toward "limited-time" deals delivered through ad feeds.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Arielle Waldman, Features Writer at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

Ransomware has moved beyond encrypting systems and stealing data. Increasingly, attackers are pressuring organizations by targeting the people around their leaders: spouses, children, relatives, and close friends.

The "Semperis 2026 Ransomware Risk Report" found that 37% of attacks involved threats against employees' friends or family members. In other words, if attackers can't break your defenses fast enough, they may try to break your people instead. AI is accelerating this shift by making reconnaissance faster and cheaper, and threat actors can mine social media, public records, leaked data, and digital breadcrumbs to map relationships, impersonate trusted contacts, and build highly convincing social engineering campaigns.

For Cybersecurity Awareness Month, organizations should expand executive protection beyond the corporate perimeter. Start with digital footprint reduction: Encourage executives and family members to limit public exposure, remove unnecessary personal details from social profiles, and use aliases or less identifiable display names where practical. Establish family verification procedures, including safe words or challenge-response phrases, but rotate them regularly because any phrase used in a compromised channel should be treated as burned.

Most importantly, extend basic cyber hygiene to the household. Require strong unique passwords, enforce MFA on personal and shared accounts, secure home networks and connected devices, and train family members to recognize urgency-based scams, impersonation attempts, and suspicious content. A child's gaming console, a spouse's reused password, or a relative's overshared profile can become the opening attackers need.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Fahmida Rashid, Editor-in-Chief at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

Security awareness works better when it feels practical and relevant, not like a mandatory lecture. But one lesson is worth stating plainly: Some employees need more protection simply because they hold more power, more access, and more sensitive information. That starts with the C-suite, but it also applies to executive assistants, finance leaders, admins, and anyone else with privileged access.

Executives are high-value targets because they combine authority, visibility, and convenience-driven work habits. They approve payments, access sensitive strategy, and often log in from airports, hotels, and personal devices. That makes them especially attractive for phishing, impersonation, business email compromise, deepfake scams, and data theft. The right response is not to make life easier for them. It's to add smart friction in the places that matter most.

A strong executive protection program should include:

Phishing-resistant MFA, ideally hardware-based rather than SMS codes

Just-in-time privileged access instead of standing elevated permissions

Dedicated, locked-down devices for sensitive work

Stronger email and DLP controls to catch unusual forwarding, sharing, or exfiltration patterns

Focused coaching for executives and their inner circle, including assistants and chiefs of staff

Guidance for family and home networks because executive risk doesn't stop at the office

Organizations can focus on "white-glove" security, which means tighter controls, better support, and faster escalation when something looks off. If a control feels mildly annoying, that may be a sign it is doing its job.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Arielle Waldman, Features Writer at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

These design tricks train people to click quickly, surrender data reflexively, and ignore warning signs. Over time, that weakens judgment. Employees who get used to manipulative prompts may be less likely to notice when a request is truly malicious — whether that's a fake consent banner, a spoofed login page, a bogus app permission screen, or a prompt asking for sensitive information. Dark patterns blur the line between annoying and dangerous.

Another good rule: If you didn't sign up for a tool, don't create an account just because an email nudges you to. Unapproved sign-ups can create shadow accounts that IT and security teams can't monitor or secure.

Finally, build a reporting culture around anything that feels off — surprise charges, mystery accounts, unusual permissions, or suspicious prompts. The more comfortable employees are raising small concerns, the easier it is to catch bigger issues before they spread.

Everyone knows password hygiene remains a challenge for most businesses, but risk in the login journey increasingly extends to the other seams around identity — the moments where users, devices, sessions, and recovery workflows intersect.

The threats include quishing, where a user scans a QR code from an email, Web page, or physical sign and lands on a convincing but malicious login screen. There's also push fatigue, where attackers bombard a user with approval requests until one gets accepted. And it includes session hijacking and token theft, where the attacker skips the password entirely and hops into an already authenticated session. Add SIM swapping to intercept SMS-based recovery, and the modern login chain starts to look brittle in several different places.

The long-term fix is to move toward phishing-resistant authentication, including FIDO2 security keys and passkeys, backed by enterprise controls that verify context, not just credentials. That requires checking device posture, monitoring session behavior, requiring managed devices for sensitive systems, and reauthenticating when risk changes. In short: Don't just trust the login — trust the device, the session, and the user behavior behind it.

However, if this kind of full passkey rollout is not on the docket yet, here are some practical steps organizations can take now to reduce login risk:

Turn on number matching for push-based MFA

Reduce or eliminate SMS-based authentication where possible

Shorten session lifetimes for high-risk apps

Require managed-device access for sensitive systems

Trigger reauthentication when device posture changes

Meanwhile, employee training should focus on a few clear habits: Don't scan login QR codes from unsolicited messages or unverified sources, for one, and never approve an unexpected SMS verification push.

To prevent session hijacking, log out of accounts when you finish using them, rather than just closing the browser tab. And avoid public Wi-Fi when you're doing something sensitive.

Finally, on the SIM-swapping front, switch from SMS MFA to Authenticator Apps that can't be intercepted via a phone network. You can also request that account changes require physical ID in-store or multilayered, out-of-band authentication before processing SIM changes.

Account takeover attacks are a bugbear that is unlikely to disappear anytime soon, but increasing friction and cost for attackers throughout the login process can truly help and, hopefully at the very least, get you out of the low-hanging-fruit category.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Rob Wright, Senior News Director at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

Fall youth sports season means many parent-professionals are working from the sidelines — at soccer fields, hockey rinks, football stadiums, and school gyms — often on whatever free Wi-Fi happens to be available. That may not sound as risky as logging on at a major airport or hotel, but it still creates an opportunity for mistakes that attackers, pranksters, or opportunistic snoops can exploit.

So, although sophisticated nation-state actors are probably not camping out at your local rink, there's still considerable risk if you connect to the wrong network. A hotspot with a name that closely resembles the venue's legitimate Wi-Fi can be enough to trick a busy parent checking email between periods or joining a meeting from the bleachers. Even a spoofed network set up as a joke can expose traffic, credentials, or session data if employees are careless.

Business readers that want to avoid their employer's penalty box should treat public connectivity anywhere as untrusted by default. Before joining a network, verify the exact Wi-Fi name with venue staff or posted signage. Disable auto-join so your device does not connect to similarly named networks without your knowledge. Use only approved secure remote access tools, keep endpoint protections enabled, and avoid handling sensitive work, such as admin access, financial approvals, or password resets, over public Wi-Fi unless it is absolutely necessary.

If you need connectivity, a personal hotspot is often the safer option — but only if it is configured properly. Use a strong password, change the default network name if it reveals your identity, and make sure the hotspot is not left open to nearby devices.

The broader lesson for Cybersecurity Awareness Month: Low-profile locations can still produce real security failures. The setting may feel routine, but the network risk is not.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Alex Culafi, Senior News Writer at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

SEO poisoning turns a routine Google search into an attack path. Threat actors either build lookalike websites or compromise legitimate ones, then manipulate content and code so those pages rank highly in search results. The idea is that a user searching for software, a login page, or a partner site might simply click the top result, which happens to be poisoned, and subsequently hand over credentials or download malware.

Guidance on spotting fake websites specifically warns that SEO poisoning can push malicious sites to the top of search results, and Trend Micro's 2026 research on more than 35,000 fake World Cup-related sites shows how easily attackers can industrialize fake-site campaigns around high-interest topics.

For business users, the safest habit is to stop trusting search rankings as a signal of legitimacy. Before clicking, inspect the URL for misspellings, extra words, odd country codes, or brand names that look slightly off. After clicking, be suspicious if the page immediately pushes a download, asks for credentials too early, triggers repeated redirects, throws pop-ups, or trips a browser warning. Those are strong signs that something is wrong.

Organizations should reinforce a few simple rules in awareness training:

Use bookmarks or manually typed URLs for key business apps, vendors, and partner portals.

Verify domains before downloading software or entering credentials.

Treat urgent install prompts and so-called ClickFix instructions as red flags.

Report suspicious search results, spoofed pages, and accidental downloads to IT immediately.

Isolate the device and change credentials quickly if a user may have interacted with a fake site.

The practical message for Cybersecurity Awareness Month: Search is a convenience layer, not a trust layer. Employees don't need to become threat hunters, but they do need to slow down long enough to verify where a search result is actually taking them. That pause can prevent a compromise.

#10059. France blames Iran for supermarket hack meltdowns

The 'first cyber offensive campaign carried out purely for the purpose of sabotage on national territory'

France has turned up the heat on Iran over destructive cyberattacks targeting refrigeration controllers at more than 700 grocery stores in October, spoiling food and sparking fires. The country vowed to take action using “all available means of response.”

The supermarket attacks, which affected Casino, Leclerc, Coopérative U, Metro, Carrefour, and Intermarché groups, started at least 15 fires and caused food losses in the tens of millions of euros, according to a Monday report by France’s Cyber Crisis Coordination Centre (C4).

The C4 includes the National Cybersecurity Agency of France, the Directorate General for External Security, the Directorate General for Internal Security, the Directorate General for Armament, and the Cyber Defence Command.

“This is an unprecedented campaign in terms of its scale and level of aggressiveness, thus constituting the first cyber offensive campaign carried out purely for the purpose of sabotage on national territory,” France’s Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs said in a statement.

Both the report and the statement attributed the refrigeration controller hacks to the Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ (IRGC) Shahid Kaveh cyber unit. The Shahid Kaveh unit, which French national security officials say is led by Reza Salarvand and Mahdi Lashgarian, is better known by its hacktivist personas, including CyberAv3ngers.

This is the same crew suspected of involvement in the July attacks that targeted more than 100 internet-exposed water systems in America. While the US government hasn’t attributed the intrusions to any country or group, private-sector security analysts blamed Iran, and specifically CyberAv3ngers.

The IRGC-affiliated hacking crew has been breaking into industrial controllers for years, and in 2023, American national security and law enforcement agencies attributed a series of cyberattacks against "multiple" US water facilities to CyberAv3ngers.

“The Iranian cyber threat against French interests is not new,” according to the Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs. “Iran has already carried out several destabilizing acts against us, notably targeting the weekly magazine Charlie Hebdo in 2023 and the organization of the Paris Olympic Games in 2024.”

Since at least June 2024, the Shahid Kaveh unit has had the ability to scan, access, and control industrial control equipment from Schneider Electric, Siemens, and Rockwell, the French government said in its report. It pins the refrigeration controller hacks on this particular Iranian crew for a couple of reasons.

First: the infrastructure used to carry out the October supermarket attacks was also used during this timeframe to conduct reconnaissance on Schneider Electric equipment, zeroing in on small- and medium-sized energy and water production units. “The techniques used during these actions are known to have been used by the Shahid Kaveh unit since at least April 2026,” the report says.

It also notes that investigators found “traces of Farsi use” in the attack infrastructure. Plus, Iranian media outlet CyberbanNews, which is reportedly linked to the Shahid Kaveh unit, publicized the incidents that occurred late on October 11 and into October 12 extremely quickly: “as early as October 13.”

In early November, similar cyberattacks on commercial refrigerators and freezers were reported across Europe, with grocery stores in Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden reporting widespread food losses after miscreants spiked temperatures to as high as 122°F (50°C).

Last week, the US federal government urged owners and operators to take security measures to prevent these types of attacks from spreading to America.

The French government, for its part, said that it would “use all available means of response, including within the European Union and alongside its European and international partners, to anticipate, prevent, deter and respond to destabilizing and destructive actions targeting it in cyberspace.”

This includes proposing additional EU sanctions against Iranian entities and individuals involved. France also vowed to express “its strongest condemnation of these cyberattacks” to the Iranian ambassador.

However, the country didn’t rule out responding with more than just harsh words: “France reserves the right to take any additional measures, public and non-public, deemed necessary and proportionate to respond to these cyberattacks.” ®
