#10056. Anthropic's super bug-finding Mythos model is going into Cisco and IBM products

Enterprise security tools will offer its capabilities without handing customers the model itself

Anthropic has started extending access to its bug-finding Mythos model by allowing Cisco and IBM to make it part of their security products.

Cisco announced its integration today at an event in Melbourne, Australia, where it revealed that the red teaming tools in its AI Defense suite, which looks for weaknesses and inappropriate activity in AI models, agents, and applications they power, will be able to call Mythos to test customers’ setups.

“At a very high level, AI Defense has the ability to look at models and break them,” said Jeff Schultz, Cisco’s senior vice president for portfolio strategy and marketing. He said the tool is now “super-charged by Mythos” and will identify more danger that AI Defense will then address.

AI Defense already uses AI-powered red teaming to find flaws. Mythos will become another option. Cisco will make it available under users’ existing licenses, without additional cost.

Natalie Mead, Anthropic’s head of applied AI for the Asia-Pacific, said the company has a long queue of buyers who want to use Mythos, and working with Cisco will make it easier to satisfy that demand.

Anthropic initially made Mythos available under "Project Glasswing," a program that gave vetted organizations access to the model to test their codebases, but has since expanded access through other controlled programs, an arrangement that makes considerable sense because in the wrong hands Mythos could help attackers exploit software flaws.

The Cisco deal exposes the functionality of Mythos to end-users, without letting them use the model itself.

The Register asked Mead if Anthropic has similar deals with other third parties and she demurred. That may be because a few hours after Cisco told us about its use of Mythos, IBM announced that it will also integrate Anthropic’s model into a product – namely its Concert tool, which uses AI to scan applications for risks and weaknesses.

IBM says it will use Mythos “to uncover weaknesses traditional scanners miss, determine which pose real risk and generate fixes for developer approval.”

We have asked Anthropic if these integrations represent a decision to open Mythos to more users in more ways. We will update this story if we receive a substantial response.

Also on Monday, Anthropic introduced version 5.2 of Mythos and Fable, which the company says generate outputs up to 30 percent faster than version 5.1 yet cost less: $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens.

Users can choose to run both models in “fast mode,” which speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times, and doubles prices to $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens.

Anthropic says it “ran extensive prerelease safety testing on the model that underlies Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. This included developing novel evaluations that give deeper insight into specific concerning behaviors like sandbox escapes.”

After those tests, the company concluded “high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low, and the model performed as well as, or better than, our recent models on most alignment measures.

“Fable 5.2’s cyber and biology safeguards are as robust as those of Fable 5.1 but produce fewer unnecessary blocks, and we have implemented our strongest-ever protections against distillation attacks.”

The latter is a telling admission, given Anthropic believes Chinese AI labs use distillation to effectively clone its models without doing expensive training work. ®

#10053. Cisco to link all future products to its SaaS-y Cloud Control management tool

Global rollout of unified portal finally happening in 2027

Cisco will no longer create products that don’t integrate with Cloud Control, its SaaS-y management platform that offers netadmins a single tool to manage all of the networking giant’s devices and much of its software portfolio.

It appears Cisco is now satisfied it has sorted out those issues. Jeff Schultz, Cisco’s senior vice president for portfolio strategy and marketing, today told the company’s Live conference in Australia that Cloud Control will come online in the European Union, UK, and Down Under in February 2027. Japan, India, and Canada will get their turn in May.

Schultz said Cisco is “working tirelessly” to deploy Cloud Control across the world as soon as possible.

He also revealed that, starting next year, Cisco will no longer ship products that don’t integrate with Cloud Control.

That doesn’t mean those products will be manageable only if they can connect to Cloud Control. Instead, the decision reflects Cisco’s belief that the main thing stopping its customers buying more of its products is the complexity of operating them in concert. Schultz also feels that Cloud Control represents “platform advantage” for Cisco, because when users integrate networking, security, and observability the result is better manageability and resilience.

Schultz also told the conference that Cisco will bundle its Thousand Eyes observability and security tool with the “Essentials” and “Advantage” licenses. “We admit it was hard to license and deploy,” he said during his keynote speech, adding that the tool will be deployed automatically with Wi‑Fi 6E and Wi‑Fi 7 hardware.

Another product Cisco plans to bring to more customers is Live Protect, a tool that implements compensating controls for flaws that organizations can’t immediately patch. The product has become particularly useful since Anthropic's Mythos model, and similar AI offerings, made it possible to quickly find more software bugs and flaws and overwhelmed tech teams whose patching apparatus was not set up to handle hundreds of montly CVEs.

Live Protect currently works on some of Cisco's datacenter switches, plus SD-WAN and WLAN controllers. From December, Cisco will extend it to 8000 series routers, secure firewalls, campus gateway, and to Cloud Control itself. From May 2027, Live Protect will work with Cisco’s ASR 9000 series service aggregation routers and Network Convergence System.

"Expect this to be a major investment area," Schultz added. ®

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds

What Americans actually have saved — the gap between average and median tells the real story.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Before comparing your balance to anyone else's, you need to know what the benchmarks actually include. Most retirement savings data from Vanguard, Fidelity, and the Federal Reserve covers:

What these numbers typically exclude: taxable brokerage accounts, real estate equity, HSA balances invested for retirement, pension values, and Social Security. For FI-minded savers, this distinction matters enormously — your total investable net worth is almost certainly larger than your "retirement savings" as defined by these surveys.

The gap between average and median retirement savings is one of the most important distinctions in personal finance. The average gets pulled upward by high-balance accounts — a single person with $5 million in their 401(k) dramatically inflates the average for their age group. The median (the middle number when all balances are ranked) gives you a far more honest picture of what a typical American actually has saved.

Notice how the gap widens with age. By 65+, the average is 3.3 times the median — meaning a small number of disciplined savers (or high earners) are pulling the average far above what most people actually have. The median tells you what a typical person in each age group actually holds. If you are above the median, you are doing better than half of Americans your age. But "better than average" and "on track for a secure retirement" are very different standards.

Vanguard's annual "How America Saves" report and Fidelity's quarterly retirement analysis provide the most comprehensive snapshots of what Americans hold in their workplace retirement accounts. These numbers reflect defined-contribution plan balances only — primarily 401(k) and 403(b) accounts.

Average balance: $13,265. Median balance: $5,400. Most savers in this bracket have been contributing for fewer than five years. The biggest advantage this group has is time — a 25-year-old contributing $6,000 per year with a 7% average return will accumulate over $1.2 million by age 65 without ever increasing their contribution. The FI community emphasizes that getting started early matters far more than starting with large contributions.

Average balance: $53,300. Median balance: $21,000. This is where employer matches start compounding meaningfully. Fidelity data shows that employees who have been contributing consistently since their 20s have balances 2.5 to 3 times higher than those who started in their 30s. The typical employer match adds 3-6% of salary — effectively free money that many employees still leave on the table. According to Vanguard, roughly 25% of eligible employees do not contribute enough to capture their full employer match.

Average balance: $142,069. Median balance: $60,763. Earnings typically peak in this decade, making it the critical window for aggressive savings. FIRE-path savers in this age bracket commonly have $500,000 to $1 million or more saved by maximizing their 401(k) ($24,500 in 2026), HSA ($4,400 individual / $8,750 family), and Roth IRA ($7,000) — then directing additional savings into taxable brokerage accounts.

Fidelity's guideline of 1x salary by 30 and 10x salary by 67 is a reasonable starting point for traditional retirement planning. But for FI seekers, these benchmarks are the floor, not the ceiling. The ChooseFI community consistently demonstrates that saving 40-60% of income — rather than the national average of 4.6% — compresses the timeline from 40 working years down to 10-17.

If your balance is below the median for your age group, you are not alone — and you are not stuck. The math of compound growth means that aggressive action in your 40s and 50s can still produce a secure retirement or even an early one.

The IRS provides additional contribution room for savers age 50 and older. In 2026, the 401(k) catch-up contribution is $7,500 on top of the standard $24,500 limit, for a total of $31,000. IRA catch-up contributions add $1,000 to the standard $7,000 limit. HSA catch-up for those 55+ adds another $1,000. Combined with employer matching, a 50-year-old couple can potentially shelter $80,000 or more per year in tax-advantaged accounts.

Most financial advice focuses on investment returns, but the variable you control most directly is your savings rate. Moving from a 10% savings rate to a 30% savings rate has a dramatically larger impact on your retirement timeline than chasing an extra 2% of investment return. A household earning $120,000 that increases from 10% to 30% savings — a shift of $24,000 per year — adds roughly $600,000 to their retirement balance over 15 years (assuming 7% average returns).

The FI community's core insight is that savings rate is the primary driver of financial independence. At a 50% savings rate, you can reach FI in roughly 17 years regardless of income level. At 60%, it compresses to about 12 years. At 70%, you are looking at under 10 years. These numbers are independent of salary — they depend only on the ratio of savings to spending.

The average American contributes 4.6% of salary to their 401(k), receives a 3-4% employer match, and saves little outside of that. FIRE-path savers typically max every available tax-advantaged account, maintain savings rates of 40-60%, invest in low-cost index funds, and direct overflow savings into taxable brokerage accounts. The result: FIRE savers in their 40s commonly have $500,000 to $1.5 million in total investable assets — 5 to 10 times the national median for their age group. The difference is not income; many FIRE success stories come from median-income households that simply saved aggressively and avoided lifestyle inflation.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

If you are 40 with $50,000 saved and feeling behind, shifting from a 10% savings rate to a 40% savings rate on a $100,000 income adds $30,000 per year to your investment accounts. At 7% average returns, that alone grows to over $950,000 in 15 years — before counting the $50,000 you already have. Starting late is not ideal, but a high savings rate compresses the timeline dramatically.

Add up every 401(k), IRA, Roth IRA, HSA, and other retirement account balance. Include employer-sponsored plans from previous jobs — many people have orphaned 401(k) accounts they have forgotten about. Exclude your home equity and Social Security for now.

Use the age-bracket tables above to see where you stand. If you are above the median, you are ahead of most Americans your age. If you are below, calculate exactly how far behind and what it would take to catch up.

Most employers allow you to change your 401(k) contribution rate at any time. Increasing by 2% of salary is small enough that you will barely notice the paycheck reduction, but it compounds dramatically over time. Repeat this increase every six months until you are maxing out your 401(k).

Roughly one in four employees leaves free employer match money on the table. If your employer matches 50% of contributions up to 6% of salary, you need to contribute at least 6% to capture the full match. This is an instant 50% return on your money — no investment can beat it.

A Roth IRA provides tax-free growth and tax-free withdrawals in retirement, with no required minimum distributions. The 2026 limit is $7,000 ($8,000 if 50+). If your income exceeds the Roth limits, use the backdoor Roth conversion strategy to contribute indirectly.

Fidelity recommends having 1x your annual salary saved by age 30. For someone earning $55,000, that means $55,000 in retirement accounts. The FI community targets higher — $50,000 to $100,000 by 30 is common among aggressive savers. The national median for under-35 is only $13,000, so if you have more than that, you are already ahead of most peers.

The average is pulled upward by a small percentage of very high-balance accounts. If nine people have $10,000 saved and one person has $1,000,000, the average is $109,000 but the median is $10,000. The median gives a far more accurate picture of what a typical American has saved. Always compare yourself to the median, not the average.

Yes — employer matching contributions are part of your retirement savings balance. In a typical arrangement, an employer matches 50% of your contributions up to 6% of salary. On a $75,000 salary, that adds $2,250 per year in free money. Over a 30-year career at 7% returns, that match alone grows to roughly $213,000.

Generally no. While your home is part of your net worth, it is not liquid retirement savings you can draw from to cover living expenses. You would need to sell or reverse-mortgage your home to access that equity. Retirement planning should focus on investable assets — accounts you can convert to income without selling your primary residence.

A common guideline is 10-12x your pre-retirement income. For a household earning $100,000, that means $1,000,000 to $1,200,000 in retirement savings. The 4% rule suggests you can withdraw 4% of your portfolio annually with a high probability of not running out over 30 years — so $1 million supports roughly $40,000 per year in withdrawals.

It is never too late, but the urgency increases with age. A 40-year-old saving $20,000 per year at 7% returns will accumulate roughly $1 million by age 65. A 50-year-old has access to catch-up contributions ($7,500 extra in a 401(k)) and can still build $400,000 to $600,000 in 15 years with aggressive saving. The key is maximizing savings rate immediately rather than trying to make up ground through risky investments.

The average retirement savings benchmarks are useful directional guides, but they should not define your target. Most Americans are dramatically undersaved — the median 401(k) balance at retirement age is under $72,000, which supports only about $2,860 per year in withdrawals using the 4% rule. That is not a retirement plan; it is a supplement to Social Security at best. The FI community takes a fundamentally different approach: define your actual annual spending, multiply by 25, and work backward to a savings rate that gets you there. Whether your number is $750,000 or $3 million, the path is the same — maximize tax-advantaged accounts, invest in low-cost index funds, maintain a high savings rate, and let compound growth do the heavy lifting. If you are behind the benchmarks, the single most impactful action is increasing your savings rate, not chasing higher returns.

#10048. Microsoft teaches schools that free email was just a phase

Office 365 A1 and Student Use Benefit face retirement, leaving institutions to budget for paid replacements at renewal

Microsoft is retiring its free education email service, leaving schools, colleges, and universities facing new licensing bills if they want to keep students' mailboxes.

The company announced plans last week to retire Office 365 A1, the Student Use Benefit program, and free Exchange Online for Alumni. The changes generally take effect at institutions' first renewal or extension on or after January 1, 2028.

Office 365 A1 provides eligible institutions with web-based Office applications, Teams, and email at no charge. Its replacement, Microsoft 365 Education A0, excludes Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Teams. Eligibility also depends on paid faculty licensing and students actively using Windows devices for education.

A spokesperson for the UK's Department for Education told The Register: "We are disappointed that Microsoft has made this decision. However, we are pleased to have successfully negotiated some additional concessions for the UK, giving schools, colleges and universities the time they need to be able to successfully transition to new licensing agreements."

An industry insider said the loss of free Microsoft-hosted email could add thousands to institutions' bills. Another organization noted "significant concerns… around affordability, equitable treatment across the sector, and the longer-term implications of the changes."

A spokesperson for UK education technology body Jisc told The Register that its "focus has been on ensuring that UK education providers are well supported and have sufficient time to assess their options."

"We continue working closely with Microsoft and sector partners to support those discussions and help institutions make informed decisions about their future requirements."

Also being retired are free Exchange Online for Alumni – which lets graduates retain their mailboxes – and the Student Use Benefit, providing student licenses at no additional charge when institutions purchase qualifying faculty licenses. Microsoft plans a paid alumni replacement.

The Windows giant is also changing storage entitlements and introducing Microsoft 365 Education A7, its "most advanced education offering," which adds AI, security, governance, and device-management features.

Asked why it was removing those services from the free tier, Microsoft framed the overhaul as a response to institutions' changing needs.

"Microsoft is updating the portfolio now to provide a clearer path from foundational access to advanced capabilities, while enabling institutions to adopt technology according to their needs and readiness. This evolution reflects both the value Microsoft 365 Education has gained since the last pricing change nearly a decade ago and the structure of the new portfolio.

Office 365 A1 stopped accepting new web-direct orders on November 5, 2026, with partner-channel sales ending on May 1, 2027. Retirement is scheduled for January 1, 2028, but existing agreements remain valid through their current terms. Institutions that need continued service must move to replacement licenses at the applicable renewal or contract expiry. ®

#10044. Royal Navy stands up first autonomous boat squadron

Force deploys an operational squadron to gain experience in uncrewed systems as part of its Hybrid Navy vision

Britain’s Royal Navy has formally commissioned its first uncrewed boat squadron, operating seaborne drones on front-line operations as part of its “Hybrid Navy” strategy.

The force says the 1st Autonomous Squadron officially entered active service on November 5 at a ceremony in Portsmouth Naval Base. It comprises around 180 personnel, about the same as a Type 23 frigate, split into two watches to enable operations around the clock.

This active squadron replaces Project Beehive, the navy’s experimental program to build a fleet of autonomous and remotely operated vessels, through which it obtained 20 uncrewed boats from UK-based Kraken Technology Group.

The force is understood to be using both Kraken’s K3 Scout, and the SM400 from SYOS Aerospace, known by the Royal Navy as the Rattler.

The K3 Scout is an 8.4 m boat capable of 55 knots and can carry a payload of up to 600 kg. It has a range of up to 650 nautical miles and  endurance of up to 7 days. The maker describes it as capable of a range of missions, including anti-ship and anti-submarine to detecting and countering other drones and even casualty evacuation.

The Rattler boat is 7.2 m and has a 500 kg modular bay, with a range of up to 950 nautical miles. It was used last year in a demonstration during which 5 of the uncrewed boats were remotely-piloted to escort patrol ship HMS Tyne and mine countermeasures mothership HMS Stirling Castle

Part of the new squadron’s mission will be to act as pathfinder for drone operations, working on bringing additional types of uncrewed surface vessel (USVs) into fleet service and conducting a range of operations alongside other organizations – both as single vessels and as part of a task group.

The “Hybrid Navy” concept was outlined by First Sea Lord General Sir Gwyn Jenkins earlier this year, who made the case that uncrewed vessels would be vital in filling the gaps left by the Royal Navy’s much depleted surface fleet.

Speaking at the launch of the autonomous squadron, Fleet Commander Vice-Admiral Steve Moorhouse hailed it as an historic occasion, but warned that the seas are becoming more contested, more dangerous and harder to operate in.

“A hybrid navy is about giving our people better tools. It means more reach, more striking power and more options,” he stated.

Last week, the force also launched strike drones from one of its aircraft carriers for the first time. Nyan one-way drones made by BAE Systems were launched from the deck, as well as a Tekever AR5 fixed-wing uncrewed aircraft, the same kind the British Army has selected to replace its troublesome Watchkeeper fleet.

Elsewhere, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) says it has launched a British-built satellite called Titania into orbit, claiming it “gives the Armed Forces a new pair of eyes in space.” However, the original purpose of the orbiter was understood to be to test high-speed optical communications from low Earth orbit directly to Earth, using laser beams that are harder to intercept than radio links.

Titania is the second satellite in the UK’s growing constellation of military satellites in orbit, following the launch of Tyche in October, and will be operated by UK Space Command as part of the ISTARI* program.

The latter aims to deliver satellites and supporting ground systems to expand space-based intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, the MoD said.

However, while the satellite is British-made, it got into space via an American rocket, riding on SpaceX’s Transporter-18 mission. ®

* What is it with the tech industry and Tolkien references?

#10042. Germany Busts 'Crime-as-a-Service' Investment Fraud Outfit

Authorities seized more than 100 servers and arrested seven as part of a crackdown on a fraud network spanning more than 50 countries.

You see an online advertisement promising quick returns from trading cryptocurrency, foreign currencies, and stocks. You give the "investment firm" your information, and an operator calls you and convinces you to transfer a small amount of money into a platform. You make early profits quickly, so you deposit increasingly large sums of money. But when you attempt to withdraw your earnings, the operator stalls for a while until finally cutting off contact.

This pattern is familiar to victims of investment fraud, a multinational criminal industry that relies on social engineering to convince would-be investors that they're about to make substantial gains before pulling the rug out from under them.

Europol today shared news of the disruption of one such operation, an investment fraud scheme with potential victims across more than 50 countries and a company allegedly supplying fraudulent trading platforms and leads to criminal groups. According to a press release, Europol and Eurojust supported an international operation involving authorities in Albania, Cyprus, Finland, Germany, Israel, Kosovo, and North Macedonia.

Related:Black Hat India 2026 Makes a Landmark Debut in Bengaluru, Bringing the Global Cybersecurity Community to India

The German Itzehoe Public Prosecutor's Office led the operation, targeting a company suspected of supplying phony trading websites and multiple call centers to criminal groups; investigators estimate losses to exceed 4 million euros.

International authorities searched 17 locations, including a call center in Kosovo, leading to the seizure of 100 servers and the arrests of seven suspects.

The law enforcement action reflects a multiyear investigation that began in 2022, according to Europol, when a German couple reported they could not withdraw money invested through an online trading platform. This led to two previous "action days" by authorities, one in 2022 (involving two arrests and the seizure of evidence) and another in 2025 (involving more arrests and seizures of money and evidence).

"Analysis of the material recovered exposed the suspected infrastructure provider and its links to call centre operators, paving the way for the latest operation," the press release read.

A Eurojust press release provided further detail regarding the extent of the operation. The analysis of evidence seized during the second action day exposed a company based in Cyprus and Israel allegedly offering "crime-as-a-service," supplying criminal groups with fraudulent websites that funnel targets into the central investment scam.

The data of potential victims visiting these websites and expressing interest would be sold as leads to call centers, which contacted the victims to persuade them to invest their money, leading to repeated demands for additional investments. Authorities identified suspected call center-operating clients of this company in Albania, Kosovo, and North Macedonia.

Related:PwC's CISO on AI, Robots & What's Next for Security

The fraud operation guaranteed significant returns for trades in cryptocurrencies, foreign currencies, or stocks, according to Europol. But authorities found that the seemingly legitimate platforms were run by "brokers" that used phony profits and social engineering tactics to convince victims to keep investing. Additionally, investigators also found the operators used affiliate marketing services and deceptive advertisements to lure in potential victims.

Austin Anderson, director of threat intel at cybercrime disruption firm Netcraft, tells Dark Reading that operations like these that target upstream providers can help disrupt investment fraud operations at scale.

"Fraudsters have increasingly specialized in one piece of an attack's supply chain, as seen in this scheme where websites collected personal data that was sold to call centers to ultimately coerce funds from victims," he says. "While this can breed sophistication in each actor's niche, it also introduces fragility when a large dependency like the call center is disrupted. Ultimately, without arrests that remove fraudsters from the market, these operations only temporarily disrupt operations while actors rebuild their infrastructure."

Related:NIST: Solo Shouldn't Mean Less Secure

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. After cutting his teeth writing for independent gaming publications as a teenager, he graduated from Emerson College in 2016 with a Bachelor of Science in journalism. He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

He has received numerous awards, including TechTarget's Writer of the Year in 2022 as well as more than 10 Azbee awards for his reporting between 2022 and today.

#10040. EU's €212M border IT project lands IBM and Atos in legal water

After years of missed deadlines, ballooning costs, and a blame game over who was responsible, Brussels has finally called in the lawyers

The European Union has dragged IBM, Atos, and Leonardo into court over years of delays to its troubled €212 million smart border system, which finally went live after missing a string of deadlines and leaving travelers stuck in airport queues.

The lawsuit dates back to December 22, 2025, when eu-LISA, the agency behind the EU's fingerprint-and-facial-image border checks for non-EU travelers, filed its claim in an Estonian court.

The lawsuit was buried in eu-LISA's 2025 financial accounts, published in July, with no mention of who was being sued. The Financial Times has since named the three companies after obtaining letters exchanged with the agency.

In a statement to The Register, eu-LISA confirmed it had initiated proceedings "in line with the Agency’s responsibility to protect the EU’s financial interests."

"The proceedings concern the system’s development phase and have no impact on its current operation. EES (entry exit system)  is fully operational," the agency said, declining to discuss the ongoing case.

The EES was supposed to be ready in 2022 yet wasn't live until October 2025 and was only fully operational from April. Travelers have since had to contend with hours-long airport queues and fingerprint scanners that reportedly struggle with sweaty fingers. Behind the scenes, things weren't going much better, with the consortium and eu-LISA spending years arguing over missed deadlines, financial penalties and who was to blame.

IBM Belgium and Atos Belgium were already arguing over penalties back in October 2021, when they disputed a fine from eu-LISA and pointed to the COVID-19 pandemic and other factors beyond their control as reasons for the delays.

By February 2022, the consortium was pushing back against another set of deadlines, warning that the agency's timetable was unrealistic.

"Ignoring reality is not prudent and will not help to achieve the plan," the companies wrote, according to the FT. "On the contrary, working with an unrealistic plan will cause frustration for all stakeholders."

The consortium also criticized eu-LISA's "overall governance," suggesting relations between the two sides had become rather frosty.

The fallout wasn't cheap. The contract had already grown from €142 million to €212 million in 2021, and the delays kept adding to the bill.

In its 2022 accounts [PDF], eu-LISA acknowledged difficulties with the consortium and warned of additional costs, with the setbacks also holding up other EU IT projects. By 2023, it had nearly doubled its annual EES budget to €40 million by diverting funds from elsewhere, partly to cover rising hardware and software maintenance costs.

The FT also reported that IBM agreed in March 2022 to let eu-LISA withhold certain payments while the dispute over damages was resolved.

The original contract expired last year, with a new consortium taking over implementation, although IBM, Atos, and Leonardo remained responsible until August.

The project has attracted scrutiny for more than its ballooning budget. Last year, Atos reportedly used its Moscow office to procure software for the system, raising questions about Russian involvement in sensitive European border infrastructure.

The EU's anti-fraud office, OLAF, found sufficient grounds for further investigation, according to an internal report seen by the FT. However, it referred the matter back to eu-LISA despite describing the agency's initial assessment as insufficient.

Estonia's Harju County Court confirmed that the civil case had been filed, although no hearings have taken place or been scheduled.

IBM and Atos did not respond to The Register's questions.

The EES may finally be up and running, but the argument over who should foot the bill for getting it there looks far from settled. ®

#10037. Microsoft is giving Claude the keys to UK Copilot tenants by default

Admins have until December 9 to review access settings as Anthropic processes data in the US

Microsoft will enable access to Anthropic's Claude models by default for UK Copilot tenants next month, giving administrators a deadline to decide whether US-based processing fits their compliance requirements.

From December 9, UK tenants whose administrators have not already chosen a setting will have Claude access enabled. Administrators can disable it, but leaving the setting untouched means opting in.

In this instance, Anthropic operates as a Microsoft subprocessor, and Claude models are already on by default for most customers in the Windows giant's commercial cloud. The exceptions, notably, include the European Union, the European Free Trade Association, and the UK.

However, UK tenants aren't in scope for Microsoft's EU Data Boundary - launched at the start of 2023 - and so Redmond is flipping the switch for the country.

Anthropic processes the relevant data in the United States, Microsoft's documentation states. Administrators therefore have until December 9 to review whether that meets their organization's data-handling requirements and set access accordingly.

Microsoft is also retiring the setting that restricts Claude access to Microsoft 365 alone.

"This affirms Microsoft's commitment to offering choice between leading AI models while maintaining enterprise-grade security and compliance," the Redmond-based biz said.

So long as you don't mind processing happening in the US. ®

#10036. Slightly better interpolating spline

Today I'm introducing a new interpolating spline. Its name is S9. Without further demagoguery, here it is -

You can click on knots and drag to see how this thing works.

For comparison with other splines, here is a demo. And here you can find the implementation source.

For decades people were used to manually clicking and dragging cubic BÃ©zier points until they developed Stockholm syndrome for it. Sometimes experienced designers will even tell you about having some magic rules like "keeping control arm lengths to about a third of chord length" which is good advice, but only if no better option is available. The fact is, humans cannot manually come up with good looking sequences of curves. The problem is inability to see subtle variations in the curvature of polynomial curves.

So what is this curvature anyway? The best way to explain is using a related concept called osculating circle. It is an approximation of how the curve is bending at any point on it. Take a look at this demo -

If you play with this for long enough, you will see a pattern. If a circle size along the curve changes very little, the curve looks better. If it changes a lot, the curve looks worse. This smoothness of how the circle changes along the curve is called curvature variation. Less variation is better.

We can visualise this in a different way. If we record the reciprocal of osculating circle radius on every step of the curve, we get curvature profile of a curve.

Now you can see another pattern. If this plot is smooth, the curve also looks smooth.

However, it can be very difficult to see how smooth or not smooth this blue function is. Especially in absence of large spikes and multiple turns. Instead, let me show you another related plot. Here, in red, is a plot of a function representing curvature variation of the curve. And the rule is simple - thinner this plot gets, less curvature variation the curve has. We want the red part to be as close to the horizontal grey line as possible. For example, a section of a circle will have an integral (red number next to function plot) of this function equal to zero.

As you can see, it can be quite hard to get this red function to relax. But it can still be worse though. This is just one segment. How about we connect two curves?

See now you have to juggle more than two balls - you need to make individual curves smooth, but also keep the connection between the curves continuous too. In other words, the blue function must not have any gaps and the red function must stay as flat as possible.

This gets worse with every additional curve because polynomial curves have this property where changing one side of it will change curvature on the other side as well.

At this point you should see that trying to get harmony out of 20 or 30 connected curves has the same entertainment value as colonoscopy. This is what splines solve. Automatic smoothness of individual segments and continuity between curves.

The goal for S9 is to look good and to adapt to changes smoothly so it is useful in interactive CAD applications. This requires the following -

The primary goal is roundness. I want a spline which feels natural for forming fundamentally round and smooth objects.

At the moment there are very few splines that are optimized for the same goal as S9. In my opinion, the best published G2-continuous interpolating spline is this one. In fact, it is very good, only using one cubic curve to connect a pair of knots. I doubt you can do much better than this with a single cubic. Second best is Îº-Curves, which is implemented in Adobe Illustrator as a "Curvature" tool. Using quadratic curves, but has a few fundamental problems where the solver can fail without special case handling. Then there is Hobby spline. A very old one. It does not guarantee G2 continuity, but the solver is much simpler. Apple Keynote and some other applications use it.

There are some other, more famous splines like Catmull-Rom. I'm sure they have use cases even today, but they have no use in any even remotely serious CAD application. In fact, I would argue that any locally solved spline would have a flaw somewhere that cannot be fixed.

I decided to call this spline S9 because it is my 9th attempt to come up with a decent spline. I still have the first 8.

Fundamentally this spline works in a similar way to Hobby spline. It has two separate elements to it -

The solver part is not a problem. The issue is how to come up with a curve parametrized by two angles. And it is harder than it looks.

The final and the most important part is the curve this spline is made of. After years of attempts, the best I was able to do is to describe the curve as a function of arc length.

For greek letter connoisseurs, here is an implementation of the curve in Desmos graphing calculator. That thing is powerful.

Curve math is explained in detail in comments for S9 curve. Weight computation rules are sprinkled around in the solver.

The curve solver is given two tangent angles and two weight parameters which are somewhat abstract, but the idea is as follows -

For two weights of 1, the curve is identical to the Euler spiral. This formula also has extra knobs to control curvature change near ends when weights decrease.

Weights are calculated from start and end angles. Which, like velocity function for Hobby spline, reduces a number of free parameters to two.

Input is two tangent angles you can adjust with sliders.

This curve, when used with automatic weight computation, will form high curvature spikes at the ends for large angles. This is a requirement for this type of spline. But for low to medium angles, it does have very little curvature variation which was the goal.

The source repository includes implementation of both curve solver and spline solver. However, it is not meant to be a full implementation of path construction solution for CAD. For example, it does not include G2-continuous transitions from straight to curved segments, sharp corners or angle locking. These features would be independent additions.

Here is a minimal list of resources for anyone interested in curves and splines -

Minimum Curvature Variation Curves, Networks, and Surfaces for Fair Free-Form Shape Design. Henry Packard Moreton. 1992. From Spiral to Spline: Optimal Techniques in Interactive Curve Design. Raphael Linus Levien. 2009. Typographers, programmers and mathematicians, or the case of an Ã¦sthetically pleasing interpolation. BogusÅaw Jackowski. 2013. Îº-Curves: Interpolation at Local Maximum Curvature. Zhipei Yan, Stephen Schiller, Gregg Wilensky, Nathan Carr, Scott Schaefer. 2017.

#10033. Google DeepMind melds humans and AI agents to vet Signal's secure messaging techniques

Post-quantum handshake and Triple Ratchet get a formal security check

Google DeepMind researchers have completed a formal verification of Signal's messaging security, marking what they claim is the first time AI has helped devise a proof that links protocol-level security guarantees to a widely used cryptographic implementation.

They did so using AlphaProof Code, a multi-agent framework for formal software specification and verification. AlphaProof Code relies on a human-guided agent that writes a Lean specification, assesses machine code semantics, and crafts an agent-authored proof that the Lean kernel checks against the specification.

In this instance, AlphaProof Code verified Signal’s post-quantum PQXDH handshake and Triple Ratchet, thereby validating the design of libsignal's forward secrecy, authentication, post-compromise security, and handshake secrecy.

In so doing, the Google/DeepMind team – Swarat Chaudhuri, Andrew Ferraiuolo, Anton Kovsharov, Tej Chajed, Sam Schlesinger, Karn Seth, Jonathan Katz, Charles Sutton, and Pushmeet Kohli – has taken a step toward a challenge the Beneficial AI Foundation issued in April to formally verify the Signal protocol and Signal app with Lean.

The AlphaProof Code process involves working with various models to turn Signal's security goals into a human-reviewed mathematical specification. Based on this spec, the researchers assigned Gemini Carbon agents to generate Lean code proving the correctness of the libsignal implementation. After the agents generated 6.5 million lines of Lean code, they undertook an auditing pass and flagged bits that required human review.

The result is theoretical in that it assumes perfect cryptography and doesn't guarantee the computational secrecy of bytes. But it's still a meaningful assertion of correctness.

"It's a system that is fundamentally built for human AI collaboration," said Swarat Chaudhuri, research scientist at Google DeepMind and a professor at the University of Texas at Austin, in an interview with The Register.

Traditionally, said Chaudhuri, you start proving theorems with well-defined problems formulated by a mathematician that get submitted to an AI agent for proof. In this case, the researchers had to figure out what to prove.

"In formal methods, we always had this belief that verification is the hard bit," he said. "There's thirty or forty years of work on how to scale up verification. Now we are able to do that. So now the question is what are we verifying? … That process is fundamentally human-in-the-loop, but we devised a process of trying to scale it up to the extent possible with AI."

As Chaudhuri and his colleagues note in their research paper, "AlphaProof Code: Verifying Signal’s Security at the Machine-Code Level," formal verification used to require heroic efforts. Formally verifying the seL4 microkernel took 20 person-years, while developing the verified CompCert C compiler took six years.

AlphaProof Code, they believe, can drastically reduce the cost of formal verification, though their Signal work still took four weeks for a team of five people and "quite a few tokens."

"The dream is definitely to scale this up," said Chaudhuri. "So you know there's been this rise in offensive AI capabilities, right? There are a lot of insecure systems around the world, and they're going to be exploited.

"So what we really need to do is to apply this kind of technology to code at large all over the world and figure out what is it that you want to guard against? How do you write those properties, how do we specify those properties? That's going to be super important, but we have to figure that out."

Pointing to a related DeepMind project, AlphaProof Nexus, which is focused on mathematics, Chaudhuri said the next step is to apply this technology during the software design process – not just to cryptographic protocols but code in general.

"We really believe that the next frontier is not going to be proof but specification in this kind of research," he said. "And so that's why we took on this domain where that was actually a hard problem. And I think that we have some really good insights now about how to go about this, although not the last word by any means." ®

#10031. A faster Easter date function

This post is a fun little side quest to kickstart my journey optimising regional calendars.

Computing the date of Easter faster is not going to matter in any real application. Even in places where it might seem to matter, like high frequency trading applications, it is probably better to just use an in-memory lookup table for holiday dates...However, no "Fast Date" series would be complete without some mention of this classic problem.

The rules for Easter were broadly decided at the First Council of Nicaea, organised by Emperor Constantine in 325 AD, and later modified by Pope Gregory XIII in 1582 (referred to here as "Gregorian Easter"), with the first Easter under the new rules applying in Catholic countries the following year. The Church of England first observed the new date of Easter in 1753, but Eastern / Orthodox churches continue to follow the old rules.This article is about the new "Gregorian" Easter, because it is much more complex and slow to compute.

The code below runs really fast.It's around twice as fast as a standard easter function that you might find in a typical date library, and I suspect it may be the fastest one made so far ð¤·.Part of that speed is attributable to using only 5 multiplications (whereas typical reference algorithms have 10 or more multiplications).

The accuracy range of around -11m â +16m years might seem a bit of overkill, but the reason I targeted this range is so that any date library that expresses dates via a signed or unsigned 32âbit "rata die", is covered by this function. This means that if you decide to not clamp the logic to years after 1582, at least it will return something resembling the correct rules, rather than garbage.

Note that this function contains more terms than traditional Easter functions, but bear in mind that the compiled assembly will be a lot smaller. So if you don't care about the speed, but want a tiny impact on binary size, that could be a reason to consider this function.

The rest of this post will briefly explain the tricks used in this function:

You'll notice that the very first thing we do is add a strange value SHIFT to the input value. This is done for two reasons:

For example, most Easter algorithms have a term like (5 + 8 * c) / 25, where c is the century (year / 100 + 1). The term 25 in the calculation of shift is responsible for aligning the century such that the constant 5 can be removed, resulting in c * 8 / 25, which is then approximated in the final algorithm with a single mul-shift: (u64) c * M25 >> 32.

Other terms in SHIFT: 19, 400, 30 are all doing similar things related to the 19-year-cycle, 400-year-cycle, and mod-30 steps.The term * 2 is different. Without this term, the range of coverage would be -5,403,600 â +22,363,835; which doesn't quite cover the range we wanted, which for signed 32-bit rata die, is Â±5.88m years. Including * 2 increases the value of shift by exactly 5,700,000, which is how many years it takes for the Easter pattern to repeat, and gets the range we are after.

If you like this type of optimisation, but are not a fan of the low-level bit-shifting and so on, then you might prefer to use this function here below. It is a much more readable version of the function, which only has these higher-level optimisations applied.

Note that unlike in the main function presented earlier, MOD 30 needs to be a positive-modulus function (even for positive dates), and that the nextSunday helper is anchored to the internal logic of the function, not related to Unix day-counting.

Note: a variant in the C++ repo has some small optimisations not shown here (fast day-of-week and fast mod 30), and a range of [-73,803,600 .. 70,208,581].

Computing year % 19 is a staple of Easter algorithms.It's related to the Metonic cycle, where every 19 years there are nearly exactly 235 full moons.

It is traditionally used in Easter algorithms in two ways:

We are going to compute these same things using a single multiplication.These steps seem unavoidable at first, but they can be eliminated. We'll begin by expanding the first one:

(11 * (year % 19) + ... ) MOD 30(11 * (year - year / 19 * 19) + ... ) MOD 30(11 * year - year / 19 * 209 + ... ) MOD 30(11 * year + year / 19 + ... ) MOD 30

The last step there might be the least obvious. It works because we can add any multiple of 30 to the multiplier and get the same result (a property of MOD), so add 30 Ã 7 = 210, which means we can remove the multiplication by 209 and just invert the sign.

This leaves us with only two terms related to year which can be computed efficiently in parallel, however using a 64âbit multiplier, we can actually merge these into one (fixed-point multiplication by 11 1/19):

u64 constexpr M19 = (1 << 32) / 19 + 1 + (11 << 32)((year * M19 >> 32) + ... ) MOD 30

This is the only 64âbit multiplication in the function, and a 32-bit compiler should have no trouble turning that back into the previous pair of multiplications.

The algebra above relies on MOD 30, which is different to % 30 in C for negative numbers.The value being computed does not go negative over our range, so the substitutions remain valid.

Now on to the other term: (year % 19) > 10. It is a well known trick to use the low bits from the mul-shift of division by 19 as a comparison cutoff, and the version used in my function is u32(b) > 0x90000000. The extra term in our multiplier (11 << 32) has no effect in the lower 32âbits, so this still works. Cassio Neri has written about things like this, if you want to read more you can start with this Overload Edition 154 .

So, this is just one multiplication plus the MOD 30, which is usually an additional two multiplications, but we'll eliminate those later in Trick #4.

There's always a % 7 term in these Easter functions, which is then subtracted from a final result. This is because Easter is on the âfirst Sunday after [...]â.

Clearly we are going to use the fast-mod-7 trick from the weekday article. If you haven't read that article, you should. You won't understand this section otherwise, and frankly, it's a better article than this one.

The same mod-7 trick as before, but notice that the mapping is reversed? (The numbers track anti-clockwise)

So why not just subtract the result of % 7 like everybody else? Well, that would make the final line be: j - m + C (for some constant C). This does not fit the pattern of a single-operation LEA instruction on x86.

Instead, we adapt the fast-mod-7 code to use a fixed-point multiplier of 6 / 7 (rather than 1 / 7) before the right-shift-29, which means this line actually counts mod-7 backwards for us! This means the final line can be j + m + C, which fits LEA and saves... one cycle ð (depending on the compiler and CPU...).

This one is pretty obvious if you've been following this blog series.MOD 30 can be calculated faster by using our favourite identity:

This was introduced and proven in the weekday article, and utilised more notably in the time-of-day article.Here setting D = 30, c = 2 gives us the useful version where we can apply MOD 32 (same as & 31).

This final bit, I'm not sure if it's been done before exactly like this.

Easter can only ever be in March or April (month 3 or 4), and luckily March is 31 days long, which means we can use % 32 to truncate dates there. A straightforward modulus would cause March 32 to overflow to April 0, a non-existent date, so we add the term v >> 7 which increments the date when it overflows (a lucky coincidence relying on April, month 4, being a power-of-2).

I have seen similar things done before using % 31, but I have not seen this with the clean bit-mask approach.

So, that's it. A bunch of fussing about to make a simple streamlined function that is next to impossible to read... but fast.

This article was prompted by Twitter/X user Dirk Loss replying to one of my posts with a link to a ChatGPT thread, where he used AI to compute Easter faster. See ChatGPT thread.

The AI actually did a pretty good job. It used learnings from my prior blog posts to apply various optimisations, but also came up with new twists on these ideas. It produced a function that is really fast, and that is accurate over the range 1498â14,544. The range is a fairly reasonable choice given that the modern rules for Easter took effect after 1582, and nobody really needs Easter further into the future.

In a serious case of "Not Invented Here" syndrome (on behalf of human kind), I had to see if I could beat the AI. I clearly did, otherwise there wouldn't be this blog post. The wider-range algorithm presented in this article has around 5-15% higher throughput across tested platforms, and similar latency (despite the wider range).

My algorithm was adapted from the one presented in Calendrical Calculations (Reingold and Dershowitz).I did not apply any learnings from the ChatGPT one, though we settled on several similar steps.

I suspect this function could be optimised more, as it still has the same overarching structure of existing algorithms going back a very long time.I tried for a little while to find a shortcut solution using the Python "Z3 Theorem Prover", which found an alternative which is a further 15-20% faster than my main one, however it's only accurate over a micro range [1894 .. 2199]. It is available in the testcase repo . If you can find a function of similar or faster speed with a wider range, feel free to let me know and I will update the repo and this page!

Although I beat the AI in this case, itâs a pretty mild victory as it was just a basic model with a moderate amount of compute. Itâs sad to know that if frontier models were pointed at the problems Iâve been tackling in this blog series, they would probably unearth every last jewel of optimisation left in the blink of an eye. I hope that I have time to explore this space more before it becomes barren.

If you enjoyed this post, you should follow me on X to get notified when I publish more date and algorithm related articles.

Exhaustive tests of the ranges asserted in this article can be verified via the testcase code: https://github.com/benjoffe/fast-world-calendars .

The same repository is used for benchmarking, where a large set of random years are loaded into memory and tested.

All results were obtained by running the benchmark with -repeat=10 and recording the median results.The -batch flag runs each computation 3 times before loading the next entry from memory. This ensures that the processor is not bottlenecked by memory access.Latency results use the same command but replace the batch flag with -latency. This mode feeds the result of each computation into the next, so there is no parallelisation.

The number in a small font size represents the number of nanoseconds per year computation.The larger number is the ratio of these results compared to the New function as a baseline.

Note: the benchmarks compute "Days since 22 March" (not day and month), as some of the reference algorithms only return this value.If my optimisation of the day/month step is novel, then the speedup would be larger than presented here.

#10029. Smart meters to cost the UK billions: 2G switch-off means replacing 12-13 million

Sunset of legacy cellphone tech means forced upgrade for many millions of smart energy meter users

Between 12 and 13 million UK smart meters could stop working properly when  2G and 3G networks are switched off by 2033, and replacing them all is likely to cost around £4 billion ($5.3 billion).

Smart meters have long been a controversial topic thanks to the British government's botched rollout of the technology; they were supposed to be fitted into 80 percent of households by 2020.

But numerous delays and technical hitches, such as consumers finding their meter stopped being smart if they switched energy supplier, hindered progress.

Now, a report from connectivity biz Wirepas, "The European Connectivity Trilemma," shows that it isn't just Brits who have problems, but that other European countries also have their share of smart meter issues and that no two countries have adopted the same approach.

The UK's issues center on the fact that early meters used 2G or 3G cellular connections to transmit energy usage back to the supplier. These continued to be fitted until 4G versions began arriving at the end of 2024, the report says.

This issue was covered by The Register back in 2023, and again in 2024.

However, the government had already announced measures to phase out 2G and 3G networks by 2033 several years earlier, back in 2021, so it was known that any meters being fitted would have a limited lifespan.

In fact, 3G services have now already been withdrawn by the networks, and they all plan to phase out 2G ahead of the 2033 deadline. BT/EE will begin closing its network from May 2029, VMO2 will start the same summer, and Vodafone aims to switch off in spring 2030.

The report claims the UK now faces two substantial areas of expenditure as a result. The first covers newer, second generation (SMETS2) meters, where only the communications module needs swapping out, but even this is likely to cost £1.3 to £1.4 billion (c $1.7 to $1.9 billion) before the hardware cost of each new hub is even factored in.

The other is for an estimated 7 million older, first-generation (SMETS1) meter installations, which have the cellular comms hard-wired in, so the whole meter typically needs replacing. The report authors estimate this will cost another £2.1 billion to £2.45 billion ($2.8 billion to $3.3 billion), at an indicative replacement cost of £300 to £350 per installation.

This results in the estimated £4 billion in gross replacement costs, which will ultimately feed into household energy bills, adding to the very costs the government is currently trying to reduce.

We asked the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ), which oversees smart meters, for comment.

While some of these older meters would naturally have been due for replacement as part of normal asset renewal cycles, the cell network shutdown makes the replacement program unavoidable and dictates when much of the expenditure must occur.

According to the report, the SMETS2 replacement largely applies to central and southern Britain, as second-gen meters in the north use a long-range radio network and are not subject to the 2G/3G cut-off. However, the issue of older SMETS1 meters applies nationwide.

Wirepas' interest in all of this is that it specializes in IoT connectivity and is pushing NR+ as a solution to the issue. Based on the DECT-2020 New Radio standard developed by the European Telecommunication Standards Institute (ETSI), this is designed to be scalable and operates in the license-exempt and globally available 1.9GHz part of the spectrum.

When 4G technology reaches the end of its life, (which isn't likely to happen until the 2040s, and there is no planned date) the UK's smart meters will need to be replaced once again, the report asserts. However, this is sufficiently far in the future that it is unlikely to trouble policymakers anytime soon. ®

#10026. What are you doing this week?

What are you doing this week? Feel free to share!

Keep in mind it’s OK to do nothing at all, too.

I'm organizing a programmer meetup, Chilean style, in Santiago. We are going to have a nice barbecue outdoors (it's summer here!) and I'm expecting about 30 attendees. Looking forward to it :)

Celebrating another revolution of the sun completed. New toys include a new waterproof coat, (new old stock), Wayfarer mk2 sailing dinghy (secondhand but ready to go) and iPad mini (new, so thin! Nano-texture!)

Off to see a live show of the Smith n Sniff podcast, and hopefully getting the Z4 back from having an exhaust blow cut out and new pipes welded in, in time for a trackday at Donnington Park on Friday. Not done a trackday before (taking the Focus estate round the Nurburgring excepted) and quite looking forward to it, but also somewhat nervous.

in time for a trackday at Donnington Park on Friday.

That’s the track where Senna went from 5th to 1st in half a lap finding grip in a completely different lane right? Amazing :-)

I am still contemplating if I am going to take part in the 6H race in Serres circuit in two-three weeks. The problem is that we will race with an Elise and safety-wise is not ideal, especially in rainy conditions. But we have experience, as a team, so we’ll see. Have fun!

That’s the track where Senna went from 5th to 1st in half a lap finding grip in a completely different lane right? Amazing :-)

That’s the one. It’s on the flight path for the East Midlands airport too, so I think can be quite slippy in the wet due to things like fuel vapour that falls out occasionally and lands on the track.

I wrote up a list of all the projects I started this year and turns out I started almost exactly one every month. Didn't finish any of them. For the rest of the year, I am going to focus on polishing and shipping all the ones I still find interesting.

Starting with emmer (a Wayland notification daemon, inspired by Sonner).

I'm on paternity leave so mostly looking after my newborn son. But in the "off hours" (which are at weird hours), I'm working through Nystrom's "Crafting Interpreters" and am in the process of implementing the first interpreter (jlox) in Zig (https://codeberg.org/hgrsd/lokz)

I moved one of my internal tools for my company to emacs/elisp. I live in emacs so it makes sense to replace some webapps only used by me with buffers and completing-read

How is WoW? I haven't played in a very long time (and I'm hesitant to try again, I need to protect myself lol).

So far I'm having a blast. I played from Classic to WotLK and then I dabbled in the other expansions. Forever feels like Classic but with a lot of QoL improvements. It's slow, large and a great excuse to be unproductive (after the last months have given me productivity anxiety).

Going back to tanking dead mines with randoms has been a great experience.

I've been writing and editing documentation for the GoActivityPub library. If anyone has 10m to kill and read through it, I'd appreciate some feedback (and owe you one <3).

Found an index optimization few days ago that largely eliminates pointer chasing, so I've been updating the buffer pool with io_uring to make use of that. Getting io_uring to actually deliver the performance that Patterson, Gimlin et al. suggests is pretty hard in real world scenarios where IOPS go brr is not the only outcome you're looking for.

Next is actually adjusting the index to make use of the async fetching capabilities.

Wallowing in existential dread as AI is becoming more and more scary to me.

Also working on my receipt printer project and finally getting a UPS for my home setup

Looking for engineering jobs in Amsterdam area, and maybe spend some time to polish my application launcher.

Dinner with a friend on Wednesday. Going to Cambridge for the Retro Computer Festival 2026 at the Centre for Computing History on Saturday & Sunday.

As my work has continued to push LLMs on me (and my promotion has not materialized nor disappeared yet) I am going to write an MCP server for Citrix. My replacement will surely make use of LLMs and it would be nice if I could simply tell them to point their agents at an MCP server to get good diagnostics / other information.

Got some miniPCIe LTE modems that my workplace was throwing out, so I'm waiting on a SIM card (on a cheap 19 DKK/month PAYG plan) and USB adapter to arrive. First task is to figure out which of them still work, and after that I'm not sure. I don't have anything that urgently needs cellular connectivity.

I'm also going to be moving my home network back to my own router (a N100 or N150—I can't remember—mini PC with 2 NICs and 4 ethernet ports running OpenBSD). After my recent move, it was easier to just use the ISP router until I had some time to clear the space I need under the stairs. I still don't have ethernet everywhere, but my wifi mesh is good enough for most things.

I have another project turning my Marantz PM6005 amplifier into a smart speaker, using an ESP32, a tinkerboard, raspotify, and home assistant. At the moment it communicates over IR, but I plan to hook the ESP32 up to the remote control RCA jack at the rear so it doesn't need line of sight any more (right now the biggest blocker is a literal one, a spanish galgo that likes to stand right between the ESP32 and the IR receiver). I'm not sure whether I'll bother with much of a write up for this, the tinkerboard, raspotify and home assistant stuff is fairly standard, and the ESP32 firmware is mostly vibecoded, so not that interesting to read about. I know many here are skeptical and highly critical of LLMs, but I've been finding them more and more useful. As someone who has struggled with executive function all my life, they've actually allowed me to get projects done that I would have in the past indefinitely postponed.

listening to joy division and staring into the void

I finalized porting the compression lib zxc (libzxc.org) to native go with the help of Claude opus 5.5. We had to rewrite a big part of it in AMD64 and ARM64 assembly to reach the C lib speed.

ZXC is a compression format allowing ultra fast decompression (faster than zstd) which might be of interest for game development to provide compact ressources.

The Go package is available here: https://github.com/chmike/zxc-go.

Probably spend too much time reading Lobs and HN articles about “how the world is changing.”

When not distracted with that, I’m playing with some IoT prototypes in the ag space using the Nordic9151. This is my second go at zephyr in a few years, and I’m having a much better experience this time. It’s either the improved stability of the tooling AND/OR the presence of AI tools to make sense of what is otherwise a pretty complex beast (compared to classical bare metal programming). The Nordic chip is pretty impressive.

There’s a cloud side to the efforts I’ll be pursuing as well. I’ve always liked MQTT, but I’m leveraging version 5 in these efforts and rather happy with the results so far. Quite impressed with EMQX (broker) as well as mqttx library in Elixir.

Working on my toy graph-based DSP https://github.com/giann/zsynth Started as afternoon tinkering to better understand signal processing, now i kinda want to bring it to the point where i can design actual synths with it and use it as a VST plugin.

I want to do some minor site touch-ups to the Nixtamal site now that 3.0.0 was released over the weekend. I still like keeping in somewhat homemade looking since it doesn’t make it look like slop even if I would consider it sloppy for my own design work.

This week I'm polishing CabFuse, a small utility I built to bring tabs to Windows 10 File Explorer.

I originally started it to solve some everyday annoyances with File Explorer, and I've been using it myself ever since. It's been especially rewarding to see other people finding it useful too.

Pursuantly, I'll be generalising my implementation of fibers into one of effects after a lightbulb moment. Fibers share a storage location for the yield target, but if you make that a parameter, you get effects. So it's analogous to a labeled break. I think that's how effects are supposed to work? Seems to be similar to how OCaml does it anyway. Also simultaneously halfway through rewriting the parser (said Sisyphus).

#10024. Ransomware threat blares from Vanderbilt University computers during cyberattack

BYOD claims extensive data theft as campus Wi-Fi returns, most systems remain restricted, and classes carry on

Classes at Vanderbilt University are proceeding as scheduled today, although access to most university systems remains restricted following a cyberattack claimed by ransomware group BYOD.

Vanderbilt announced on Monday morning that it was dealing with "an active cybersecurity incident," and that the fallout may affect university devices, systems, and cloud-based services.

The Nashville-based university initially told students and staff to shut down university devices and disconnect from campus Wi-Fi. It warned them to watch for unexpected prompts, altered files or permissions, unfamiliar applications, and unsolicited authentication requests.

Campus computers reportedly began playing an audio threat attributed to BYOD. Student newspaper The Vanderbilt Hustler cited posts on campus social network Fizz showing the message.

"You have been compromised by BYOD," the recording said. "We suggest you reach out to us as soon as possible. Instructions have been placed on your desktop. Failure to communicate will result in this estate being brought to the ground completely. Make the right choice or rot with the wrong one."

By Monday evening, Vanderbilt had restored access to campus Wi-Fi, but warned that access to most systems remains restricted.

"We know this has disrupted important work and caused frustration across the university," it said. "Vanderbilt Information Technology is working with government agencies and other partners to manage this situation."

Students were told to attend classes as scheduled on Tuesday and contact instructors about flexibility on coursework deadlines. Staff were instructed to report to work normally.

Vanderbilt's Athletics department said that its ticketing system was unavailable, and that students were unable to claim tickets for the college's football game against Alabama on Saturday.

BYOD claimed responsibility for the attack on Vanderbilt on Monday, along with extensive data theft.

"If you could not tell already, your databases are locked [and] we have your entire estate and research data," it said via its leak site.

"Over 1 million SSNs, full names, email addresses, phone numbers, student and employee records, full takeover of your DC, whatever was on your network, we possess."

Vanderbilt has not confirmed BYOD's claims about the extent of its access or the data allegedly stolen.

BYOD may be a familiar name to some. The group previously claimed attacks on the University of New Mexico and Trump Mobile's customer database.

BYOD also claimed responsibility on Monday for an attack on Texas Health and Human Services. The agency has not publicly confirmed an incident and did not immediately respond to our questions. ®
